title: Charter Check-in
note: Scenario questions on the charter check-in, written for study: taking over a bareboat at the base — papers, the walk-round, engine, electrics, water and gas, instruments, safety gear, ground tackle — and handing it back. Not an IYT course and not any charter company's procedure; the contract and the base's briefing are the authority. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults.

questions.q: The base's confirmation e-mail reminds you to bring your papers to check-in. What goes in your hand luggage?
options: Your skipper's licence, VHF certificate, every passport and the crew list
The boat's registration and insurance, printed from the base's website
Your logbook and the sailing-school certificates of each crew member
Your own passport only — the base has the crew from the booking form
questions.why: The base checks the skipper's licence and VHF certificate and files a crew list with passport numbers for the port police.

questions.q: You fill in the crew list at the desk and the manager asks whether anyone else will sleep aboard this week. What do you say?

figure.title: Crew list
lines: A friend joins Wednesday in Lefkas
Two crew fly home on Thursday
Port police may check at any harbour

options: Yes, but you will write him on the list yourself when he arrives
Yes — name the Wednesday guest now and tell the base again when the crew changes
No — a guest for two nights is not crew and does not go on the list
No — the list is for the people who signed the charter contract
questions.why: Everyone who sleeps aboard is on the crew list; a change mid-week is reported to the base, which amends the list for the port police.

questions.q: Reading the deposit clause, your crew ask what it costs if the dinghy flips and the outboard goes to the bottom. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Contract — deposit
lines: Held on card or in cash at check-in
Limit of liability for insured damage
Dinghy and outboard: at full value

options: Half the price — the base shares losses that are nobody's fault
Nothing — the boat's insurance covers the tender and its motor
The full price of the outboard — the deposit does not cap a lost dinghy or outboard
At most the deposit — that is exactly what the deposit is for
questions.why: The deposit caps insured damage only; the contract lists what is charged in full — negligence, grounding, the dinghy and outboard.

questions.q: The desk offers you this waiver. Your crew say that with it nothing can be charged to you. What do you tell them?
options: They are right — the waiver replaces the deposit and ends your liability
It covers the hull only; everything else comes off the full deposit
It is the boat's insurance; without it the base cannot let you sail
It lowers the deposit, but the items listed as excluded are still charged in full
questions.why: A waiver cuts your exposure, not the exclusions: negligence, grounding, dinghy, outboard and sails stay on the charterer.

questions.q: The technician hands you this folder at the chart table. Where does it live during the week?
options: In the chart table, aboard, ready for a port police check in any harbour
At the base — the originals are too valuable to take to sea
In your bag, to show at the desk when you hand the boat back
At the marina office of your first harbour, with the crew list
questions.why: The boat's papers sail with the boat: port police check the registration, insurance, radio licence and charter permit.

questions.q: Your crew want to cross to Italy on Tuesday night and be back by Thursday. You read this clause. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — navigation limits
lines: No sailing between sunset and sunrise

options: Go by day only — the clause forbids night sailing, not the crossing
Ask the base for written consent before you leave; without it the crossing is off
Go — the limits bind the boat's insurer, not the skipper
Go, and call the base from Italy so that they know where the boat is
questions.why: Outside the contract area or at night the insurance and the deposit cap fall away; only the base's written consent moves a limit.

questions.q: Your crew point at the late-return clause and say you must leave now. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday 07:00, Kioni
lines: Forecast: NW 6–7 all day and Friday
Contract: no leaving port above F6

options: Leave under engine only — the wind limit is about sailing, not motoring
Leave at once with two reefs — the wind limit is advice, the penalty is money
Stay in port, call the base now and agree with them what happens about the return
Leave on Friday at dawn instead; one day of F7 is a smaller risk than two
questions.why: A wind limit in the contract is a limit; the base would rather move the return than have the boat out in F7.

questions.q: The manager runs through the chart briefing fast, pointing at the wall chart. What do you do with what he says?

figure.title: Chart briefing
lines: Reef off the cape: keep 0.5 M off
Bay with the cable: no anchoring

options: Note the no-go areas only; the rest is local colour
Photograph the wall chart and work out the details at sea
Listen — the pilot book covers it all and you can read it on passage
Write it on your chart as he goes and ask him to repeat anything you missed
questions.why: The chart briefing is local knowledge the pilot book lacks: hazards, no-go bays, harbours untenable in a given wind.

questions.q: The technician offers to do the technical briefing on the pontoon in five minutes, 'since you have sailed this type before'. What do you say?

figure.title: Technical briefing
lines: Gas: bottle in locker, valve under sink

options: Ask to go through each system aboard, hands on, with every switch and valve shown
Accept, but ask for the briefing on paper to read on passage
Accept, and read the owner's manual aboard tonight instead
Accept — the same model has the same systems at every base
questions.why: Every charter boat is wired and plumbed differently; switches, valves and quirks are shown aboard by the one who knows them.

questions.q: The manager ends the briefing with this slide. What do you do with it every morning of the week?
options: Look at the sky and the barometer; forecasts are for open-sea crossings
Check the named sources before deciding the day's passage, and call the base if in doubt
Wait for the base to call before leaving harbour each day
Check your phone's weather app — the sources listed are for the base's own use
questions.why: The briefing names the forecasts the base trusts for its area; the daily decision to sail starts with them.

questions.q: On Wednesday the forecast shows a gale for Friday, so you plan to be back at the base on Thursday evening. What does the contract say about that?

figure.title: Charter contract — return
lines: Return: Friday by 18:00, at the base
Early return: no refund of unused days
Late return: a fee per hour started

options: The unused day is refunded at the daily rate
You must stay out until the return time in the contract
Nothing is refunded for the unused day; the berth is yours from Thursday — tell the base you are coming
The deposit is reduced by one day's charter
questions.why: Coming back early is your call and costs nothing extra; unused days are not refunded; call the base so a berth is free.

questions.q: Your crew want to spend Friday night in a bay an hour from the base — the flights are not until Saturday noon. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Contract — times
lines: Boat in base marina: Friday by 18:00
Late return: a penalty per hour, plus costs

options: Fine — the base can check the boat out in the bay if you call them
Fine, if you leave the bay at 06:00 and refuel on the way in
Fine — check-out is at 09:00 and an hour's sail gets you there in time
No — the boat is in the base marina on Friday evening; Saturday morning is the check-out
questions.why: The contract wants the boat back the evening before: the base checks her out, refuels and cleans her before the next crew.

questions.q: The technician fills in the form as you walk round and hands it to you to sign. What do you do before you sign?
options: Read every line against what you saw, add what is missing, then photograph the form and the boat
Sign — the technician's copy is the one that counts and he has written it all down
Sign, and e-mail the base a list of everything else you can remember
Sign, and photograph the boat later in the evening when it is quieter
questions.why: The check-in form is what the deposit is settled against; anything not on it counts as new damage at check-out.

questions.q: Your partner also holds a licence and will skipper half the week. The contract looks like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Charter contract — crew
lines: Crew: 6 adults on the crew list

options: Nothing — once the skipper is checked, anyone aboard may take the helm
Have the base add them as co-skipper now, licence shown, before the contract is signed
Carry their licence aboard and show it only if the port police ask
Add their name to the crew list and leave the contract as it is
questions.why: Only the skipper named in the contract is covered at the helm; a co-skipper is added at the base, with their licence, before signing.

questions.q: At the office the desk asks you to sign the contract and the check-in form together, 'the technician will walk you round afterwards'. What do you do?
options: Sign neither until the technician has walked you round the boat
Sign both — the walk-round is a formality and the form can be amended by e-mail
Sign the contract; the check-in form only after the walk-round, with what you found on it
Sign both, and photograph the boat so that you have your own record
questions.why: The check-in form records the state of the boat as you took her over; it is signed after the walk-round, not before.

questions.q: It is 19:30 on Saturday, the base is handing over twelve boats, and the technician says 'she's fine, sign here, I'll come by tomorrow if anything is wrong'. What do you do?
options: Sign — he has seen the boat, and you will phone the base about anything tomorrow
Refuse to sign, sleep ashore and come back on Sunday morning when it is quieter
Sign now, then e-mail the base a list of defects first thing on Sunday
Walk round yourself now, write what you find on the form, and have the base countersign it tonight
questions.why: The walk-round is yours, not the base's; what is not written and countersigned before you sign is yours to pay for.

questions.q: Friday 16:00, the base is in sight and the tank is at three-quarters. Where do you take the boat first?

figure.note: Fri 18:00, tanks full · base refuels at fuel + €80

options: A — fill up, then berth at B and report to the base
B — berth; the base's refuelling costs the same as the pontoon
C — the visitor quay for the night; the return berth is for Saturday
B — berth; the base fills up from the berth on Saturday morning
questions.why: Full to full: the boat comes back with full tanks; refuelling by the base is charged on top of the fuel.

questions.q: Your crew say you can hand-haul the anchor all week and mention the windlass on Friday. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday, Vathi, 12 M from base
lines: Windlass stops with 20 m of chain out
Contract: no sailing with a known fault

options: Hand-haul for the week and write the windlass on the check-out form
Call the base now, report it, and sail on only as they instruct
Sail on to the next big harbour and find a mechanic there yourselves
Open the windlass and repair it yourselves so that nothing is charged
questions.why: Under the contract the skipper reports a fault at once and does not carry on with it; the base decides the repair.

questions.q: The other skipper is holding out the cash. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday, Fiskardo
lines: A departing motorboat hits your bow
Their skipper offers €200 cash to settle
Base number on the chart table

options: Take the cash and write the damage on the check-out form on Friday
Let him go, and have the pulpit straightened at the yard here today
Refuse the cash, take the boat's name, port, insurer and photos, and call the base at once
Take the cash — it will cover the gelcoat and the base need not know
questions.why: A third-party collision is settled between insurers: the base needs the other boat's details, photos and your report at once.

questions.q: In your first harbour the port police come aboard and ask for the boat's papers. What do you hand them?

figure.title: Port papers
lines: Transit log, stamped at the base

options: A photo of the papers on your phone; the originals stay at the base
The charter contract — it shows that the base is responsible for the boat
Your skipper's licence and passport — the rest is the base's business
The document folder: transit log, crew list, registration and insurance
questions.why: Port police check the transit log and crew list against the registration and insurance; they must be aboard and current.

questions.q: The desk takes an imprint of your card for the deposit and your crew say €3,000 has just left your account and want to split it tonight. What do you tell them?
options: Nothing has left: it is a hold on the card's limit, released after check-out if nothing is charged
It has — the base charges the deposit now and repays it in cash at check-out
Nothing has left: the base keeps the card number and charges only if something breaks
It has — the deposit is charged now and refunded by bank transfer the week after
questions.why: A card deposit is a pre-authorisation: the sum is blocked on the card, not taken, and the block is lifted after a clean check-out.

questions.q: Reading the deposit clause at the desk, you realise your card will not cover it. What do you do?

figure.title: Deposit — payment
lines: Credit card: hold placed before the keys

options: Ask the base to hold €2,000 now and take the rest on your co-skipper's word
Put a second card up for the rest, or pay the balance in cash against a receipt
Leave your passport with the base as security for the difference
Sign now and bring the rest on Monday, once your bank has raised the limit
questions.why: The deposit is in place in full before the boat is handed over; a second card or cash with a receipt is the usual way round a card limit.

questions.q: Wednesday evening, after the gelcoat quote, your crew say the €500 excess is used up and nothing more can be charged this week. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Waiver — the excess
lines: Wednesday: gelcoat on the quarter, €700 quote

options: They are right — the excess is the ceiling for the week, whatever else happens
They are right, but the base will want a new €500 before you may leave harbour
The excess is per incident: another scrape on Thursday costs up to €500 again
They are wrong the other way: two incidents in a week cancel the waiver altogether
questions.why: A waiver's excess is charged on each incident unless the contract says otherwise; two incidents mean two excesses.

questions.q: Your crew ask whether the boat's insurance covers their injuries and luggage. What do you tell them?
options: No one is covered; that is what the deposit is for
Yes, for injuries aboard; luggage is covered out of the deposit
Yes — everyone on the crew list is insured under the boat's policy
No — the policy covers the boat and third parties; each of you needs travel insurance that covers sailing
questions.why: A yacht's policy insures the hull and liability to others; crew injury, luggage and cancellation are the charterer's own travel insurance.

questions.q: Your crew ask whether, if one of them is at the helm when the boat hits a quay, that person pays the deposit. What do you tell them?
options: No — the skipper named in the contract answers to the base for any damage; how you share it is between you
Yes — the base charges whoever was at the helm, so everyone should keep their card handy
Yes — that is why each crew member signs the contract at check-in
No — damage with a crew member at the helm is the base's risk, not the charterer's
questions.why: The contract makes the named skipper responsible for the boat and crew; the base settles the deposit with the skipper, not with the helmsman.

questions.q: A poster in the base office invites charter boats to Wednesday's club regatta and your crew are keen. What does the contract say?
options: Yes — a club regatta is sailing in company, which is cruising, not racing
No — racing is excluded; without the base's written consent you do not enter
Yes, if you sail under mainsail alone and keep clear of the marks
Yes, if you enter the cruising class and pay the entry fee yourselves
questions.why: Racing is excluded from the charter and from its insurance; only the base's written consent could change that.

questions.q: Monday in Lefkas, a friend of your crew asks to come along for the day sail only. You are eight. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Boat's licence
lines: Lefkas, Monday: a friend asks to join for the day

options: Yes — the limit counts berths for sleeping, and he goes home tonight
Yes, if you call the base before you leave the quay and give his name
No — eight is the licence's limit for anyone aboard under way, a day guest included
Yes, if he signs a note that he sails at his own risk
questions.why: The boat's licence and insurance cap the persons aboard under way; a day guest counts, and the port police count heads.

questions.q: The booking form asks for each child's age and weight and your crew ask why the base cares. What do you tell them?
options: The base needs the ages for the crew list; children are not counted as persons aboard
Children under 12 sail free and the base needs the ages for the invoice
So the base can fit cots; children are not entered on the crew list
The base sizes their lifejackets and the children count as persons aboard under the licence
questions.why: Children are crew: on the crew list, within the persons limit, and in a lifejacket of the right size, which the base supplies.

questions.q: Your crew want to bring the dog for the week. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — pets
lines: Pets: only with the base's written consent
Pet passport for the port police

options: Ask the base in writing before you book it in, bring its pet passport and budget for the cleaning fee
Bring it and tell the technician on the pontoon; the fee is settled at check-out
Bring it — a small dog is not a pet in the sense of the contract
Bring it, but leave it off the crew list so the port police need not know
questions.why: A pet comes with the base's written consent, a cleaning fee and its own papers; sprung on the base at the pontoon it can be refused.

questions.q: A yacht hails you on ch 16 and asks for a tow into harbour. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday 15:00, off Meganisi
lines: Yacht with a dead engine asks for a tow, 4 M
Wind F2, flat sea, no one hurt
Contract: no towing of other vessels
Coast guard on ch 16; base number aboard

options: Tow her, once her skipper has signed a note accepting any damage to either boat
Stand by her, relay her call to the coast guard and tell your base; tow only if she is in immediate danger
Sail on — the clause means you may not even stop for a boat that is not in distress
Tow her — the duty to help at sea overrides any clause in a charter contract
questions.why: The duty to assist is to life in danger; a tow for convenience is excluded by the contract and uninsured — the coast guard or a tow service does it.

questions.q: The forecast has come true and the only shelter downwind is a harbour the contract forbids. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday 14:00, 15 M from base
lines: Nearest shelter: harbour marked X in the contract
Contract: harbours marked X not permitted
Base's 24 h number on the chart table

options: Stay out and beat to the base; the clause is absolute and the fine is worse than F7
Go in — safety overrides the contract, and you tell the base about it at check-out
Call the base now, explain, and go in with their consent; they can allow for shelter what they forbid for a visit
Anchor in the open bay outside the mole; the clause names the harbour, not the bay
questions.why: A forbidden harbour is a contract matter, not a law of nature: the base can consent for shelter, and a call now beats a surprise at check-out.

questions.q: Your crew want to press on to the planned harbour. What do you do?

figure.title: Monday 17:30, under way
lines: Planned harbour: 14 M, you make 5 kn
Harbour abeam, 6 M: sheltered, free quay
Contract: no sailing between sunset and sunrise

options: Press on — it is the open sea the clause means, not the last hour into a lit harbour
Press on under engine with the nav lights on; the clause is about sailing, not motoring
Press on and call the base from the quay so that they know you arrived safely
Divert to the harbour 6 M off and be in before sunset; 14 M at 5 kn puts you in after dark
questions.why: 14 M at 5 kn is 2 h 48 min — arrival 20:18, after sunset; the no-night-sailing clause has no allowance for the last hour.

questions.q: Monday 18:00, the quay attendant waves you to the free space at A. What do you do with the briefing's note?

figure.note: Briefing: ferry wash on the N quay 07:00 and 19:00

options: Ask for B, or anchor at C; the ferry wash will throw you onto the quay twice a day
Take A — the attendant knows his harbour better than the base does
Take A and double the fenders — wash is what fenders are for
Take A for tonight; the ferry comes at 07:00 and you leave at 06:30
questions.why: The briefing's harbour notes are the base's own experience of its boats damaged on that quay; the attendant fills spaces.

questions.q: Monday 07:00, leaving the bay, you see two orange flags ahead between you and the cape. What do you do?

figure.title: Briefing — fishing nets
lines: Nets set at dusk, lifted by 08:00
Two flags = a net between them, up to 500 m
Pass outside both flags, never between
Net on the prop: call the base, do not dive

options: Go between them under sail only; a net cannot foul a boat with no prop turning
Pass outside the outer flag, well clear — the net runs between the two
Pass between the flags — they mark the ends and the net lies on the bottom
Pass inshore of the inner flag — nets are set to seaward of their flags
questions.why: Flagged nets run between their flags near the surface; the rule is outside both, and a net on the prop is a call to the base, not a dive.

questions.q: Monday 18:00, N 3 and dying, your crew want A: it is flat calm and closest to the taverna. What do you do?

figure.note: Briefing: E bay — night gusts to 40 kn in N wind

options: Anchor at A and move to B if the gusts come; it is only across the bay
Anchor at A with all the chain out and an anchor watch — that is what the briefing was for
Anchor at B — the briefing's gusts come after dark in exactly this wind, however calm it looks now
Anchor at A — F3 is light, and a briefing always exaggerates
questions.why: Katabatic gusts fall from the cliffs after dark in a northerly; the briefing names that bay so that you do not learn it at 02:00.

questions.q: Your crew prefer the phone app and want Thursday's planned 25 M leg. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday 18:00, base's daily post
lines: All yachts: sheltered harbour by Thu 12:00
Call the base when you are in
Your phone app: NE 5 on Thursday

options: Follow the app and sail; the base's post is advice for its less experienced crews
Sail until the wind reaches 6, then look for shelter — that is what the wind limit means
Stay in the bay you are in; it has been calm since Monday
Follow the base: a harbour sheltered from NE by noon, and call in; its instruction binds you under the contract
questions.why: The base's instruction to its boats in weather is binding under the contract, and the Meltemi forecast the base names beats a phone app.

questions.q: As the technician starts the technical briefing, your crew say it is the skipper's job and head for the supermarket. What do you do?
options: Keep one other aboard for it, and walk the rest through gas, heads, seacocks and lifejackets yourself tonight
Let them go — the briefing is for the skipper, and the crew need only know the heads
Let them go and give them the base's briefing sheet to read on Sunday
Insist they all stay — the base will not sign off the briefing otherwise
questions.why: The skipper answers for the crew knowing the boat; a second pair of ears at the briefing and a crew briefing aboard are how that is done.

questions.q: The technician leaves this pack at the chart table. What do you do with it before you sail?

figure.title: Briefing pack
lines: Phone list: base, technician, coast guard

options: Leave it in its bag — the pilot book is for the base's own skippers
Check it is complete against the inventory, read the harbour notes tonight, keep it at the chart table
Photograph the phone list and hand the pack back; it is heavy and not yours
Read the harbour notes once you are in the first harbour and need them
questions.why: The pack is the base's local knowledge and is on the inventory; the harbour notes are read before the first harbour, not in it.

questions.q: Your crew ask who to call if the engine stops on Sunday, when the office is shut. What do you tell them?
options: 112 — it is Sunday and the base office is shut
Ch 16 — the coast guard will pass the message on to the base
The technician's 24 h number; the coast guard and ch 16 are for danger to life or the boat
No one until Monday 09:00; anchor and wait for the office to open
questions.why: The base keeps a 24 h technical number for its boats; the coast guard and ch 16 are for distress and urgency, not a dead engine at anchor.

questions.q: At the desk the manager reads your licence and says the base cannot accept it. What do you do?
options: Show the manager your logbook — twenty years of miles outweigh a date on a card
Sail as planned — the licence is checked at the base, not at sea
Ask the base to write 'renewal pending' on the contract and renew it online from the boat
Have the co-skipper named as skipper on the contract, or hire the base's skipper for the week
questions.why: No valid licence, no bareboat: the base's options are a licensed co-skipper named as skipper or its own skipper at a daily rate.

questions.q: The form asks who will operate the VHF. What do you write?

figure.title: Radio — the form
lines: Ship's radio licence: in the folder
Crew member Anna: SRC, in date

options: Anna, as radio operator; her certificate is filed with your skipper's papers
Yourself — the ship's radio licence covers whoever is at the set
Nobody — then the base must take the VHF off the inventory
Nobody — the VHF is for emergencies, and anyone may call MAYDAY
questions.why: The ship's licence covers the set; the operator needs a certificate, and the base files the certificated crew member as operator.

questions.q: Sunday morning, your crew ask how much to budget for harbours this week. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Charter price
lines: Included: base marina, first and last night
Not included: harbour and marina fees
Cruising tax: paid by the base, receipt aboard

options: Only the marinas; town quays are free to charter yachts
Every marina and town quay is paid by you each night; only the base marina is in the price
Nothing — the base refunds harbour fees against the receipts you bring back
Nothing — the charter price covers mooring anywhere in the cruising area
questions.why: Mooring during the week is the crew's cost, paid on the spot; the contract includes the base's own berth and nothing else.

questions.q: At Kioni the port police ask for the cruising-tax receipt. What do you show them?

figure.title: Document folder — tax
lines: Cruising tax: paid by the base for the month
Receipt: in the folder, second pocket
A fine for a missing receipt: on the charterer

options: Your card — the tax is paid by the crew in the first port of call
Your charter contract — it proves the base, not you, owes the tax
The receipt in the document folder — the base paid it and the boat carries the proof
Nothing — the tax is for private yachts, not for charter boats
questions.why: The cruising tax is paid before the boat sails and its receipt lives with the boat's papers; the port police check it with the transit log.

questions.q: The supermarket's van arrives at the pontoon as the briefing starts. What do you do?

figure.title: Provisioning delivery
lines: Delivered: 9 boxes, cold items on top

options: Leave the boxes on the pontoon until the briefing is over, then check them
Sign it — the base placed the order, so the base chases any shortage
Sign the note now and sort the boxes out after the briefing
A crew member checks the boxes against the order and stows the cold food; the note is signed when it tallies
questions.why: The delivery note is your acceptance; shortages are claimed now against the order, and the cold chain does not wait for the briefing.

questions.q: Your crew want to refill the empty bottle in the marina today so that nothing is charged. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Thursday 08:00, gas
lines: Contract: one empty on return is fine

options: Don't — one empty bottle on return is in the policy; a refill ashore is your money and the base will not refund it
Do — an empty bottle on return is charged, whatever the policy says
Do, and keep the receipt: the base refunds a refill at check-out
Do — the spare must also be full at check-out, or it is charged too
questions.why: The contract allows one empty bottle at check-out; a refill ashore is the crew's money and is not refunded.

questions.q: Wednesday, your crew find their flights leave from Preveza, not Corfu, and want to end the week in Lefkas after all. What do you do?

figure.title: One-way charter
lines: Transit log: handed to the Corfu base
Change of return base: base's consent, fee

options: Sail back to Lefkas — the boat belongs there and the base will be glad to have her
Call the base now — the return base is fixed in the contract and changes only with its consent and a fee
End in Corfu as agreed and leave the boat on the visitor quay with the keys at the office
Finish in Lefkas and pay the base the Corfu berth fee you saved
questions.why: A one-way charter names the base that checks the boat out and takes the transit log; a change is the base's decision, not the crew's.

questions.q: Your flight lands at 22:30 on Saturday. What do you arrange with the base?

figure.title: Check-in times
lines: Late arrival: by arrangement, key at the marina office

options: Ask to sign the check-in form by e-mail on Saturday so that Sunday is yours
Nothing — find the boat on the pontoon and check her in yourself by the inventory list
Tell them now; collect the key as agreed, sleep aboard, and do the walk-round and briefing on Sunday before you leave
Nothing — sleep aboard and leave at dawn; the briefing is for first-time charterers
questions.why: A late arrival is agreed in advance; the walk-round, the form and the briefing still happen, just on Sunday morning, before departure.

questions.q: The walk-round is done and the form is signed. Which photos do you take before the light goes?

figure.title: Check-in photos
lines: Scratch, stbd quarter: close up and from the quay
Fenders: all six in one frame
Hull from the quay, both sides

options: The saloon and the cabins — the hull is the base's business, not yours
The form only — the technician photographs the boat for the base's file
A short video round the deck, e-mailed to the base so that it is time-stamped
Each mark close up and from far enough to see where it is, the whole hull from the quay, and the signed form
questions.why: A photo proves a defect only when it shows what, where and when; the base's own pictures are not yours to rely on.

questions.q: Reading the form again on Sunday morning you find this line. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-in form, Sunday 08:30
lines: No size, no side, no photo

options: Call the technician over now, have each scratch located and measured on the form, and photograph them together
Leave it — 'minor scratches' covers anything found on the bow at check-out
Cross it out and write a precise description yourself, with your initials
Photograph the bow yourself and e-mail the pictures to the base from the first harbour
questions.why: A vague line on the form protects no one; a located, measured, countersigned entry with a photo does.

questions.q: Your crew say nothing happened and the diver on Friday will see nothing. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday 11:00, bay entrance
lines: Keel touched sand twice at 2 kn; boat off
Contract: inspection as the base decides

options: Write it in the log and tell the technician on Friday at check-out
Call the base now, report it, note it in the log, and let them decide on a diver or a lift
Say nothing — sand does not mark a keel, and the Friday diver will see nothing
Snorkel over the keel yourselves and report it on Friday only if you find a mark
questions.why: A grounding is reported at once: the base and its insurer decide the inspection; a grounding found later at check-out is treated as hidden.

questions.q: It is 16:30 at the base in Lefkas. The technician hands you the form and says he will start with the engine. How do you run the walk-round?

figure.title: Check-in, Lefkas
lines: Form: boat outline and a remarks box
Three more boats waiting for him

options: Engine and inside first, the hull from the quay once he has left
Whatever order he prefers, as long as the engine runs before you sign
Outside first from the quay, bow to stern on both sides, then the deck, then the rig
Deck and rig first while it is light, the hull from the dinghy tomorrow
questions.why: A fixed order — hull both sides, deck, rig — is how nothing gets missed; the hull is the deposit.

questions.q: At 17:10 the technician says this and heads for the next boat. What do you do?

figure.title: Technician
lines: 'Walk round yourself, I have three more'
'Bring the form to the office by 18:00'
Form still blank for hull and deck

options: Agree; a photographed walk-round is as good as a witnessed one
Walk round alone and list everything; the office will accept the list
Sign the hull section now and photograph the boat after he leaves
Ask him to stay for the walk-round — what you find alone is disputed on Friday
questions.why: Damage goes on the form with the base's technician present and initialling; notes made alone are your word against theirs.

questions.q: On the port bow, 40 cm aft of the stem, you find this. It is not on the form. What do you do?

figure.title: Port bow: gelcoat chip 3 cm
lines: Below the toe rail, 40 cm aft of the stem
Form: nothing marked at the bow

options: Photograph it with a coin for scale, write 'chip 3 cm, star cracks' on the outline, have him initial
Write 'scratches, port bow' in the remarks box and move on to the deck
Ask the base to fill and polish it before you leave the dock
Leave it — chips under 5 cm are normal wear and are never charged
questions.why: Size, place and a photo with scale; star cracks mean impact, so write cracks, not scratches.

questions.q: From the quay you look along the port side at the waterline. What goes on the form?

figure.title: Waterline, from the quay
lines: Stern 5 cm low: tanks full, 6 bags aboard
Stbd quarter: brighter gelcoat patch, sound

options: Nothing — the waterline and old repairs are not deposit items
'Weed on waterline' and 'old repair, stbd quarter' with a photo — neither is yours
A request for a diver before you sign — fouling slows the boat and heats the engine
'Crack, starboard quarter' — so the repair cannot be charged to you later
questions.why: Fouling and old repairs are the base's; writing them down with a photo is what keeps them the base's.

questions.q: Moored stern-to in Alimos, the water is clear enough to see the keel. What do you do before you go aboard?

figure.title: Stern, from the quay
lines: Keel leading edge: scuffed, paint gone

options: Note the rudder only; the keel is below the waterline and is not on the form
Note nothing; the technician has seen the keel and says it is only sand
Photograph both, write them on the form, and watch the rudder while he turns the wheel lock to lock
Ask for a haul-out before you accept the boat — a scuffed keel means a grounding
questions.why: A keel scuff at check-in that is not on the form becomes your grounding at check-out.

questions.q: You check the bathing platform before the crew arrives with the bags. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Bathing platform
lines: Platform hinge: 1 cm play, lifts with a clunk

options: A tape repair on the rung yourself; note the hinge and the shower
The hinge rebuilt before you leave; the rung and the shower are wear
Nothing fixed — write all three on the form and manage with a bucket
The rung and the shower head fixed before you leave; the hinge play on the form with a photo
questions.why: A cracked rung breaks under a wet crew member; the rest is noted so it is not charged on Friday.

questions.q: You lean on the starboard guardrail by the gate and find this. What do you do?

figure.note: Starboard side, at the gate

options: Ask the base to fix all three before you leave — the guardrail is what keeps the crew aboard
Write all three on the form and seize the hook with a lanyard
Tell the crew to use the port side and note it on the form
Tighten the stanchion yourself; the wire and the hook are cosmetic
questions.why: A loose stanchion or a frayed lifeline fails when someone falls on it; the base fixes it, not the form.

questions.q: In the forecabin you look at the hatch and the portlight. What do you do?

figure.title: Forecabin hatch
lines: Lens: 8 cm crack from the hinge corner
Seal perished; hatch does not dog down tight

options: Ask for the portlight handle freed; the hatch is noted as wear
Photograph the crack and ask for the lens taped and the seal replaced — a wave fills that bunk
Note all three and ask for a tarpaulin for the foredeck
Note the crack; keep the hatch shut all week and the bunk stays dry
questions.why: A hatch that does not seal takes green water on the foredeck; a cracked lens is a deposit item unless noted.

questions.q: Walking the port side deck you press with your heel by the chainplates. What goes on the form?

figure.title: Side deck, port
lines: Non-slip worn smooth by the shrouds
Soft spot 20 × 20 cm by the chainplate
Genoa track: two bolts standing proud

options: The soft spot only — worn non-slip and proud bolts are wear
Nothing — deck wear is never a deposit item
All three with photos; the soft spot and the raised bolts the technician initials
A request for the deck re-cored before you sail
questions.why: A soft spot is structural and may be blamed on your week; written and initialled now it stays the base's.

questions.q: You open the cockpit lockers against the inventory. What do you do?

figure.title: Cockpit lockers
lines: Lazarette: padlock missing, lid does not latch

options: Ask for everything moved to the saloon so you can count it
Note 'lockers OK'; a lid that does not latch is tied with a line
Sign the inventory — the count is the base's job, the latch you tie down
Count against the list; ask for a padlock, a latch that holds and the drain cleared
questions.why: An unlatched locker lid opens at sea and floods the lazarette; a blocked drain floods the cockpit.

questions.q: At the binnacle you turn the wheel and work the lever with the engine off. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Binnacle
lines: Wheel: a quarter turn of play before the rudder moves
Wheel lock: slips under hand pressure
Throttle: stiff, two hands into astern

options: The steering cables and the throttle cable adjusted now; the lock on the form
The wheel lock replaced before you leave; play is normal, the lever you learn
A spray of lubricant on the lever yourself; note the play and the lock
Nothing adjusted — note all three, charter wheels are always loose
questions.why: Play in the steering is a loose cable or chain; a stiff throttle costs the moment you need astern in a berth.

questions.q: You check the canvas before the afternoon sun goes. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Sprayhood & bimini
lines: Sprayhood window scratched; port zip open at the foot
Bimini frame bent; one strap missing
Bimini: 15 cm tear at the aft seam

options: The tear only; the zip, strap and frame are how the boat came
The zip, strap and tear fixed before you leave; the window and the frame on the form with photos
A new bimini fitted before you leave the dock, the sprayhood noted
Nothing fixed — canvas is wear, write all five items on the form
questions.why: A tear grows in the first blow and a missing strap lets the bimini fold; what cannot be fixed now goes on the form.

questions.q: You check the standing rigging at deck level on both sides. What do you do?

figure.title: Standing rigging, from deck
lines: Port cap shroud: turnbuckle split pin missing, no tape
Starboard lower: one broken strand at the swage

options: Fit a pin yourself; one broken wire of nineteen is fine for a week
Note both; tape the strand and ask for a split pin at your first port
A broken strand means the base's rigger before you sail; the split pin and tape are fitted now
Ask for the rig tuned and tensioned before you accept the boat
questions.why: A broken strand at the swage is the start of a failure; a turnbuckle without a split pin unwinds.

questions.q: You stand at the mast foot on deck. What do you check by eye?
options: Push the mast at the gooseneck to feel for play in the step
Count the halyards and read the makers' label at the gooseneck
The wind vane turning; the rest needs a bosun's chair
Up the groove: a straight mast, spreaders level with boots on; the collar sealed, the deck flat round the foot
questions.why: A bend, a drooping spreader or a dished deck round the foot are seen from the deck; the base's rigger does the rest.

questions.q: You swing the boom and look at what holds it up. What do you ask the base for?

figure.title: Boom
lines: Gooseneck pin: worn, boom knocks when swung
Rigid kicker holds the boom; no topping lift
Preventer: no line aboard, no pad-eye forward

options: The gooseneck pin looked at now and a long line to rig a preventer; the rigid kicker needs no topping lift
Nothing — all three are how the boat was built and how it sailed last week
A new gooseneck fitting; the preventer is for ocean passages, not the Ionian
A topping lift rigged to the masthead; the gooseneck play is normal and a sheet makes the preventer
questions.why: A rigid kicker carries the boom; a worn gooseneck pin and no preventer are what hurt crew in a gybe.

questions.q: At the cabin-top winches you run each halyard and clutch. What do you do before you sign?

figure.note: Clutch #2 jammed shut · 2 of 3 winch handles found

options: Ask for the halyard replaced and a new self-tailer; the handle you buy
The clutch freed and the third handle found now; the chafe and the jaws on the form
Sign — a jammed clutch is opened at sea with a winch, two handles are plenty
Note all four on the form and free the clutch with pliers once out
questions.why: A clutch that will not release is a halyard you cannot drop; a missing handle is a deposit charge on Friday.

questions.q: At the bow you work the roller, the stopper and the cleat by hand. What do you do?

figure.title: Bow fitting
lines: Bow roller: pin bent, roller does not turn
Port bow cleat: moves under hand pressure

options: Note all three; the windlass holds the chain and the starboard cleat does for mooring
Ask for the roller only; a loose cleat and a stopper are the base's wear
Ask for all three fixed before you leave — the cleat and the stopper take the mooring and anchor loads
Tighten the cleat from below yourself and note the roller and the stopper
questions.why: The chain stopper, not the windlass, holds the anchor load; a loose cleat is a line gone in a Meltemi night.

questions.q: The technician says the masthead was checked at the start of the season. How do you check it yourself before you sign?
options: Send a crew member up in the bosun's chair with the technician on the winch
Switch the instruments on — a wind reading means the masthead is fine
You cannot from the deck; write 'masthead not inspected' on the form
Through binoculars from the quay: wind vane and cups turning, VHF antenna upright, light lenses whole
questions.why: Binoculars show a missing cup, a leaning antenna or a cracked lens from the quay; the season's start was months ago.

questions.q: You find the pulpit bent to port. The technician says this. What do you do?

figure.title: Pulpit bent to port
lines: Technician: 'That's old, it's on the form already'
Form, boat outline: nothing at the bow

options: Write 'pulpit bent, port' on the outline now, photograph it and have him initial
Write it in the remarks box as 'general wear' to match the office
Ask the office for last week's check-out form before you continue
Take his word — he knows the boat and the office has last week's form
questions.why: What counts on Friday is this form; 'general wear' and the technician's memory are not entries.

questions.q: In the catamaran saloon you find this, and the manager wants the form signed before the briefing. What do you do?

figure.title: Saloon forward window
lines: Crack 25 cm from the lower corner
Manager: 'sign now, we correct it Monday'

options: Sign with 'see photo' beside the entry; the photo is dated and the office has a copy
Do not sign until the entry reads 'crack 25 cm' with your photo — 'scratched' is your crack on Friday
Sign and e-mail the office the photo tonight so the record is complete
Sign; a correction on Monday is in writing and better than an argument now
questions.why: You sign for the boat as the form describes it; a crack recorded as a scratch is charged to the deposit.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician walks you along the quay and down the steps and says the hull is done. What have you still not seen?

figure.title: Catamaran 42 ft, stern-to
lines: Walked: port and starboard outer sides
Dinghy in the water at the stern

options: Only the keels, which are below the waterline and never on the form
Nothing — a catamaran's hulls are seen in full from the quay and the steps
The inner faces of both hulls and the bridgedeck underside — from the dinghy
The deck between the hulls, which you walk once the bags are aboard
questions.why: Between the hulls nothing shows from the quay; a scrape under the bridgedeck found on Friday is yours unless noted.

questions.q: From the quay you see the boat sitting like this, before any bags are aboard. What do you do?
options: Nothing — a charter boat always lists a little with full tanks
Note 'list to port' on the form and trim her with the crew's bags
Ask for the port tank pumped down so that she floats level
Have the bilge and the port lockers opened to find the weight before you sign
questions.why: With both tanks full, a list means weight on one side — often water in the bilge or a locker. Find it before it is yours.

questions.q: From the dinghy at the stern in Göcek you push the rudder blade sideways and feel this. What do you do?

figure.title: Rudder, from the dinghy
lines: Blade pushed side to side by hand
Clunk at the hull, about 5 mm

options: Show the technician, note 'rudder bearing play' and let the base pass it as safe
Refuse the boat outright and ask the base for another yacht
Note nothing — every spade rudder moves a little in its bearing, it is normal
Grease the rudder stock from the cockpit and test it again tomorrow
questions.why: Bearing play grows under load; on the form it is the base's, and the base decides if it sails — not you, alone at sea.

questions.q: You lift the saloon floorboards over the keel and find this. Outside, the front of the keel joint has fresh paint. What do you do?

figure.title: Bilge, over the keel
lines: Hairline crack in the floor beside bolt 3

options: Note the rust only; fresh paint means the base has already repaired it
Ask for the boat's grounding record and a keel check before you sign — not 'keel OK'
Sign — a dry bilge proves that the keel and its bolts are sound
Tighten the nuts yourself and write 'keel bolts serviced' on the form
questions.why: Weeping bolts, a cracked floor and new paint at the joint point to a grounding; unrecorded, it is blamed on your week.

questions.q: The aft cabin has a fixed window in the topsides. From the quay you see this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Hull window, port aft
lines: Sealant cracked along the lower edge
Inside: white salt line on the frame
Heeled to port, it is under water

options: A note on the form and a towel along the frame for the week
Fresh sealant along the edge, run by your crew on Monday
A hose test from outside while you watch inside, and the result on the form
Nothing — fixed hull windows are bonded in and do not leak
questions.why: A hull window is under water when heeled; a hose test finds the leak at the pontoon, not on your first beat.

questions.q: Walking the starboard side deck you look at the toe rail aft. What goes to the base?

figure.title: Toe rail, starboard quarter
lines: Gelcoat cracked along the joint below
Last crew's fender lines tied round it

options: Nothing — a toe rail is trim and is never charged
A note on the form; your fenders go on the same rail all week
Nothing yet; you tap the bolts back in and write 'toe rail fixed'
A photo, a line on the form, and the bolts and sealant put back before you leave
questions.why: The toe rail bolts through the hull-deck joint; lifted, it lets water in and pulls further with every fender line.

questions.q: A crew member offers to take the photos while you write on the form. What do you ask for, for each mark?
options: One wide shot that shows where on the boat, then a close-up with a coin beside it
Close-ups of only the marks not yet on the form, to save time
A video of the whole hull at walking pace, nothing else
One sharp close-up of each mark, with the flash on
questions.why: A close-up alone cannot be placed on the boat; the wide shot ties it to the outline, the coin gives its size.

questions.q: In the saloon you look up at the headlining under the side decks. What do you do?

figure.title: Saloon headlining, port
lines: Brown stains round two stanchion-base bolts

options: Note nothing; stains in the headlining are old and only cosmetic
Photograph it, note it, and ask for the stanchion bases rebedded before you leave
Put a towel over the bolts and keep the crew's bags off that berth
Seal the bolts from below with tape and mention it to the base on Friday
questions.why: Damp round the bolts is a deck fitting leaking now; rebedded it stays dry, and noted it is not your damage.

questions.q: The walk-round is done but the form is not signed. A boat leaving the next berth swings into you. What do you do?
options: Call to the other boat and settle it with its skipper in cash
Sign as it is; the new scuff is between you and the other skipper
Get the technician back, add it to the form with photos and the other boat's name
Photograph it and tell the base on Friday if they ask about it
questions.why: Anything before your signature goes on the form; the base claims from the other boat, not from your deposit.

questions.q: The technician lifts the cockpit table leaves with you. What goes on the form?

figure.title: Cockpit table
lines: Port leaf: support arm broken, leaf droops

options: 'Table OK' — it stands firm and the starboard leaf holds
Nothing — a table leaf is not a deposit item on any charter
Nothing yet; you ask the base for a new table before you sign
'Port leaf support broken' with a photo — so on Friday it is wear, not damage
questions.why: A fault written at check-in is the base's on Friday; one that is not becomes damage from your week.

questions.q: You load the starboard primary winch with the genoa sheet and feel this. What do you do?

figure.note: Starboard primary · clicks unevenly

options: Ask the base to service the winch now — a slipping pawl lets the sheet run back
Oil the drum yourself and try it again under sail on Sunday
Note it and take two extra turns on the drum to hold the load
Use the port winch for both sheets and note the starboard one
questions.why: Pawls stop the drum turning back; worn or stuck, they let the sheet run out under load and take a hand with it.

questions.q: At the pontoon you shake each cap shroud by hand. What do you do?
options: Sail and check it again on the first beat, when the load comes on
Ask the base's rigger to tension it before you sail — not you on the turnbuckle
Turn the port turnbuckle yourself until it matches the starboard
Note it; the shroud on the side away from the quay is always slack
questions.why: A slack cap shroud lets the mast move and shock-loads the rig; tuning it is the rigger's job, not a risk for your deposit.

questions.q: Your crew ask why the foot of every shroud is wrapped in tape. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Shroud turnbuckle
lines: Split pin through the threaded stud
Tape over the pin and its ends

options: It keeps salt off the wire; the pin needs nothing over it
It marks the shrouds the base has tuned this season
It covers the pin's sharp ends so sails, sheets and hands do not snag on them
It stops the turnbuckle turning — the pin is only a backup
questions.why: The split pin stops the turnbuckle unwinding; the tape covers its sharp ends and is peeled back to check the pin.

questions.q: In the saloon you open the panel over the port chainplate. What do you do?

figure.title: Port chainplate, from below
lines: Wood round the bolts dark and damp
On deck: sealant cracked round it

options: Wipe off the rust and write 'chainplate cleaned' on the form
Sail, and keep the load off it by reefing early all week
Nothing — rust stains at a chainplate are normal on a charter boat
Photograph it, put it on the form and ask the base's rigger to look before you sail
questions.why: Water at a chainplate corrodes it where no one sees; the whole load of the shroud runs through it.

questions.q: From the end of the pontoon you look at the spreaders through binoculars. What do you do?

figure.title: Spreaders, by binoculars
lines: Port lower spreader droops below level
Its tip boot gone; shroud kinked there

options: Ask the base to send someone aloft to reset it before you sail, and note it
Tape a rag round the tip at the next harbour and sail on
Sail on starboard tack only until Friday and note it
Note it — a spreader angle does not matter at charter loads
questions.why: A drooping spreader pushes the shroud off line and can fold under load; it is reset from aloft by the base.

questions.q: At the stern the technician points at the backstay adjuster and says 'leave it alone'. You look at it. What do you ask for?
options: Nothing — he said leave it alone, so its setting does not matter
The ram checked for the leak, and the setting the base wants, in writing
How to pump it to the top of the gauge to get the forestay tight
A rag to wipe the oil, and 'adjuster serviced' on the form
questions.why: A leaking ram lets the backstay go slack and the forestay sag; the base sets it, and you need its number.

questions.q: Reading the form again on Sunday before you cast off, you see the scrape you photographed is not on it. You signed last night. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-in form, Sunday
lines: Stern: scrape 15 cm, your photo 17:52 Sat

options: Leave it — yesterday's dated photo is proof enough on Friday
Show the photo at check-out, if the scrape is mentioned
Go to the office before you leave and have it added, dated and initialled
E-mail the photo to the base tonight from the first bay
questions.why: Friday is settled on the signed form; an entry initialled before you sail closes the gap a photo alone leaves.

questions.q: The 36 ft boat steers with a tiller. You work it and look at the fittings. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Tiller, 36 ft
lines: Tiller head: bolt loose, 1 cm play on the stock

options: Nothing fixed; a little play at the tiller head is normal
The bolt on the form; you steer all week without the extension
Nothing now; you tighten the bolt at sea if it gets worse
The head bolt tightened and a new extension before you leave
questions.why: Play at the tiller head grows until the tiller comes off the stock; a cracked extension breaks when you lean on it.

questions.q: On the catamaran you turn each wheel lock to lock while a crew member watches the rudders from the steps. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Catamaran, two helms
lines: Port wheel: both rudders follow at once
Starboard wheel: 1/4 turn before they move

options: The starboard steering and the tie bar adjusted before you leave
Grease for the starboard wheel; rudders line up under way
A note on the form; uneven rudders are normal on twin helms
Nothing — you steer from the port helm and note the starboard
questions.why: Slack at one helm and rudders out of line mean a loose cable or tie bar; it gets worse, and it fights you in a berth.

questions.q: On the catamaran the forestay comes down to a bridle on the front beam. You look at both legs. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Forestay bridle, front beam
lines: Port leg: broken strand at the thimble

options: Less halyard tension, so the bridle carries less all week
The port leg replaced before you sail — it carries the forestay
Tape over the broken strand and a look at it each morning
A note on the form; the two legs share the load between them
questions.why: Each bridle leg takes the forestay load in turn; one broken strand is the start of the wire going.

questions.q: On the catamaran the crew are already lying on the trampoline. You look at it. What do you do?

figure.title: Trampoline
lines: Lacing chafed through at the front beam, 30 cm
Net sagging by the port hull
Crew of six, two of them children

options: Lace the gap with spare line yourself and note it on the form
Note it; the net only matters at sea, not at the pontoon
Ask for it relaced before you leave, and keep everyone off it till then
Note it and tell the crew to keep to the starboard half
questions.why: Chafed lacing lets the net open under a body; at sea that is a fall between the hulls ahead of the beam.

questions.q: At the stern of the catamaran you look at the davits before the dinghy goes up. What do you do?

figure.title: Davits
lines: Port arm: crack at the weld to the beam
Dinghy 3.1 m with a 6 hp outboard

options: Note it and hoist anyway; davits are built to take far more than that
Lash the dinghy tighter to that arm and note the crack on the form
Tow the dinghy all week and leave the crack off the form
Ask the base to look at the weld before the dinghy hangs on it
questions.why: A cracked weld under a dinghy and outboard in a seaway can let both go; found now, the repair is the base's.

questions.q: On the catamaran you slide the saloon door open and shut. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Saloon sliding door
lines: Jumps off the lower track half open

options: The track and the lock fixed before you leave — a loose door slams under way
Only the lock; a door off its track is how these doors are
A note on the form; the door stays open all week in this heat
A note on the form; a cushion wedges it shut when you sail
questions.why: A door that will not latch runs and slams in a seaway; broken glass is a deposit item and a cut hand.

questions.q: Coming back from a swim, your crew pull themselves into the cockpit by the bimini frame. What do you tell them?
options: Fine, but only when the bimini is folded and the canvas takes no load
The frame is light tube and bends — use the pushpit and the grab rails
Fine — the frame is bolted through the deck like the stanchions
Fine on the windward side, where the straps brace the frame
questions.why: A bimini frame bent by a hand is new damage at check-out; the pushpit and grab rails are built to take a body's weight.

questions.q: Monday, at anchor, a crew member reaches for kitchen roll to wipe the salt off the sprayhood window. What do you tell them?
options: Kitchen roll and a squirt of galley spray clean it fastest
Leave the salt on — the base cleans the canvas on Friday
Rinse it with fresh water and dab it with a soft cloth — dry salt scratches
A dry towel, rubbed hard, before the salt sets on the window
questions.why: Clear vinyl scratches under dry salt and cleaners; a window you cannot see through at check-out is charged.

questions.q: Tuesday, creeping into a bay at 2 kn, the keel touches sand and you back off under engine. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday, 13:00
lines: Touched sand at 2 kn, came off astern
Your check-in photos of the keel on the phone

options: Report it on Friday at check-out, when the diver goes down
Call the base only if water shows in the bilge this week
Carry on — a soft touch on sand leaves no mark and needs no report
Check the keel bolts, snorkel and photograph the keel, and call the base today
questions.why: The contract wants a grounding reported at once; your check-in photos and today's show what is new and what is not.

questions.q: Monday evening, after a wet beat on port tack, the starboard aft cabin locker is wet and the bilge is dry. What do you do?

figure.title: Aft cabin, starboard
lines: Water runs down from under the side deck
Salty; only wet when heeled to starboard

options: Photograph it, call the base, and keep that side up until they look at it
Head straight back to the base; salt water means a hole in the hull
Nothing till Friday — it was on the form, so it is the base's problem
Seal the joint from inside with tape and leave it out of your report
questions.why: Salt water only when heeled is the deck joint, not the hull; reported now, the base fixes it and wet bedding is not charged to you.

questions.q: Wednesday, under way, the steering feels like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday, 11:00
lines: Half a turn of play before the rudder moves
A knock under the cockpit floor

options: Open the binnacle and tighten the cables yourself under way
Call the base now and motor gently to the nearest harbour to meet their technician
Carry on under autopilot so that the wheel takes no load
Carry on and tell the base at check-out; the play is on the form
questions.why: Play that grows with a knock is a cable or quadrant going; the base fixes it in harbour before it parts at sea.

questions.q: Thursday evening at anchor, your crew want the bimini left up for the morning sun. What do you do?
options: Take the side panels off and leave the top up for the morning
Leave it up, with a line tied in place of the missing strap
Take the panels off, fold the bimini and lash it — it is not built for that wind
Leave it up; it was noted at check-in, so damage is the base's
questions.why: A bimini up in 30 kn gusts tears or bends its frame; damage from your week is yours, noted strap or not.

questions.q: Thursday, 28 miles from the base, your morning look at the rig finds this. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday, 07:00
lines: Stbd lower shroud: 2 broken strands at the swage
Forecast: NW 6 from noon; the base lies NW

options: Leave it for Friday's check-out; one more day on it is fine
Sail back reefed, on the tack that takes the load off that shroud
Tape the strands and sail back early, before the wind arrives
Call the base now; stay, or motor back sails down, as they decide — not sail on it
questions.why: Broken strands mean the wire is going; with a beat ahead the rig must not be loaded — the base sends a rigger or agrees a return.

questions.q: Saturday, 16:30, light wind. The technician ticks 'Sails: OK' and says they were checked yesterday. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Check-in form — sails
lines: Wind at the pontoon: F2, no swell
Main in the stackpack, genoa furled

options: The main hoisted and the genoa unrolled now, while it is calm
A look inside the stackpack and the sail bags, unhoisted
To unroll them yourself on the first morning and phone in faults
Nothing — it was checked yesterday and the form says OK
questions.why: Sails are checked hoisted: at the pontoon in light wind, not at sea; a faulty sail found on Sunday is your problem.

questions.q: The genoa is fully unrolled. You look at the furling drum and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Genoa fully out · rest of the line slack on deck

options: Three turns taken off the drum so the sail unrolls fully
The line rewound tight on the drum with the sail fully out
Nothing — the drum should be empty when the sail is out
The slack on deck coiled, tied off to the pulpit and left
questions.why: With the sail fully out the drum must hold enough line to roll it all in; one turn left means the line runs out mid-furl.

questions.q: Halfway through furling the genoa the line goes solid. The technician reaches for a winch handle. You look up and see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa furler — jammed
lines: Halyard wound twice round the forestay above the swivel
Furling line: solid, two turns on the drum

options: Sheet the genoa in hard on the winch to drag the wrap down the foil
Note 'stiff furler' on the form and grease the swivel yourself once at sea
Stop him — unroll, clear the wrap, and have the base fix the halyard lead
Let him winch it — a halyard wrap pulls itself out once under load
questions.why: A halyard wrap jams the swivel; winching it damages the foil and the halyard. The halyard angle at the masthead is the base's job.

questions.q: The technician runs the genoa sheet through the car for you. You check the car itself and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Starboard car lashed to the track with cord · port car OK

options: Nothing — the cord lashing holds the car where it is
A shackle through the car to the toe rail once at sea
The port car moved across to starboard; one car is enough
The plunger pin replaced so the car locks in the track
questions.why: A car that is not pinned slides under load: the sheet lead goes and the car can hit the end stop; the pin is a base fix.

questions.q: The genoa is out. You walk the leech and see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa leech
lines: UV strip: stitching gone along 1.5 m, strip hanging
Leech line: cleat at the clew broken, line flapping

options: Photograph both, note them on the form, ask for the strip restitched today
Nothing — the UV strip is cosmetic and a leech line is only a trim aid
Sign now and mention both at check-out if they have got any worse
Tape the strip down and tie off the leech line yourself, then move on
questions.why: A loose UV strip tears off and takes stitching with it; the leech line flogs the leech. Both are quick fixes at the base, not at sea.

questions.q: At the genoa clew you find this. The technician says it has sailed like that all season. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa clew
lines: One loop chafed through, one frayed
Sheets tied with bowlines, no shackle

options: Note it on the form and ask for a reduced deposit for the week
Insist the base repairs the clew now — it carries the whole sheet load
Tie the sheets to the ring with a round turn and two half hitches instead
Accept it — two of the three loops are still holding the ring
questions.why: A clew lets go in a gust and the sail flogs itself to pieces; a chafed clew is the base's repair, not a note.

questions.q: The main goes up at the pontoon and you see this. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Mainsail hoisted
lines: Batten 3: snapped, bends in the middle
One luff slide cracked; stackpack zip slider missing

options: The zip fixed now; battens only matter with the full main up
Everything on the form — you will be sailing on reef 1 most days anyway
Battens and the slide replaced now; the zip photographed and on the form
A spare batten and a spare slide to fit yourself at the first anchorage
questions.why: Missing battens let the leech flog and tear; a cracked slide jams the hoist. The zip only keeps the cover shut.

questions.q: You run the genoa sheets to the winches and look at them. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Port 14 m · starboard 16 m · spare lines: list 2, found 1

options: Both sheets swapped for the spare lines and the old sheets noted on the form
The port sheet end-for-ended so the chafe sits at the tail end
Nothing — a sheet lasts the week; the spare takes over if it goes
The port sheet replaced and the second spare line found before you sign
questions.why: A bare core fails under load and a 14 m sheet will not reach the winch on a wide genoa; spares are counted, not assumed.

questions.q: The boat has in-mast furling. The technician asks you to unfurl the main yourself. How do you do it?

figure.note: In-mast main · outhaul on the winch, furling line in a clutch

options: Outhaul out on the winch, the furling line eased with a little tension kept on
Furling line cast off fully first, then the outhaul hauled out on the winch
Outhaul winched out with the furling line still shut in its clutch
Furling line and outhaul hauled together so the roll stays tight
questions.why: The roll must stay firm as it leaves the mast: slack on the furling line lets it bunch and jam in the slot; never winch against a closed clutch.

questions.q: Now the technician furls the main back in. You watch the boom and the lines. What do you ask him to change?

figure.title: In-mast main — furling in
lines: Topping lift eased: boom end below horizontal
Furling line pulled fast, by hand

options: Boom lower still on the topping lift so the sail drops into the mast on its own
Boom up to the base's mark on the topping lift, a little outhaul tension kept
Furling line pulled faster, two hands, so the roll stays tight in the mast
Outhaul let fully go so that nothing at all resists the roll into the mast
questions.why: The boom at the set angle feeds the luff square into the slot; a loose roll creases and jams, and a jammed furler is never forced.

questions.q: The technician points at the clutches and says 'reefs are there'. What do you ask for before you sign?
options: The colour code written on the form so you can look it up when you need it
The reef lines coiled and stowed below; you will try them out at sea
Reef 1 put in at the pontoon, so you see which line does what and runs free
A spare clutch handed over in case one of the reef clutches fails at sea
questions.why: A reef is practised at the pontoon in calm, not worked out at 25 knots; a jammed reef line is then the base's fix.

questions.q: You look at the gooseneck and the reef lines. What does this tell you about reefing at sea?

figure.title: Reefing gear
lines: Cockpit: one line per reef, to the clew cringle

options: The luff reefs with the halyard alone; the horns are spare fittings, unused
The horns take the tack only; the reefs are single-line, pulled from the cockpit
Single-line: one pull from the cockpit reefs both the luff and the clew together
Two-line: the luff cringle is hooked on a horn at the mast, then the clew line hauled
questions.why: Horns at the gooseneck mean the luff is hooked by hand: plan who goes forward, clipped on, before you need a reef.

questions.q: The main is sheeted in at the pontoon and you see this. What do you settle with the base before you sign?

figure.title: Boom & bimini
lines: Main sheeted in: boom end 3 cm above the bimini frame
Bimini: folds aft in a minute

options: Whether the bimini folds under sail or the boom is held clear — and who pays if it tears
Nothing — it is only canvas; the boom slides over it on a gybe without harm
The bimini taken off and left ashore at the base for the week, fitted again on Friday
The boom held up high on the topping lift and cleated there for the whole week
questions.why: A boom that meets the bimini on a gybe tears it, and the damage comes off your deposit; agree the rule now, in writing on the form.

questions.q: The genoa is out in F2 and the luff looks like this. The technician says it always does. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa luff
lines: Genoa halyard: in a clutch at the mast

options: Ease the backstay a turn — the scallops come from forestay sag, not from the halyard
Tension the halyard until the scallops just go, then check the furler still turns
Leave it — a slack luff rolls up tighter on the furler and sets better
Winch the halyard bar-tight; a furling genoa can never be too tight
questions.why: Scallops mean a slack luff; set the halyard so they disappear, no more — an over-tight halyard stiffens the furler and wraps.

questions.q: Your check of the mainsheet, traveller and vang gives this list. What goes to the base to fix now, and what on the form?

figure.title: Mainsheet, traveller, vang
lines: Mainsheet lower block: one cheek cracked
Traveller control line: cover chafed, core sound

options: Everything on the form — nothing has actually failed yet, so nothing to fix
Both replaced now before you sign, or you do not take the boat at all
The cracked block replaced now; the chafed cover photographed and on the form
The chafed line replaced now, the block noted — rope fails before metal
questions.why: A cracked block under mainsheet load can burst and hurt someone: repair now. A chafed cover on a sound core: note it, watch it.

questions.q: The inventory lists a preventer. You find this in the cockpit locker. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Inventory — deck
lines: Preventer line: 1 — found: 6 m, snap hook

options: A boom brake instead of it; a preventer line is only for racing boats
A second 6 m line so you can rig one on each side at the same time
Nothing — 6 m from the boom end to the toe rail amidships is how it is rigged
A line long enough from the boom end to the bow and back to a cockpit winch
questions.why: A preventer runs from the boom end forward to the bow and back aft, so it can be eased from the cockpit; a short strop to the rail breaks the boom.

questions.q: The inventory lists the sails below. You open the forepeak. What do you do before you sign?

figure.title: Inventory — sails
lines: Found: bag 'Gennaker' (sail + sock); bag 'Storm jib' — empty

options: Have the storm jib found or struck off the list, and the count on the form
Take the technician's word that it is in the office and will be put back
Count the bags, not the contents: two bags on the list, two bags found
Sign — you will not fly a storm jib in August in the Ionian anyway
questions.why: What is on the signed list is what you hand back on Friday; a sail you never had is charged against your deposit.

questions.q: Sunday, your first sail. Off the headland the genoa furling line goes solid with the sail half rolled. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 1 — off Lefkas
lines: Genoa half rolled, furling line solid

options: Leave it half out, hoist the main and carry on under both to the anchorage
Ease the sheet, try again by hand, and call the base for instructions — cut nothing
Cut the furling line at the drum and roll the sail by hand round the foil
Put the furling line on the electric winch and grind the sail in, turn by turn
questions.why: A jammed furler is a base problem: forcing or cutting it turns a phone call into a damaged foil and a deposit claim.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician says 'the main goes up like on any boat'. You look at the lazy bag and the head of the sail. What do you ask to see?

figure.title: Catamaran mainsail
lines: Square-top main: headboard on two cars
Lazy bag zip: 2.6 m above the coachroof
Boom reached from the coachroof steps

options: Only the sail number on the bag — a catamaran's main hoists like any other mainsail does
That the bag can stay zipped shut and the main hoisted straight up through it
The main hoisted and dropped once: how the square top goes into the bag, and where you zip it
A ladder added to the inventory so you can reach the zip from the deck at anchor
questions.why: A square top with two headboard cars needs the lazyjacks and the bag opened right, at a height; see it done once at the pontoon.

questions.q: At the briefing you are given this. What does it mean for your week?

figure.title: Contract & briefing — wind
lines: Sailing permitted up to F6 on the base forecast
Reef 1 at 18 kn, reef 2 at 25 kn
Above F6: stay in port, call the base

options: The reef numbers apply only with the full genoa out; with the main alone they do not
Reef when the boat feels overpressed; the numbers are a guide for beginners
The limit is for the forecast only; at sea you carry on as you judge best
Reef at those numbers and stay in port above F6 — they are contract terms, not advice
questions.why: Sailing above the contract limit, or unreefed when told to reef, can void the insurance and put the damage on you.

questions.q: You follow the genoa furling line from the drum aft along the side deck and find this. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Furling line, drum to cockpit · list: 4 blocks, fitted: 3

options: A lead block fitted at the gap so the line runs fair, not over the stanchion base
A spare furling line put aboard in case this one chafes through
The line lashed to that stanchion with a short cord so it cannot move
Nothing — the line only touches the base while the sail is fully out
questions.why: A furling line chafing on a stanchion base jams or parts mid-furl; the lead blocks are the base's fittings, counted like the rest.

questions.q: Reading the inventory again, you compare it with the number on the genoa's clew. What do you do before you sign?
options: Ask for the genoa with the number on the form to be fitted instead of this one
Have the form corrected to the number on the sail — that is the sail you hand back
Write the main's number on the genoa clew with a marker so the two agree
Nothing — the base swaps sails between boats and the form is only indicative
questions.why: On Friday the inventory is checked by number: a sail listed wrongly is 'missing' and charged against your deposit.

questions.q: On the hoist the technician stops winching at this point. Your crew ask what the tape is for. What do you tell them?

figure.note: Main at full hoist · black tape 5 cm short of the clutch

options: It marks reef 1: the sail is lowered to the tape for the first reef
It marks a worn spot on the halyard; move the tape when the chafe moves
It marks full hoist: stop there, or the headboard jams against the masthead sheave
It is the base's inventory tag; the lines are counted by their tapes
questions.why: A halyard winched past its mark drives the headboard into the sheave: the halyard stretches, the sail will not come down.

questions.q: Your crew are already planning a gennaker day. At the briefing you read this clause. What does it mean for the week?

figure.title: Contract — gennaker
lines: Use only with the base's written OK
Max 12 kn true, daylight, sock rigged
Damage to it: not covered by the waiver

options: Leave it in the bag all week; a gennaker on a charter boat is never for the crew
Fly it only after raising the deposit to cover it; the base adjusts the hold
Fly it whenever the wind allows; the clause is advice to keep beginners off it
Ask for the base's written OK now, keep to 12 kn and daylight — a torn gennaker is paid in full
questions.why: The gennaker is usually outside the damage waiver: the clause sets who, when and the limit, and you carry the whole repair bill.

questions.q: Your crew ask where the topping lift is before the main comes down. You look at the boom and see this. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Boom support
