lines: Mainsheet eased, main down: boom stays up

options: There is none: the rigid vang holds the boom up with the sail down — just ease the mainsheet
Pull the vang control line on hard before the drop so the boom cannot fall
Rig the spare halyard to the boom end as a lift every time before the drop
Hold the boom up by hand at the drop; without a lift it falls on the bimini
questions.why: A gas-strut vang replaces the topping lift: it carries the boom when the halyard is let go; a strut that sags is a base repair.

questions.q: The main halyard goes to an electric winch. The technician shows you the button. What rule do you give the crew?

figure.note: Push-button at the coachroof · two speeds · halyard 10 mm

options: Hold the button until the winch stalls; the motor's cut-out protects the sail
Short pushes, eyes on the sail, stop at any snag — never hold the button against a load
Only the skipper touches the button; the crew hoist by hand with the handle
Use the button only for the last metre; the first part is hoisted by hand
questions.why: An electric winch does not feel a snag: a batten in a lazyjack or a jammed slide tears before the motor notices.

questions.q: The technician hands you the furling line to roll the genoa in. It takes everything you have, though there is no wrap aloft. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa furler
lines: Sail fully out, sheet eased, F2
Rolls in by hand: barely, with both hands
Masthead by binoculars: no halyard wrap

options: Lead the line to the electric winch and roll it in on the button
Spray the drum and swivel with lubricant yourself and sign
Ask the base to check the drum and swivel bearings now — in F2 a furler rolls in by hand
Note 'stiff furler' and furl the genoa only in light winds this week
questions.why: A furler that needs the winch at the pontoon will not furl at all at 25 kn; bearings are the base's job and no amount of spray fixes them.

questions.q: The genoa is out in F2 and looks like this. The form says it is fine. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa in F2
lines: Cloth stiff and crackly, UV strip faded

options: Nothing — the age of the cloth is not something the check-in form records
Demand a new genoa before you sign; the contract promises sails in good condition
Ask for a lower deposit for the week since the sail is likely to blow out
Photograph luff and leech, write 'genoa: aged, stretched' on the form, and plan to reef it early
questions.why: An old sail is not damage the base repairs, but its state goes on the form so a blow-out this week is not charged as new; sail it conservatively.

questions.q: Main hoisted, you walk the leech from the cockpit and spot this. The technician points at the locker. What do you do?

figure.title: Mainsail hoisted
lines: Tear 10 cm at the leech, above batten 3 pocket
Technician: 'sail tape is in the locker'

options: The tear sewn or patched by the base's sailmaker before departure, and written on the form
Nothing — a tear that small is within normal wear for a charter sail
Note it and keep reef 2 in all week so that part of the leech stays rolled away
Tape it on both sides yourself; a tear this size does not grow in the Ionian
questions.why: A tear at the leech grows with every flog; sail tape is a sea-going stopgap, and a tear you accept unrepaired is yours at check-out.

questions.q: Hoisting the main at the pontoon, your crew member on the winch feels it stop and asks whether to keep winching. You look up and see this. What do you say?

figure.note: Hoist stops at two-thirds · lazyjack across the batten pocket

options: Drop the main, pull all the battens out, hoist it and refit them aloft
Stop — ease a little so the batten drops clear of the lazyjack, then hoist again by hand
Let the lazyjacks go altogether; they only get in the way of the hoist
Keep winching — the batten end pops through once the halyard is tight
questions.why: A batten end winched against a lazyjack tears the pocket; slack the lazyjacks forward or head to wind, and hoist with eyes aloft.

questions.q: The 36 ft boat is simpler than your last charter. You read its sail handling on the form. What does this change for Thursday evening, coming into the bay?

figure.title: 36 ft — mainsail
lines: Slab reefing at the mast, no lazyjacks, no stackpack
Halyard and reef lines at the mast

options: Drop the main in the bay once the anchor is down; the sail flakes itself
Keep the main up until the anchor is set; it steadies the boat in the bay
Someone clipped on at the mast to flake the main onto the boom as it drops, head to wind under engine, before the bay
Nothing — the main drops onto the boom and into the cover like a stackpack
questions.why: Without lazyjacks the dropped main falls over the deck and the helm's view: plan the drop outside, with a crew member at the mast.

questions.q: You unclip the main halyard from the headboard to look at it. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Main halyard shackle
lines: Pin held by a cable tie

options: Nothing — the headboard cars hold the sail if the shackle lets go
A second cable tie through the pin and a line on the form
The halyard tied to the headboard with a bowline instead of the shackle
The shackle replaced before you sign — one that opens drops the main and sends the halyard aloft
questions.why: A halyard shackle carries the whole luff load: a stripped pin held by plastic is a failure waiting for a gust, and a lost halyard ends the week.

questions.q: You take the binoculars to the masthead before the main goes up and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Masthead by binoculars
lines: Main halyard and topping lift crossed twice above the sheaves
Main stops 1 m short of full hoist
Spare halyard: wrapped round the forestay

options: The base sends someone up the mast to clear it now — a crossed halyard is a mast job
Go up in the bosun's chair yourself with the technician on the winch
Hoist the main anyway: the last metre comes with the halyard winched hard
Tie the spare halyard off at the bow and live with the crossed lines
questions.why: Halyards crossed above the sheaves chafe through each other and stop the hoist short; it is cleared from aloft, by the base, before you leave.

questions.q: Main sheeted in at the pontoon, you load the mainsheet by hand and the tail creeps through the cleat. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Sheet loaded by hand · tail creeps 10 cm, then holds

options: A figure-of-eight in the tail behind the cleat so it cannot run out
The cam cleat replaced before you sign — a mainsheet that will not hold cannot be trusted on a gybe
Lead the mainsheet to the genoa winch instead for the week
A note on the form; it only slips above twenty knots anyway
questions.why: The mainsheet must hold on its own cleat under full load; worn cam teeth let the boom out in a gust, with crew in the way.

questions.q: Your crew ask what the fitting under the boom is and whether a preventer is still needed. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Under the boom
lines: Boom brake: line through the drum, led to both toe rails
Control tail: cam cleat at the cockpit

options: A boom brake: it locks the boom like a preventer, so no preventer is needed
A second vang: pull it on hard upwind and leave it slack on a run
A boom brake: set its line before a downwind leg so the boom crosses slowly — it slows a gybe, it does not stop one
A dinghy-hoist fitting; nothing to do with the boom under sail
questions.why: A brake lets the boom come across under friction on a gybe; it never pins the boom, so an accidental gybe still happens, only slower.

questions.q: The gennaker is on the list. You find this in the forepeak. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Inventory — gennaker
lines: Gennaker with sock: 1 — found in bag
Tack line, gennaker halyard: on the list, not found
Tack fitting: ring on the bow roller

options: The sock taken off; a gennaker without a sock is simpler for a crew
Nothing — a gennaker is checked by flying it on the first downwind leg
The sail pulled out of the bag on the pontoon and looked over for tears
The gennaker hoisted in its sock at the pontoon, sock raised a metre and lowered, tack line and halyard found
questions.why: The sock's uphaul, the tack line and a dedicated halyard are what let a crew get the sail down; find and try them where help is at hand.

questions.q: With the main up you look along the leech at spreader height and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Mainsail — leech
lines: Port spreader patch: worn through, cloth under it thin

options: The worn patches replaced now — on a run the leech lies on the spreader and the cloth under goes next
Nothing — patches are there to be worn through; that is their job
The spreader tips taped instead; then the sail needs no patches
Sail tape over the patches, and a note on the form
questions.why: Spreader patches are sacrificial, but once through the sail itself chafes; a sailmaker's patch at the base is an hour, a torn leech is a week.

questions.q: Monday, 09:30, leaving the bay. Your crew member on the helm asks how you want the boat for the hoist. What do you say?

figure.title: Monday — leaving the bay
lines: Wind N 10 kn, bay open to the south
Crew: two adults, both new to it

options: Sail out on the genoa and hoist the main outside, running downwind
Motor clear of the moorings, head to wind at slow ahead, autopilot in compass mode, and hoist with eyes aloft
Autopilot in wind mode so it follows every shift while you hoist
Hoist at anchor among the moored boats; the bow lies to the wind by itself
questions.why: Head to wind the slides run free and the battens clear the lazyjacks; the autopilot holds the heading while two of you work the halyard.

questions.q: You ask for the main dropped into the lazy bag as a test and watch it come down. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Main drop — pontoon
lines: Halyard let go: sail stops at batten 2
Technician: 'pull the luff, it always wants a hand'

options: Silicone spray on the track yourself before you sign
A note 'sticky slides' and a crew member at the mast for every drop
The track cleaned and the bent slide replaced so the main drops on its own — at sea nobody should be hauling it down
Nothing — a main always needs a hand on the luff to come down
questions.why: A main that will not fall on its own cannot be dropped fast in a squall; a dry track and a bent slide are the base's fix, before departure.

questions.q: Reef 1 went in fine. You try reef 2 at the pontoon and get this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Reef 2 — pontoon
lines: Reef 2 line: 1 m tail, runs out before the clew cringle is down

options: Take the line out and keep it as a spare sheet; reef 2 is for storms
Tie an extension onto the tail with a sheet bend and note it
Accept it — reef 1 and a rolled genoa is reefed enough for F6
The reef 2 line re-led or replaced long enough to pull the reef in from the cockpit, before you sign
questions.why: Reef 2 is the reef you need when it is already too rough to improvise; a line that runs out before the cringle is down is no reef at all.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician says there are no genoa sheets to run — the jib tacks itself. What do you check?

figure.title: Catamaran foresail
lines: Self-tacking jib, curved track ahead of the mast
One sheet, to the mast winch
Overlapping genoa: on the list, in the forepeak

options: The car runs the whole track with its end stops in, and the single sheet pulls through its blocks to the winch
Nothing — a self-tacker has no sheets, cars or leads to go wrong
That the car is lashed in the middle of the track so it cannot move
That the overlapping genoa from the forepeak is bent on instead; it is faster
questions.why: A self-tacking jib still has one sheet, one car and two end stops; a car that leaves the track or a sheet that jams tacks nothing.

questions.q: Thursday, 14:00, 22 kn on a beam reach. Your crew member says they will put the furling line on the winch. What do you say?

figure.title: Thursday — 22 kn
lines: Sheet: cleated hard on the winch
Crew: 'I'll put the line on the winch'

options: Luff head to wind and let the sail flog while the line is hauled
Bear away to blanket the genoa behind the main, ease the sheet but keep a little on it, and haul the line by hand
Drop the genoa on deck instead; a furler is not meant for 22 knots
Winch it in on the beam reach with the sheet cleated — the winch has the power
questions.why: Blanketed and with light sheet tension the sail rolls tight by hand; winched against a cleated sheet, the line or the drum goes first.

questions.q: Monday, 08:00, in a bay. The base's forecast is on your phone; your crew say you will reef when it gets strong. What do you do?

figure.title: Monday — in the bay
lines: Base forecast: NW 18–22 kn by noon
Contract: reef 1 at 18 kn, reef 2 at 25 kn

options: Stay at anchor until the base calls to say the wind has dropped
Leave the main in the bag and motor all day; the contract numbers are for sailing
Put reef 1 in at the hoist, still at anchor, and shake it out later if the wind never comes
Hoist full and reef when the first gust arrives; reefing early wastes a nice morning
questions.why: A reef is put in at the hoist, in the flat water, when the forecast says it will be needed; shaking one out is easy, reefing late is not.

questions.q: You watch the technician furl the genoa away at the end of the check and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Genoa furled
lines: UV strip: inside the roll, white cloth outside
Furling line: full on the drum

options: A cover made to fit over the furled genoa for the week
The strip pulled out and over the roll by hand without unrolling
Nothing — the strip only matters while the sail is stored ashore
The sail unrolled and furled the other way so the UV strip is outside — and ask which way the drum turns
questions.why: The UV strip protects the roll only on the outside; furled the wrong way the sail cooks all week and the sheets wrap in the wrong direction.

questions.q: Thursday, 16:00, in harbour 25 miles from the base. The base's forecast arrives. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday — base forecast
lines: Friday from 10:00: NW F6, gusts F7
Tonight and early morning: NW 10–14 kn
Base: 25 M, about 5 h · boat due Friday 17:00

options: Leave now or at first light, reefed, and tell the base your plan — Friday at 10:00 would be above the limit
Stay put and let the base fetch the boat; the limit means you may not sail
Leave Friday at 06:00 under full sail to be fast ahead of the wind
Stay and leave Friday at 10:00 as planned; F6 is within the contract limit
questions.why: The limit is read against the forecast for the passage: sailing into a forecast F6–7 breaks the contract, so the passage moves to before it.

questions.q: Tuesday, 15 kn, furling the main in. The line goes solid at halfway and your crew member on the electric winch says 'one more push'. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday — furling the main
lines: Furling line solid at half; cloth bunched at the slot
Boom: below the mark on the topping lift
Crew on the electric winch: 'one more push'

options: Hold the button — the winch has the power to pull the bunch through the slot
Stop the winch, unroll a turn to clear the bunch, boom to its mark, then furl again by hand with outhaul tension
Drop the boom further so the sail hangs slack and pulls itself into the mast
Leave the main half furled, sheet it in hard and motor to the bay
questions.why: A bunch in the slot only gets tighter under power; back off a turn and feed the roll in square, the way it was shown at the pontoon.

questions.q: Wednesday, 17:00, at anchor. Your crew admit the gennaker tore in a broach and suggest bagging it quietly. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday — at anchor
lines: Gennaker: 2 m tear along the foot after a broach
Contract: damage reported at once; gennaker outside the waiver

options: Bag it and say nothing; the inventory counts bags, not the state of the sail
Report it on Friday at check-out, when the technician asks about the sails
Call the base today, photograph it, and have it noted — hiding it costs more at check-out than the repair
Patch it with sail tape and fly it again so the tear looks like old wear
questions.why: The contract says damage is reported at once; a tear found by the base after a cover-up loses you the waiver's goodwill and the whole deposit.

questions.q: Kos, Saturday. Trying reef 2 you find this, and the base's forecast is on the board. The technician shrugs. What do you do?

figure.title: Reef 2 cringle
lines: Clew cringle reef 2: ring torn half out of the leech

options: Tie a strop through the cloth round the boom as a makeshift reef 2 and sign
Accept it with a note on the form; reef 1 and a scrap of genoa will do for F6
Postpone departure to Monday and let the base decide what to do then
A sailmaker's repair before departure or another boat — with a Meltemi forecast reef 2 is the reef you will use
questions.why: A torn cringle cannot take a reef load; in the Dodecanese in a Meltemi week you will sail on reef 2 most days, so it is fixed or the boat is not fit.

questions.q: The boat has in-mast furling and it is blowing F4 at the pontoon. The technician will not unfurl the main today. What do you do?

figure.title: Saturday — pontoon
lines: In-mast main, F4 across the pontoon
Technician: 'not in this wind, it's fine'

options: Have it rolled out a metre and back to prove it runs, and write 'main not fully seen at check-in' on the form
Sign — an in-mast main cannot be checked at a pontoon in any case
Unfurl it yourself at the first anchorage and photograph any fault for the base
Insist on the whole main out in F4 at the pontoon; it is your right
questions.why: You sign for what you were shown: a short test proves the furler turns, and the note means a fault found on Sunday is not your fault.

questions.q: Thursday, 13:00, Meltemi 25 kn. Reef 2 is in and the genoa is half rolled; your crew say it is fine. You look forward and see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday — 25 kn
lines: Sheet cars: at the aft end of the track

options: Unroll the genoa fully so the leech stops flogging, and ease the main
Move the cars forward for the smaller sail and roll a little more — a flogging half genoa wears itself out in an hour
Leave it — with reef 2 in, the main does the work and the genoa hardly matters
Roll the genoa away and motor-sail on the main alone to stay within the limit
questions.why: A reefed genoa needs its lead moved forward or the leech flogs; a flogging leech shreds the UV strip and stitching — damage you pay for.

questions.q: The technician lifts the companionway steps and lets you pull the dipstick and open the header tank yourself. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Engine bay, before starting
lines: Dipstick: at the top mark, milky grey
Belt: firm, a little black dust

options: A litre of coolant to top up yourself, with the oil colour noted on the form
Nothing — oil goes grey after a season of short runs in the marina
The base to find why the oil is milky and to fill the coolant before you leave
To run the engine hot for ten minutes and look at the dipstick again
questions.why: Milky oil is water in the oil — a heat exchanger or gasket fault; the base fixes it, not you at sea.

questions.q: You look round the engine with a torch while the technician waits. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Engine bay — hoses and tray
lines: Coolant stain under one hose clip
Raw-water seacock: under the sole, open
Tray: a film of old oil

options: Nothing — a stain and a film of oil are normal on a charter engine
A rag over the tray so the oil does not reach the bilge pump
The seacock closed while in port and opened before each start
The clip tightened and the tray wiped dry, so a new leak will show this week
questions.why: Small leaks are noted and fixed at the base; a dry tray is how you spot a new one on day three.

questions.q: The technician has already filled in the engine hours on the check-in form. You look at the panel. What do you do?
options: Have the form corrected to the panel reading and photograph the panel
Sign the form — the base counts hours from its own log
Write both numbers on the form and let the base manager choose
Note the difference and raise it at check-out if hours are charged
questions.why: Engine hours on the form are what you are charged against at check-out; write what the panel shows, with a photo.

questions.q: The technician hands you the key: 'Start it yourself.' In what order do you do it?
options: Lever a little ahead so it does not stall, key on, crank at once
Lever in neutral, key on, wait for the glow-plug light to go out, then crank
Key on and crank straight away — a warm Greek engine needs no preheat
Throttle wide open in neutral, crank until it fires, then back off
questions.why: Neutral, preheat, crank: a diesel starts in neutral and the glow plugs need their seconds, even in summer.

questions.q: The engine has started under the technician's eye and you watch the panel. What do you do?
options: Rev it to 1,500 so the pressure builds faster and the buzzer stops
Let it idle five minutes; the buzzer stops once the oil is warm
Pull the stop handle now — the alarm should stop within seconds as oil pressure rises
Turn the key off and on again to reset the alarm and carry on
questions.why: The oil alarm sounds until pressure builds — a second or two; longer than that, stop the engine before it damages itself.

questions.q: The engine is running at the pontoon. You step aft and look at the exhaust outlet: a puff of smoke, no water. The technician says 'give it a minute'. What do you do?
options: Note 'no exhaust water' on the form and check again at the fuel quay
Give it the minute — raw water takes time to come up through the strainer
Rev it to 2,000 for a moment so the pump pulls the water through
Have the engine stopped now and the seacock, strainer and impeller checked before it restarts
questions.why: No water at the exhaust means no cooling: a closed seacock, a blocked strainer or a dead impeller — stop first, find out second.

questions.q: The technician reads the spares list off the inventory. What do you ask for before departure?
options: A spare impeller and the tools to fit it, and where the puller is kept
A second belt — belts go more often than impellers in the heat
A bottle of coolant and a funnel for the header tank
Nothing — the base's mechanic comes out if anything fails
questions.why: The impeller is the usual cause of overheating; without a spare aboard a failure ends the day's sailing where you are.

questions.q: The contract says the boat is handed over with a full tank. What do you do?
options: Fill it yourself on the first day and keep the receipt for the base
Ask to see it dipped or topped up at the fuel quay, and write the gauge reading on the form
Sign for full and put in a claim at check-out if it runs short
Accept his word — gauges on charter boats are never trusted anyway
questions.why: 'Full on handover, full on return' only works if you see it full: a dip, a sight glass or a visit to the fuel quay.

questions.q: Your plan for the week is about 6 hours of motoring a day for six days. What do you decide at the briefing?
options: Nothing — a 160-litre tank is more than a week of motoring on a 45-footer
Refuel only when the gauge first shows a quarter, as on a car
Plan a fuel stop around midweek — 36 hours is about 144 litres of a 160-litre tank
Run the tank down and fill it once on the way back on the last day
questions.why: 36 h × 4 L/h = 144 L: the week's plan uses the whole tank minus reserve, and the gauge cannot be trusted to warn you.

questions.q: The technician shows you the deck fillers on the side deck. What do you do?
options: Let the fuel attendant find the right one; it is his job at the quay
Remember 'fuel is port' — the technician knows his boats
Ask for both caps to be changed to marked ones before departure
Open the port one and smell it, mark it with tape and show the crew which is which
questions.why: Diesel in the water tank ruins the week's water and the tank; mark the fuel filler and brief the crew before anyone fills anything.

questions.q: You look at the primary filter with a torch while the technician talks you through the fuel shut-off. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Fuel system
lines: Bowl: dark layer at the bottom
Fuel shut-off: on the tank, open

options: The bowl drained and the element changed now, and the change written on the form
A spare element so you can change it yourself if the engine falters
Nothing — a little sediment in the bowl is normal after a season
The shut-off closed overnight to keep water out of the lines
questions.why: The dark layer is water or sludge; it reaches the injectors in the first rough sea — the base deals with it at the pontoon.

questions.q: At the pontoon with the lines on, the technician clicks the lever ahead: the revs rise, the boat hardly pulls and something clunks under the stern. What do you ask him to do?
options: Sign for it — the gear works, the boat is just held by the lines
Go to neutral, give a burst astern to open the folding propeller, then try ahead again
Pull the button on the lever hub — it is in throttle-only mode and needs the gear in
Rev harder in ahead until the clunking stops and the lines come tight
questions.why: A folding prop's blades can stick half-open from the marina; astern opens them. Test ahead and astern with the lines on, before you leave.

questions.q: After ten minutes running at the pontoon the panel looks like this. The technician says 'the light always does that'. What do you do?
options: Accept it — a 12.1 reading with the engine running is a healthy battery
Switch to the house bank and let the charger pick it up on shore power
Ask for the belt and alternator checked before you leave — it is not charging
Idle the engine an hour at tick-over tonight and see if the light goes out
questions.why: A battery light with the engine running means no charge: a slipping belt or a dead alternator. With it, the week ends on day two.

questions.q: The technician runs the engine in gear against the lines while you look under the aft cabin bunk. What do you say?

figure.title: Shaft and gearbox
lines: Engine running: a steady trickle at the seal
Bilge: 2 cm of water, pump cycling
Gearbox oil: at the mark, clear

options: Ask for the bilge pump set to automatic and sail; the seal is doing its job
Tighten the seal's collar a quarter turn yourself until the trickle stops
A few drips a minute are normal on a stern gland — write 'OK' on the form
A dripless seal should be dry — ask the base to look at it and amend the form before you sign
questions.why: A packed gland drips a little; a dripless seal does not. A trickle plus a cycling pump is a fault for the base to fix at the pontoon.

questions.q: The boat is afloat; the technician ticks the underwater lines from memory and asks you to sign. What do you write?
options: 'Not seen' against each underwater line, and sign only for what you were shown
Nothing extra — you will check it on the first swim and amend then
'OK' — the base lifted the boat in the spring and knows the anode
'Checked by base' so the responsibility stays with them
questions.why: You sign for what you saw. An anode or a prop you did not see is 'not seen' on the form, or it is yours at check-out.

questions.q: The technician closes the port engine hatch and moves on to the electrics. What do you ask?

figure.title: 42 ft catamaran — engines
lines: Stops: pull handle at each panel

options: Whether the two hour counters can be reset to match for the form
To see the starboard engine too — it has its own strainer, filter, stop and start battery
Nothing — twin engines are the same; one is a spare for the other
Which engine to run alone on passage to keep the hours even
questions.why: Two engines means two of everything: each is checked, each hours reading goes on the form, and each stop is found before you leave.

questions.q: The technician points at the bow-thruster switch at the helm: 'Test it yourself.' How do you test it at the pontoon?
options: Leave the test until you are clear of the pontoon with room to move
Take his word for it — a thruster is either fine or the base knows
Switch it on, a short burst each way with the lines on, watch the bow wash, then switch it off
Run it a full minute each way so you know the battery can take it
questions.why: Short bursts: a thruster overheats in a minute of running. Its own breaker and battery are shown to you at the same time.

questions.q: You read the clause before signing. Your plan has two long motoring days. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract, clause 11 — engine
lines: Engine use: max 4 h per day

options: Sign and keep your own log of hours to argue from at check-out
Ask for the clause to be struck out since a sailing yacht is not a motorboat
Sign as it is — most days you will sail, so the two long days are covered
Ask the base manager whether the 4 hours is per day or averaged over the week, and get the answer on the form
questions.why: A clause means what the base says it means — in writing, before you sign, not at check-out when the excess is on the bill.

questions.q: The engine has been running a quarter of an hour at the pontoon. The technician says the sender has been like that all season. Do you accept the boat?
options: Not until the base proves the oil pressure, replaces the sender or gauge, and writes it on the form
Yes — the base knows its engine; note 'oil alarm, faulty sender' on the form
Yes, if he pulls the buzzer fuse so the crew are not alarmed at sea
Yes, with a discount on the charter price written into the contract
questions.why: An oil alarm you cannot tell from a real one is no alarm: you would not know at sea. Not a boat to sign for.

questions.q: Day three, motoring towards the harbour, the panel changes to this. What do you do?

lines: Buzzer sounding; steam at the exhaust

options: Sail the last miles and restart the engine only for the mooring
Throttle back, neutral, stop; let it cool, then check strainer, impeller and belt before restarting
Slow to tick-over and carry on; the temperature will fall at low revs
Keep going at 2,200 — the engine will last the last two miles to the harbour
questions.why: Overheat: stop before it seizes. Sail or anchor, find the cause (strainer, impeller, belt), call the base if it is beyond you.

questions.q: Key on, not yet cranked: the panel lights up and the buzzer sounds. Your crew member at the chart table says 'it's broken before we start'. What do you tell them?
options: Hold the key in start until the lamps go out; the buzzer is the glow-plug timer
Turn the key off — an oil alarm before starting means the sump is empty
This is normal — the lamps and buzzer prove themselves on key-on and go out seconds after the engine fires
Press the stop button to silence it, then crank; the buzzer is the stop circuit
questions.why: On key-on the oil and charge lamps and the buzzer come on and stay on until the engine runs and pressure builds — a lamp test, not a fault.

questions.q: The technician lifts the aft-cabin bunk and shows the whole crew a lever on the tank top. Your crew ask why everyone has to see it. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Fuel shut-off
lines: Lever valve on the tank top, aft cabin
Open: handle in line with the pipe

options: It is closed every night at anchor so the lines stay full and the engine starts clean
It is the base mechanic's valve for changing the filter; the crew never touch it
It is closed before refuelling so the tank cannot overflow into the engine bay
It is the fuel shut-off: in an engine fire you stop the engine, close it, then open the extinguisher port
questions.why: The fuel shut-off starves a fire of fuel; everyone who may be nearest to it should know where it is and which way is closed.

questions.q: A 36 ft boat with a shaft and a packed stuffing box. The technician points at a brass cup on the bulkhead: 'a turn a day'. What is the cup for?

figure.title: Shaft seal — 36 ft
lines: Remote greaser cup on the bulkhead
Drips with shaft turning: 1–2 a minute
Shaft after 10 min in gear: cool

options: Greasing the packing: half a turn each day of motoring; a drip or two a minute with the shaft turning is right
Tightening the gland: screw it in until the dripping stops completely
Sealing the shaft for the week: fill it once at the base and forget it
A spare grease reserve for the winches; it has nothing to do with the shaft
questions.why: A packed gland is kept greased from the remote greaser and is meant to drip a little when turning; tightened dry, it overheats and scores the shaft.

questions.q: Monday, 07:30, cold start in the bay: white smoke from the exhaust for the first minute, then it clears and the water flows. Your crew want to stop the engine. What do you say?
options: Carry on but at full throttle, to burn the smoke off faster
Carry on — a cold diesel smokes white for a minute; white smoke that stays with a rising temperature is the one to stop for
Stop it and bleed the fuel system; white smoke is air in the lines
Stop it — white smoke is steam, the engine is already overheating
questions.why: White smoke on a cold start is unburnt fuel and clears as it warms; persistent white smoke with a hot engine or no water is steam — stop.

questions.q: The technician shows you the raw-water seacock under the sole and says 'leave it open'. When, during the week, do you close it?

figure.title: Raw-water seacock
lines: Under the sole, forward of the strainer
Handle in line with the pipe: open

options: Never — the base opened it in spring and closes it at the end of the season
Every evening at anchor, so the engine bay stays dry overnight
Before opening the strainer to clear it, and whenever the boat is left unattended for long
Before every start, and open it once the exhaust water is flowing
questions.why: A raw-water seacock is closed to work on the strainer and when leaving the boat; closed at start, the impeller runs dry in seconds.

questions.q: The panel has a key and a red button beside it; there is no pull handle at the companionway. Your crew ask how the engine is stopped. What do you tell them?
options: Lever to neutral and key off; the red button is only for emergencies
Close the raw-water seacock and wait; the engine stops on temperature
Turn the key to off — it cuts the fuel pump, as on a petrol engine
Hold the red button until the engine dies, then turn the key off — the key alone does not stop a diesel
questions.why: A diesel is stopped by cutting its fuel — the stop button or pull handle; the key off afterwards saves the battery and the alarm.

questions.q: Monday, leaving the bay, your crew on the stern calls that the exhaust is blowing black smoke each time the throttle goes past 2,500. What do you do?

figure.title: Monday, 10:00, leaving the bay
lines: Boat sat in the marina two weeks before you

options: Ease back to 2,200 and have someone look at the prop at the next stop — black smoke at high revs is an overloaded engine
Stop the engine at once and sail — black smoke is a fire in the exhaust hose
Keep it at 2,800 for ten minutes — black smoke clears the injectors on a charter engine
Change the fuel filter now — black smoke is water in the diesel
questions.why: Black smoke is unburnt fuel from overload: a fouled prop, a carboned elbow or too much throttle; drop the revs and find the load.

questions.q: Monday, 08:00, in a bay, your daily engine check. What do you do?

figure.title: Daily check, Monday 08:00
lines: Dipstick: just below the lower mark
Yesterday: 6 h motoring, blue haze at the exhaust
Oil aboard: 1 L from the base

options: Carry on — oil between the marks is fine, and the base tops it up at check-out
Top up to the upper mark, write the litre in the log and tell the base — an engine using that much oil is theirs to look at
Fill to the top of the dipstick tube so it lasts the rest of the week
Add the litre and say nothing — every charter engine uses a little oil
questions.why: A litre in six hours with a blue haze is an engine burning oil; top up to the mark, never above, and tell the base before it gets worse.

questions.q: Monday, 09:00, in a bay: you turn the key and the panel stays dark. What do you check first?

figure.title: Monday, 09:00, in the bay
lines: Key ON: panel dark, no buzzer
Last night: switches 'all off' before bed

options: Nothing — call the base: a dark panel is a failed control box
The primary fuel filter bowl and the fuel shut-off under the bunk
The engine battery switch — someone turned it off last night; then the parallel switch if the starter bank is flat
The stop handle and the neutral position of the lever
questions.why: No lamps at key-on means no power to the panel: the engine battery switch or a flat starter bank, before anything to do with fuel.
questions.ref: Engine will not start: battery switch

questions.q: Tuesday, 08:30, leaving a town quay: the engine cranks strongly but does not fire. Where do you look first?

figure.title: Tuesday, 08:30, at the town quay
lines: Key ON: lamps and buzzer normal
Last night: stopped with the pull handle

options: The raw-water seacock — close it and crank again so the engine does not flood
The glow plugs — crank for a full minute, a cold diesel needs it
The air in the fuel lines — bleed it at the filter before cranking again
The stop handle — it was pulled last night and is still out, so the engine is cranking with no fuel
questions.why: A strong crank with no fire after an evening stop is almost always the stop handle left out; push it fully home before anything else.
questions.ref: Engine will not start: stop handle

questions.q: Wednesday at the fuel quay. The attendant hands your crew the nozzle. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Fuel quay, Wednesday
lines: Fuel and water fillers 30 cm apart
Your tape mark on the fuel cap

options: Hold it in the filler you marked, ask for a slow flow and stop at the first gurgle — the overflow goes into the sea
Fill the jerrycans first and pour them into the tank below decks later
Fill until diesel shows at the deck filler, so you know the tank is full
Let the attendant fill it to the brim — he knows the tanks of charter boats
questions.why: Charter tanks vent to the deck or over the side: fill slowly, listen for the gurgle, and stop — a diesel spill at a quay is a fine and a mess.

questions.q: You find this in the lazarette, next to the engine bay. What do you ask the base?

figure.title: Lazarette
lines: Engine-bay vent hose runs through here

options: Nothing — diesel and petrol are both fuels and both cans are sealed
Where the petrol goes on deck — its vapour sinks into the bilge and a diesel engine bay has no blower; lash the diesel can
To empty the petrol into the dinghy tank so there is no can aboard at all
To move the petrol to a cabin locker, away from the engine's heat
questions.why: Petrol vapour is heavier than air and collects in the bilge next to a hot engine; it lives on deck in a vented locker, never below.

questions.q: Monday, 19:00, at anchor, the batteries are low. Your crew suggests leaving the engine ticking over until bedtime. What do you do?
options: Leave it at tick-over till bedtime — a slow charge is what the battery needs
Switch everything off instead — a charter engine must not run at anchor
Run it at about 1,500 rpm for an hour — a diesel idled for hours glazes its bores and charges little
Put it in gear at idle so the engine pulls against the anchor and works
questions.why: A diesel is charged under some load and revs, not at idle for hours; an hour at 1,500 does more than four at 800 and keeps the engine healthy.

questions.q: 42 ft catamaran. The technician shows the generator: 'run it for the batteries and the air-con'. What do you check with him before you sign?

figure.title: Generator
lines: Own seacock and strainer: under the saloon sole
Exhaust: port quarter, at the waterline

options: That it starts from the engine battery, so it can never go flat
Only its hours — a generator has no cooling of its own to check
Nothing — it is the base's machine; it charges like the engines do
Its own seacock and strainer, water at its exhaust when running, its hours on the form and the base's rule on when it may run
questions.why: A generator is a third engine: raw water, exhaust water, hours and a stop of its own — and marinas forbid it at night.

questions.q: Monday, an hour out. Your crew at the helm says the engine must be down on power. What do you tell them?

lines: Plotter: SOG 4.1 kn, 15 kn wind on the nose

options: Nothing is wrong yet: wind and chop take two knots; the test is speed at 2,200 in flat water, and a drop there means a fouled prop
Stop and check the impeller — low speed at the right revs is a cooling fault
Push to 2,800 — the base promised six knots at 2,200, so the engine is faulty
Call the base — the tachometer is misreading and needs replacing
questions.why: SOG on the plotter is speed through water plus wind, chop and current; rpm-to-speed in flat water is the baseline you note on day one.

questions.q: The technician points at the rubber around the saildrive leg: 'diaphragm changed, nothing to see'. What do you do?

figure.title: Saildrive, from the engine bay
lines: Well around the leg: damp, salt crust

options: Ask for a new diaphragm — seven years is the limit and this one is due
Ask why the well is damp and whether there is an ingress alarm; photograph it and have it written on the form
Ask to close the saildrive seacock at night so the well stays dry
Nothing — salt in the well is condensation off the cold leg
questions.why: A damp saildrive well means a seal weeping; it is the base's answer, in writing, before you sign — not your discovery on Thursday.

questions.q: The technician skips the gearbox: 'it's sealed, nothing to check'. What do you do?

figure.title: Gearbox
lines: Dipstick under a hose, on the gearbox top
Oil on the tray below: none

options: Take his word — a charter gearbox is never opened between services
Ask for a litre of gearbox oil aboard in case it runs low this week
Pull its dipstick yourself — level at the mark, oil clear not milky — and write the reading on the form
Run the engine in gear and listen — a quiet gearbox has oil in it
questions.why: A gearbox has a dipstick like the engine; milky oil there means water from the oil cooler, and a low level means a leaking seal.

questions.q: You press the alternator belt with your thumb while the technician waits. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Belt
lines: Press midway: about 20 mm of give
Black dust on the alternator and the tray

options: Belt dressing sprayed on it so it grips until the first service
Nothing — a little dust is normal and the spare belt is in the locker
'Belt loose' on the form; you will tighten it yourself on Monday
The belt tensioned or changed now and the dust wiped off — a slipping belt stops the charging and the coolant pump
questions.why: About 10 mm of give is right; 20 mm and black dust is a belt slipping on polished pulleys — the base's job at the pontoon.

questions.q: The single lever on this 36 ft boat has no click at neutral, and the technician starts the engine with it 'about in the middle'. What do you do?

figure.title: Throttle / gear lever
lines: Engine started with the lever a little ahead

options: Have the cable adjusted until neutral clicks and the engine starts only there — you must find neutral by feel at a quay
Start it in ahead with the lines on; it is quicker to leave the pontoon
Accept it — a starter interlock is an option on newer engines only
Mark neutral with tape and leave it — cables stretch on every boat
questions.why: A neutral detent and a neutral-start interlock are safety: no engine starting in gear and no hunting for neutral while mooring.

questions.q: Monday, 17:00, mooring stern-to at a town quay in a crosswind. Your crew holds the thruster to port for 30 seconds and it stops dead. What do you do?

figure.title: Town quay, Monday 17:00
lines: Thruster held 30 s to port, then dead
Breaker: forward cabin, under the bunk

options: Run the engine at 2,000 for five minutes to charge the thruster battery, then try
Finish with the engine and lines; it is the thermal cut-out — rest it ten minutes, reset its breaker, and use short bursts from now on
Abort and anchor off — the thruster fuse has blown and the base must replace it
Hold the joystick longer — the motor needs to warm up before it bites
questions.why: A bow thruster is rated for seconds, not half a minute: the thermal cut-out trips, and it resets after cooling and the breaker.

questions.q: Thursday, 08:30, in a bay. Your crew has cranked the engine six times without a fire. What do you do before anyone tries again?

figure.title: Thursday 08:30, in the bay
lines: Six cranks of 15 s: no fire
Water spurts from the exhaust on each crank

options: Pull the stop and crank — it blows the water out of the exhaust
Keep cranking — raw water only flows once the engine is running
Close the raw-water seacock, then find the cause — every crank pumps water into the silencer and towards the engine
Open the seacock fully so the engine does not overheat when it fires
questions.why: The raw-water pump works on every crank; after a few, the water-lock fills and the next crank can draw water into a cylinder.
questions.ref: Engine will not start: cranking and raw water

questions.q: Your crew ask why a hose from the engine loops up to the deckhead and back down. What do you tell them?
options: It is where the coolant is filled on this engine, above the header tank
It is a spare hose the base left; it does nothing and can be ignored
It is the exhaust bypass: you open it if the elbow blocks at sea
It is the anti-siphon loop: it stops seawater siphoning into the engine when it is stopped, and the valve on top must stay clear of salt
questions.why: A raw-water outlet below the waterline needs a siphon break; a blocked vent valve lets water fill the exhaust and reach the engine.

questions.q: Wednesday, 14:00, F6 on the nose, 6 miles from harbour. The engine surges and dies, restarts, dies again after five minutes. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday 14:00, F6 on the nose
lines: Surges, dies; restarts, dies after 5 min

options: Sail or anchor, drain the bowl and fit a spare element, then call the base — a chop stirs the tank and blocks the filter
Motor on at low revs — the fuel will settle once the sea is flatter
Pour the bottle of biocide from the locker into the tank and restart
Bleed the injectors at sea — it is air in the lines, not dirt
questions.why: Surging and dying in a seaway is a filter blocking on a dirty tank (diesel bug); the spare element gets you in, the tank is the base's.

questions.q: Tuesday, catamaran, 8 miles to go: the port engine's buzzer sounds. What do you do?
options: Keep both running at low revs so the boat stays balanced for the mooring
Stop port and carry on at moderate revs on starboard, allowing for the pull; tell the base, and port stays off till the cause is found
Stop both and sail — a catamaran must not be motored on one engine
Swap engines every fifteen minutes so neither of them gets hot
questions.why: A cat's second engine is why it can carry on; an overheated engine is stopped, not nursed, and the base is told before the next start.

questions.q: Thursday evening, anchored 28 miles from the base; tomorrow is forecast calm. What do you decide about fuel?

lines: 22 h since check-in at ≈4 L/h; tank 160 L, reserve 20 L
Friday: 28 miles to the base, calm forecast

options: Sail the whole way and keep the engine for the marina only
Motor-sail at 1,500 rpm all the way and let the base refill at check-out
Plan on the lower figure: the gauge's 40 L leaves nothing over the 20 L reserve for a five-hour run — top up at the first fuel quay
Trust the hours: 72 L left is three times the run, and the gauge sticks
questions.why: Gauge and hours disagree: plan on the worse one. 28 miles at 6 kn is 5 h ≈ 20 L, and the reserve is not for planning.
questions.ref: Fuel: range later in the week

questions.q: You look at the exhaust elbow with a torch while the technician talks about the fridge. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Exhaust elbow
lines: Rust and white salt crust on the elbow
Black soot ring at the hose joint
Exhaust water at the pontoon: strong

options: A spare elbow in the spares locker, in case this one goes this week
Tape round the joint — it is only soot, and the water flow is good
Nothing — elbows rust from the outside; it is the exhaust water you watch
The elbow and the joint looked at and written on the form — soot at the joint is exhaust gas leaking into the boat
questions.why: A corroded elbow leaks exhaust (CO) into the bay and, when it fails, blocks the water: the base checks it, not you on Wednesday.

questions.q: Wednesday, 07:00. The catamaran lay stern to a swell all night. The port engine cranks half a turn and locks solid. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday 07:00, after a night of swell
lines: Port engine: half a turn, then solid
Port exhaust: low, at the waterline

options: Do not crank again — water has come up the exhaust into a cylinder; call the base, the engine must be drained before it turns
Crank longer with the stop pulled; it clears the water out through the exhaust
Pour a little oil into the air intake and crank it over gently
Run on starboard and keep trying port under way — the movement frees it
questions.why: A locked engine is a hydrolock: water does not compress, and forcing it bends a conrod. The base drains it; you do not.
questions.ref: Water in the engine after a swell

questions.q: You find the tool roll in the locker while the technician reads the inventory. What do you ask for before you sign?
options: Nothing — the base's mechanic comes out to any engine fault within the day
An impeller puller, spare hose clips and the engine manual, and the inventory list corrected to what is there
A note on the form that the tool roll was not checked
A full socket set, so any repair at sea can be done properly
questions.why: Spares are no use without the tools to fit them: a puller for the impeller, clips for a hose, the manual for the belt route and filters.

questions.q: Your crew member takes the helm to leave the pontoon: 'I'll give it 2,000 and click it into gear so we get away cleanly.' What do you tell them?
options: Fine, as long as the lines are off first and the bow is clear
Better 1,500 — 2,000 is too much for a marina, but the gear will take it
Gear at idle only: idle, click into gear, then throttle — shifting under revs wrecks the gearbox cone and the damper plate
Use the throttle-only button first, then drop into gear at those revs
questions.why: A marine gearbox is shifted at idle; a clunk under revs is a cone clutch or damper plate going, and that is your deposit.

questions.q: On the 36 ft boat the hour meter reads 1,000.0 and has not moved after ten minutes running. The technician says 'we go by fuel'. What do you do before you sign?
options: Sign — if the meter does not count, the base cannot charge for hours
Note the time you run the engine each day in the log and argue from that
Ask for the contract's hours clause struck out, as it cannot be checked
Have 'hour meter not working' written on the form and the base's way of charging engine use agreed in writing
questions.why: A meter that does not count is written on the form, with how the base will measure instead; otherwise it is their estimate at check-out.

questions.q: The technician opens the battery lockers of the catamaran and shows you this. What do you want to be sure of before he closes them?
options: That each engine has its own starter battery and the house bank is separate from both
That the house bank starts the engines when the starter batteries are low
That the port engine battery also runs the fridge, being the strongest one
That all five batteries are wired as one bank, for the most capacity
questions.why: Separate banks: a flat house bank after a night at anchor still leaves each engine its own battery to start.

questions.q: The technician shows you the battery switches and gives you this advice. How will you actually run them?

figure.title: Battery switches
lines: Technician: "just leave BOTH on all week"

options: BOTH on all week, as he says, so the fridge and the lights can draw on both banks together
ENGINE and HOUSE on at sea and at anchor; BOTH only for a flat-battery start; all off leaving the boat
HOUSE off under way so the alternator puts the whole charge into the engine battery
ENGINE off at anchor so the fridge and the lights cannot flatten the starter battery
questions.why: Both banks on keeps them separate; BOTH joins them, so a flat house bank takes the engine battery with it.

questions.q: First morning at anchor; you read the battery monitor before switching anything on. What state is the house bank in?
options: Overcharged — a bank at rest should read 12.0 V
Flat — anything under 13 V needs the engine now
Full — a rested bank at 12.7 V is near 100 %
Half — 12.7 V is midway between flat and full
questions.why: Rested, no load: 12.7 V full, 12.4 V about 75 %, 12.2 V half, 12.0 V or less flat.

questions.q: At check-in the technician points at the voltmeter and says the batteries are 'perfect'. What does this reading actually tell you?
options: That the batteries are new — an old bank never gets up to 13.8 V
That the bank is being overcharged and the charger must go off now
That the bank is full and will hold 13.8 V all night at anchor
Only that the charger is working — the state of the bank shows after a rest off the charger
questions.why: On charge the charger sets the volts (13.8 float, 14.4 bulk); the bank's own voltage is read after an hour at rest.

questions.q: You are going through the panel with the technician and see this. What do you do?
options: Note it on the form and ask the base to sort it before you sail — the charger is off or the bank is dead
Accept it — the bank will come up once you run the engine on Sunday morning
Switch to BOTH so the engine battery carries the house bank for the week
Move the cable to another pedestal socket, see the light come on and sign
questions.why: Plugged in, the bank should read 13.8–14.4 V; 11.8 V with current going out means no charge — and ask how old the bank is.

questions.q: The technician waves at the panel, says 'all the usual' and heads for the engine bay. What do you ask him to do first?
options: Explain the 230 V side only — the 12 V side is obvious
Switch on each breaker in turn and show you what it feeds
Hand you the boat manual to read the panel on passage
Leave every breaker on so you can find out as you go
questions.why: You will be finding these at night in a blow; VHF, instruments and the windlass each have their own breaker.

questions.q: Your crew asks whether the kettle and the hairdryer will work in the bays. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Main panel
lines: Right: 230 V AC — RCD, charger, outlets, water heater
Inverter 300 W: one socket at the chart table

options: Yes — switch the charger on and it converts 12 V into 230 V for the outlets
Yes with the engine running — the alternator powers the 230 V side of the panel
Only on shore power — at anchor the 230 V outlets are dead and the inverter runs a laptop, not a kettle
Yes — flip the 230 V main breaker and the batteries feed the outlets directly
questions.why: The 230 V side is live only on shore power or a generator; a 300 W inverter will not run a 2 kW kettle.

questions.q: The technician plugs the shore cable in and goes to fetch the inventory list. You look at the 230 V panel. What do you do?
options: Press the RCD test button to clear the warning and carry on
Turn the plug the other way round in the pedestal socket
Ignore it — polarity only matters on American 110 V boats
Unplug it and tell the base — the pedestal is miswired; no 230 V until it is fixed
questions.why: Reverse polarity leaves the live side on breakers that should be neutral; an RCD does not make it safe.

questions.q: Sunday 10:00, the technician has gone and you are ready to cast off from the pontoon. In what order do you deal with the shore power?
options: Charger and 230 V main off, pedestal switch off, unplug the pedestal end first, then the boat end, stow the cable
Leave it plugged in until the engine is running for a last charge, then pull both ends at once
Pull both ends, leave the cable on the pontoon for the base to collect, cast off
Unplug the boat end first, hand the live cable to a crew on the pontoon, then the pedestal end
questions.why: Dead before you touch it, pedestal end first so no live plug lies on deck; the cable is on the inventory.

questions.q: You ask the technician to start the engine and watch the battery monitor. What do you tell him?
options: All good — the alternator only starts charging above 2000 rpm
It is not charging — the alternator or belt needs looking at before you leave
All good — it charges the engine battery, which is not on this monitor
All good — volts must drop a little when the engine takes its load
questions.why: With the engine running the monitor should show about 14 V and current going in; 12.3 V and −8 A is no charge.

questions.q: The technician resets the breaker, the windlass runs, and he moves on. What rule do you take away, and what do you ask before he goes?

figure.title: Windlass
lines: Breaker 80 A at the chart table
Tripped on the first test, reset

options: Breaker on all week so the remote always works; and whether the base will come out if it trips again
Use it with the engine off at anchor so the alternator is unloaded; and the make of the motor
Engine running whenever you use it; and where the spare fuses are, for anything that blows instead of tripping
Start the engine only if it stalls; and whether the house bank can be switched in to help it
questions.why: The windlass draws 80–100 A; the alternator covers it and the engine is ready. A breaker resets, a fuse needs a spare.

questions.q: Evening in the bay, the fridge is the only thing running. Do you leave it on overnight?
options: Yes, and the lights and the inverter too — 200 Ah is enough for the week
No — switch it off at night; 5 A will flatten 200 Ah well before dawn
Only with BOTH selected so the engine battery shares the night's load
Yes — about 5 A for 10 h is 50 Ah, a quarter of the bank; charge with the engine in the morning
questions.why: Amps × hours = amp-hours; a lead-acid bank should not go below half, so 50 Ah of 200 is fine.

questions.q: Saturday night you switch on NAV LIGHTS and walk out along the pontoon to look at the bow. This is what you see. What do you do?

figure.note: Pontoon, 21:00 — seen from ahead, NAV LIGHTS on

options: Note the dead starboard light on the form and ask the base to replace the bulb before you sail
Sail with the tricolour instead — it shows the same arcs
Accept it — you plan to be in a harbour every night
Buy a bulb in town on Monday and fit it yourself
questions.why: Test the lights at the pontoon, at night, from outside; the base replaces what is dead.

questions.q: You switch on the ANCHOR breaker and look up from the pontoon. What have you confirmed?

figure.note: Pontoon, 21:10 — ANCHOR breaker on

options: The tricolour works — show it at anchor to save the battery
The all-round white anchor light works — the one to show every night at anchor
The steaming light works — the one to show at anchor with the engine off
The deck light works — enough for a quiet bay with no traffic
questions.why: At anchor at night a vessel shows an all-round white light (Rule 30); test it where you can see it.

questions.q: The technician reads this off the inventory list without opening the floor. How do you check it before you sign?

figure.title: Bilge pump
lines: Electric: float switch in the bilge
Hand pump in the cockpit, handle in the locker

options: Leave it on AUTO and look at the bilge again at check-out
Trust the panel light — it only comes on if the pump is wired
Switch to ON and hear it run, lift the float for AUTO, find the hand-pump handle
Set it to OFF so it cannot drain the batteries at anchor
questions.why: A pump that was never heard is a pump that may not run; AUTO stays selected all week.

questions.q: What do you do with these two before you sign, and what do you ask?

figure.title: Alarms
lines: Gas detector: sensor in the bilge, panel at the galley
CO alarm in the saloon, 9 V battery

options: Note that they are fitted — testing them trips the panel breaker
Ask for a spare detector in case this one goes off falsely
Take the battery out of the CO alarm so it does not chirp at night
Press TEST on each and hear it; ask what to do when the gas alarm sounds
questions.why: Gas alarm: close the bottle valve, no switches, ventilate; a dead CO alarm goes on the form.

questions.q: The technician says 'you will not need these' and skips them. What do you ask him to show you anyway?

figure.title: Also fitted
lines: Solar 200 W on the bimini, controller at the chart table
Generator strainer under the aft bunk

options: The solar controller charging, and the generator started with water at its exhaust; note the hours
Nothing — extras you do not use are not your problem at check-out
The generator fuel level only; a solar panel has nothing to check
The panel wiring under the bimini, with the controller switched off
questions.why: Anything on the inventory is yours for the week; a generator is checked like the engine — hours and raw water.

questions.q: The technician brings this cable to plug you in. What do you do?

figure.title: Shore cable
lines: Outer sheath cut, copper showing near the plug

options: Tape over the cut and plug in — the RCD will trip if anything leaks
Refuse it and ask for another — a damaged 230 V cable on a wet pontoon can kill
Plug it in only at night when nobody is walking along the pontoon
Use it with dry hands and keep the cut end on the boat, not the pontoon
questions.why: 230 V, seawater and bare copper: no tape, no dry hands; the base has another cable.

questions.q: The technician lifts the bunk and shows you the batteries. What do you do?

figure.title: Battery compartment
lines: Under the aft bunk, terminals uncovered
Master switches: behind the companionway steps
Technician: "check they are tight if you like"

options: Ask him to disconnect the bank so you can inspect each battery
Check the terminals are tight with the winch handle while he watches
Ask him to show you the master switches and fit terminal covers; you do not touch the terminals
Note it and plan to buy terminal covers in town on Monday
questions.why: A dropped spanner across the terminals is a fire; in a fire you must find the master switch in the dark.

questions.q: The technician asks how you plan to run the boat for the week. What is your plan?

figure.title: Power budget
lines: Fridge 5 A · instruments 2 A · lights 2 A · autopilot 4 A

options: Keep the engine idling all night so the fridge never drains the bank
Run everything — 200 Ah will see the week out without charging
Fridge off, autopilot on all night — the autopilot matters more
Engine an hour morning and evening, fridge on, instruments and autopilot off when not needed
questions.why: About 100 Ah usable; a day's draw is near that, so charge twice a day and cut what is not in use.

questions.q: Tuesday, 08:00, at anchor. You read the battery monitor before breakfast. What does the third figure tell you?

lines: Last full: Sunday at the base

options: That 76 Ah have been drawn from the bank since it was last full
That the alternator will put back 76 Ah in the next hour
That the bank has lost 76 Ah of its capacity with age
That 76 Ah are left in the bank before it is completely flat
questions.why: The monitor counts amp-hours out and in since the last full charge; 76 drawn from 200 Ah matches the 62 %.

questions.q: Saturday night on shore power, a crew member in the aft cabin complains of a humming box under the bunk. You read its display. What do you tell them?
options: It is the charger failing; switch it off until the morning
It is the charger holding a full bank; the fan hum is normal
It is the inverter; it runs whenever shore power is in
It is the bank still flat; FLOAT means a slow first charge
questions.why: Bulk, absorption, float: float is the last stage — the bank is full and the charger just keeps it there.

questions.q: Monday, the plotter and the depth go dead together. Behind the panel you find this. What do you fit?

figure.title: Fuse holder: INSTRUMENTS
lines: Spares box: 5 A, 10 A, 15 A, 20 A

options: Any spare that fits the holder, since the rating is only a guide
A 15 A spare, so that it does not blow again on the same load
A 10 A spare; if it blows again, leave it out and call the base
A 20 A spare, since a bigger fuse protects the plotter better
questions.why: A fuse protects the wire; a bigger one lets the wire burn before it blows. A second blow means a fault, not a weak fuse.

questions.q: Wednesday, 18:00, you are berthed in a marina in Kos and want shore power. In which order do you connect?

figure.title: Marina berth
lines: Pedestal: 16 A socket with its own switch
Boat inlet: in the cockpit locker

options: Both ends at once, one crew at each, then switch the pedestal on
Pedestal end first and switched on, then carry the live plug to the boat
Boat's 230 V main on first, so the panel is ready when the cable goes live
Boat end first, then the pedestal end, then the pedestal switch and the 230 V main
questions.why: Never hold a live plug: the cable goes live last, from the pedestal, once both ends are in.

questions.q: Monday noon in a bay, engine off. You read the solar controller at the chart table. What is it doing?
options: Charging the house bank at 7 A from the panels
Drawing 7 A from the bank to run the controller
Nothing yet — 19.5 V is the panels' voltage with no load
Overcharging — a bank should never read above 12.7 V
questions.why: The controller turns the panels' higher voltage into a charge: +7 A is going in, and 13.9 V is a bank on charge.

questions.q: Your crew want to stuff a towel into the small vent by the battery box under the bunk to stop a draught. What do you tell them?
options: Fine at anchor — the vent only matters on shore power
Leave it open — batteries on charge give off hydrogen that must get out
Fine — the vent is there only to let the batteries' heat out
Fine — modern batteries are sealed and give off nothing at all
questions.why: Lead-acid batteries gas hydrogen on charge, more when overcharged; with the vent blocked it collects where a spark can light it.

questions.q: Saturday, 18:00, on shore power since noon. You lift the aft bunk and find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Battery compartment
lines: One battery hot to the touch, case bulging

options: Loosen the hot battery's terminals with a spanner and lift it out
Lay a wet towel over it and let the charger finish its cycle
Charger off, hatches open, no switches or sparks near it, and call the base
Leave it — the smell is the holding tank next to the batteries
questions.why: A battery cooking on charge gives off hydrogen sulphide and hydrogen: stop the charge, ventilate, no sparks.

questions.q: Wednesday, under sail, engine off. Smoke and a hot smell come from behind the DC panel. What do you do first?

figure.title: Chart table
lines: Smoke from behind the DC panel

options: Open the panel and find the burning wire before switching off
A bucket of seawater on the panel, then the battery switches
Switch the breakers off one by one to find the faulty circuit
Battery switches off, then the powder extinguisher at the panel if it still burns
questions.why: Cut the source first: with the batteries isolated most electrical fires die; never water on a live panel.

questions.q: 42 ft catamaran at anchor. A crew member asks to use her hairdryer on the inverter socket. What do you say?
options: Yes, for a few minutes, with the generator or an engine running
No — an inverter cannot run anything that heats up
Yes, as long as she likes — 400 Ah does not notice a hairdryer
Only with the charger on, so that it feeds the inverter
questions.why: 1,600 W from 12 V is about 140 A; ten minutes is over 20 Ah — fine with a charge going in, not every morning off the bank.

questions.q: Tuesday, motoring along the coast, the INSTRUMENTS breaker trips. You reset it and it trips again at once. What do you do?
options: Move the instruments onto the fridge's 15 A breaker
Leave it off, navigate by compass and paper chart, and call the base
Tape the breaker on so that a wave cannot trip it again
Hold the breaker in by hand until the instruments come back
questions.why: A breaker that trips at once has found a short; forcing it on heats the wiring. Paper chart, compass, and the base's help.

questions.q: The technician shows you the electric winch for the main halyard. What do you ask him before he moves on?
options: Whether it runs off the starter battery so the house bank is spared
Whether the button can be held while you go forward to watch the sail
Where its isolator is, so anyone can stop it if a hand is caught
How many turns to put on so that the line can never slip off
questions.why: A powered winch does not feel a finger or a fouled line; the button at the helm and the isolator below must be known to all.

questions.q: Thursday in the marina. Your shore cable sags into the water between the pontoon and the transom, and the crew want to swim off the stern. What do you do?
options: Switch the boat's charger off and let them swim
Let them swim on the far side of the boat from the cable
Nothing — the RCD on the pedestal makes it safe to swim
Lift the cable clear and tie it up; nobody swims in the marina
questions.why: Stray 230 V in marina water can kill a swimmer; keep cables out of the water and do not swim between pontoons.

questions.q: Thursday, 15:00, the catamaran at anchor. The generator runs for the air-con and the crew are jumping off the stern steps. What do you do?

figure.title: Catamaran at anchor
lines: Generator running, exhaust at the port transom

options: Stop the generator while anyone is swimming near the stern
Ask them to swim off the starboard hull only
Run it faster so that the exhaust clears away quicker
Nothing — the exhaust goes into the water, not the air
questions.why: Generator exhaust carries carbon monoxide; at the stern, in still air, a swimmer breathes it at the waterline. Swim with it off.

questions.q: Monday, 08:00: the starter battery was flat, you switched to BOTH and the engine is now running. What do you do with the switches?
options: Stop the engine and restart it on ENGINE alone to test it
BOTH off now, and an hour's charge before you trust the starter alone
Leave BOTH on all day so the starter charges from the house bank
BOTH off and stop the engine — it has started, the job is done
questions.why: Left in parallel, the two banks drain together again overnight; separate them and give the starter time to charge.
questions.ref: Battery switches — after a parallel start

questions.q: Wednesday evening on shore power in Split. Each time the water-heater breaker goes on, the RCD trips. What do you do?

figure.title: 230 V panel
lines: RCD trips when WATER HEATER goes on
Charger and sockets: fine without it

options: Reset the RCD and hold it up until the water has warmed
Run the water heater from the inverter instead
Leave the water heater off and tell the base — it is leaking to earth
Plug into another pedestal socket and try it again
questions.why: An RCD trips on current leaking to earth; a heater element that trips it is faulty and could make the water live.

questions.q: Thursday, 08:00, in a marina in Trogir: the pedestal trips each morning as breakfast starts. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: The kettle leaks to earth — throw it out and use the stove
Morning damp in the cable — dry the plug and reset it
The pedestal is faulty — ask the marina for another berth
Heater, kettle and charger together pass 10 A — one big load at a time
questions.why: Watts ÷ 230 = amps: 3,700 W is about 16 A on a 10 A pedestal. Water heater off while the kettle boils.

questions.q: Tuesday, a town marina: your plug does not fit the pedestal socket. A crew member offers to cut the plug off and push the bare wires in. What do you do?

figure.title: Pedestal
lines: Sockets: a type your plug does not fit

options: Ask the marina office for an adapter; no bare wires in a pedestal
Do it, and tape the wires in so that they cannot pull out
Let him do it, as long as he switches the pedestal off first
Run an extension lead across from the neighbour's boat
questions.why: Bare wires in a 230 V socket on a wet pontoon can kill, and a cut plug is charged to your deposit; ask the office for an adapter.

questions.q: Wednesday, 21:00, at anchor in a bay where boats are still coming in: the anchor light has failed and you cannot fix it tonight. What do you do?
options: Show the steaming light instead until the morning
Hang an all-round white lamp in the foretriangle and call the base in the morning
Leave the cabin lights on so that boats see the glow
Go up the mast in the dark and change the bulb
questions.why: The rule wants an all-round white light where it is best seen; a lamp hung forward does that. Nobody climbs the mast at night.

questions.q: Your crew, keen to save power, are about to switch off every breaker for the night at anchor. Which stay on?

figure.title: DC panel
lines: ANCHOR LIGHT · BILGE PUMP · GAS ALARM

options: Only the fridge — the food matters more than the alarms
Anchor light only — the gas alarm has its own battery
Anchor light, bilge pump and gas alarm; the rest is your choice
None — the bilge pump runs straight off the battery
questions.why: Seen, kept afloat, warned of gas: these three keep the boat safe overnight; the fridge or the VHF is a choice.

questions.q: You shine a torch on the starter battery while the technician waits. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Starter battery
lines: White-green crust on the positive post

options: Nothing — the crust is normal on a working battery
A note on the form, and you will take it from there
A tin of grease, so you can clean it yourself on Monday
The post cleaned and the lug tightened before you sail
questions.why: A loose, corroded lug fails under the starter's load — the engine will not turn on the very morning you need it.

questions.q: 42 ft catamaran with a lithium house bank, Tuesday evening at anchor. Your crew say the volts 'look fine'. What do you tell them?
options: Trust the 25 % — a lithium bank stays near 13 V until it is almost empty
Trust the 13.1 V — the percentage is only the monitor's guess
Neither — read the starter battery to judge the house bank
Both are fine — 13.1 V on any bank means three-quarters full
questions.why: Lithium holds a flat 13.0–13.3 V over most of its charge, so the volts say little; the monitor's amp-hour count is the gauge.

questions.q: Wednesday on the catamaran, a long calm passage under power; you decide to run one engine to save fuel. Which one?

figure.title: Catamaran charging (base's sheet)
lines: Stbd alternator: stbd starter + house bank

options: The port — its alternator has less to charge, so it lasts longer
The starboard — only its alternator charges the house bank
Either — each alternator charges every battery aboard
Swap every hour so that both starters stay equally charged
questions.why: On many cats only one engine charges the house bank, and the base's sheet says which; run the other and the fridge sits on a falling bank.

questions.q: Sunday evening at anchor you find the inverter on with nothing plugged in; your crew left it 'just in case'. What do you tell them?
options: Leave it — at anchor it keeps the house bank topped up
Leave it — with nothing plugged in it draws nothing
Off unless something is plugged in — idling, it takes about 24 Ah a day
Leave it — switching it on and off wears out its fan
questions.why: An inverter draws power just standing by; a day of idling is over a tenth of a 200 Ah bank, for nothing.

questions.q: Motoring out of the bay, a crew member tidying the chart table turns the ENGINE battery switch off 'because the alternator is running now'. What do you do?
options: Leave it — once running, a diesel needs no battery at all
Switch it back on only if the battery light comes on
Leave it, and switch it back on before you stop the engine
Switch it back on at once — cutting it with the engine running can wreck the alternator
questions.why: With the battery cut the alternator's output has nowhere to go; the spike can blow its diodes. Battery switches stay on under way.

questions.q: Monday, 07:00, in a bay. The fridge was the only thing on overnight. You compare the readings. What do you do?
options: The bank has lost much of its capacity — call the base for new batteries on your route
Run the engine all day; a full charge will restore the old bank
Nothing — a fridge always takes a bank down to 11.9 V by morning
Switch the fridge off each night and carry on with the plan
questions.why: 40 Ah from 200 should still read about 12.4 V; 11.9 V means the old bank holds far less than its label. The base can swap it midweek.

questions.q: Catamaran, three nights at anchor planned. Reading the power figures at the briefing, what do you decide?

figure.title: Catamaran 42 ft — power budget
lines: Galley fridge, cockpit fridge, freezer: 12 A together
Solar 400 W: about 100 Ah on a sunny day

options: Solar alone will do — 400 W is more than the fridges use
Cockpit fridge off and an engine run twice a day — 12 A round the clock outruns the sun
All three on — 400 Ah and the solar will cover any week at anchor
Freezer off, nothing else — the fridges barely draw at night
questions.why: 12 A × 24 h is about 290 Ah a day; 100 Ah of sun and 200 usable last about a day. Cut a load and charge twice a day.

questions.q: Thursday evening in a bay: strong wind is forecast for Friday's passage back to the base. You read this. What do you do tonight?

figure.title: Thursday 19:00
lines: Friday: F6–7, 25 miles to the base
Autopilot, VHF, plotter, bilge pump: house bank

options: Save the engine for tomorrow — it will charge on the way back
Nothing — the starter battery takes over if the house runs low
Charge it full tonight and in the morning — tomorrow everything runs on it
Switch the house bank off tonight to hold it at 55 %
questions.why: Go into a blow with a full bank: autopilot, plotter, VHF and bilge pump all draw on it, and the engine may yet stop.

questions.q: Saturday 14:00, shore power off since the morning cleaning. The technician says 'the monitor says full'. What do you do?
options: Believe the monitor — it counts every amp, the voltmeter only guesses
Accept it — 12.1 V with the fridge running is a full bank
Plug the charger back in for an hour, see 100 % again and sign
Believe the volts — have the bank tested and the monitor reset before you sign
questions.why: A monitor that has lost count shows whatever it was last set to; 12.1 V under a small load is a bank near half or below.

questions.q: Tuesday, 02:00, at anchor: a hum under the saloon floor wakes you. You find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Bilge
lines: Bilge pump running, panel light on
Float switch stuck up, will not free

options: Pump to OFF, look in the bilge every few hours, and call the base in the morning
Pull its fuse for the rest of the week, since the bilge is dry
