Set it to ON so that it runs steadily rather than cycling
Leave it on AUTO — better a pump running dry than a flooded bilge
questions.why: A pump running dry burns out and drains the bank; switch it off and check the bilge by hand until the base fixes the float.

questions.q: Wednesday, 11:00, motoring between islands, you check the monitor. What do you do for the rest of the week?

lines: Battery light on since this morning

options: Switch to BOTH so that the starter battery charges the house
Call the base, make for a marina with shore power tonight, and cut every load you can
Tighten the belt hard yourself and keep motoring as planned
Carry on — the house bank will last till Friday on its own
questions.why: No charge means the bank only falls; the base can send a technician, and shore power keeps the fridge and lights going until then.

questions.q: The technician says both water tanks are full. The panel shows this. What do you do before you sign?
options: Sign — the gauge reads the tank not in use
Note 'gauge faulty' on the form and sign
Switch the selector to tank 2 and look into both fillers yourself
Ask him to top up tank 1 and sign
questions.why: A gauge reads the selected tank; a quarter-full tank 1 is the first thing to see — check both tanks at the filler before signing.

questions.q: On the side deck you find three deck caps; the lettering has worn off. Your crew is already uncoiling the pontoon hose. What do you do?
options: Fill the aft one; water fillers are always aft
Try each cap — water goes in the one that gurgles
Fill the biggest cap; the water tank is the largest
Have the technician identify each cap and mark it before any hose goes in
questions.why: Water in the diesel tank or the holding tank ends the week; caps are marked WATER, DIESEL, WASTE — if they are not, mark them.

questions.q: You are filling the water tanks at the pontoon with the marina hose. How do you do it?
options: Run the hose clear first, then fill each tank until it overflows at the filler
Fill through the galley tap so the pump stays primed
Fill only the tank the selector is on; the other fills by itself
Put the hose in, go to the shop and come back in an hour
questions.why: A hose that has lain in the sun holds stale water; fill to overflow, tank by tank, and stay with it.

questions.q: Every tap is closed, yet the pressure pump keeps running. The technician says it is just priming. What do you do?
options: Leave it; a pump stops by itself once it finds pressure
Switch the pump off and ask the base to find the leak before you leave
Sign and switch it off at night to save the batteries
Open a tap to let the air out and let it run on
questions.why: A pump that runs with the taps closed is pumping into a leak or from an empty tank — on a full tank, that water is going into the bilge.

questions.q: Monday morning at anchor. Your crew report this. What do you do?
options: Switch on the inverter so the heater element can run
Report it to the base as a broken water heater
Run the engine for half an hour — the heater element only works on shore power
Open the hot tap and wait; the element takes an hour
questions.why: The calorifier is heated by the engine's cooling water or by a 230 V element on shore power; at anchor only the engine heats it.

questions.q: You are leaving the pontoon. The heads bowl is full of water and the pump lever is on 'wet'. What do you do?
options: Leave it; the water keeps the smell down
Pump the bowl full so the seal stays wet at sea
Set the lever to 'dry' and leave the bowl full
Pump the bowl dry and set the lever to 'dry'
questions.why: A full bowl slops and can siphon when the boat heels; at sea the bowl is pumped dry and the lever left on dry.

questions.q: A crew member reads the sign over the heads and asks whether the wipes she bought can go in. What do you answer?
options: No — only what has been eaten and a little paper; wipes go in the bin
Yes, one at a time with plenty of pumping after it
Yes, in the electric heads but not in the manual one
Yes, if the packet says 'flushable' and you pump well
questions.why: Wipes do not break up; they block the pump and the holding tank, and the contract charges you for the unblocking.

questions.q: Sunday afternoon in a bay. The crew are going ashore for lunch and the boat will be empty for three hours. This is how you leave it. What do you change?

figure.title: Leaving the boat, 13:00
lines: Gas valve at the bottle: open

options: Close the seacocks; the pump must stay on for the fridge
Close the heads seacocks and the gas valve, and switch the pump off
Close the gas valve; the rest is fine for three hours
Switch the pump off; seacocks stay open to vent the heads
questions.why: An empty boat is left with seacocks shut, gas off at the bottle and the pressure pump off: nothing can flood or leak while nobody is aboard.

questions.q: The technician shows you the holding-tank valve in this position, in the marina. What do you do?
options: Leave it; direct overboard saves pumping the tank out
Set it to 'tank' and never open it; the base pumps out
Set it to 'tank' now and open it only when you are well offshore
Leave it in the marina; switch to 'tank' once at sea
questions.why: In harbour and in bays everything goes to the tank; the valve is opened only offshore, where the briefing allows discharge.

questions.q: At check-in the holding tank reads this. The technician suggests you empty it at sea tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Sign and open the valve at the first bay tomorrow
Sign and note 'tank full' so the return check is fair
Sign, and empty it over the side tonight after dark
Ask the base to pump it out before you sign; a full tank is not an accepted boat
questions.why: You take over a boat with an empty holding tank; discharging in a bay or a harbour is illegal, and the full tank is the base's job to fix.

questions.q: The electric heads flush weakly and the bowl empties slowly. The technician says they are all like that. What do you do?

figure.title: Electric heads, aft cabin
lines: Flush: a trickle, bowl empties in 30 s

options: Write it on the check-in form and ask for it to be checked before you leave
Accept it; a slow flush is normal for a macerator
Sign, and use the forward heads all week
Sign; you will clear it yourself with vinegar
questions.why: A weak flush is a blocked or tired pump that will fail mid-week; note every fault on the form and ask for the fix at the base.

questions.q: The technician hands you this list and says the seacocks are 'all fine'. What do you ask for?
options: To have the bungs counted in the tool bag
To be shown each one, turn it yourself, and have a bung tied beside each
To have the list signed by him as checked
To be shown the engine one; the others are small
questions.why: You need to know where every seacock is and that it turns; a bung tied to the fitting is found in the dark, one in a bag is not.

questions.q: You lift the sole boards and find this. The technician says it is the fridge drain. What do you do?
options: Note 'fridge drain' on the form and sign
Sponge it out yourself and sign; fresh water is harmless
Have it dried out and the fridge drain shown to you, then check it stays dry
Sign; the automatic pump will take it when it rises
questions.why: A dry bilge at check-in is your baseline: any water later is news; a fridge that drains to the bilge is a known source, but it is checked first.

questions.q: The technician says the bilge pumping is 'automatic, you never need it'. How do you check the bilge pumps?

figure.title: Bilge pumps
lines: Electric: float switch under the sole

options: Switch the electric pump to 'manual' on the panel and listen for it
Ask for the pumps' last service date to be written on the form
Pour a bucket into the bilge and wait for the float to start it
Lift the float until the pump runs, then find the handle and work the manual pump
questions.why: The float switch is tested by lifting it, the manual pump by pumping it — and its handle must be where you can find it with water over the sole.

questions.q: The technician opens the gas locker and shows you this. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Gas locker, cockpit
lines: Locker drain: blocked, 2 cm of water

options: A full spare bottle and the locker drain cleared
A note on the form that the locker holds water
A full spare bottle; the drain can wait for the base
The drain cleared; you will buy a bottle in town
questions.why: Gas is heavier than air: the locker must drain overboard, not into the boat; and a half bottle with no spare runs out mid-week.

questions.q: Tuesday evening at anchor: there is a smell of gas in the galley. What do you do first?

figure.title: Galley, 19:30
lines: Smell of gas by the stove
Stove: off, gas valve at the bottle: open

options: Switch on the fan and the lights to look for the leak at the stove
Shut the valve at the bottle, ventilate, no flames or switches until the smell is gone
Pump the bilge and open the gas valve fully to flush the line
Light a burner to burn off the gas left in the pipe and hose
questions.why: Gas sinks into the bilge: isolate at the bottle, ventilate, no sparks; then find the leak with soapy water on the joints.

questions.q: In the galley you find this. The technician says the alarm 'kept going off, so we disconnected it'. What do you do?

figure.title: Gas alarm
lines: Sensor: in the bilge under the stove
Solenoid switch at the stove: works

options: Accept it; the solenoid switch is your safety
Note it and rely on your nose for the week
Ask for it reconnected and tested before departure
Sign and plug it in yourself later
questions.why: A gas alarm that trips may be finding a real leak; it goes back on and is tested, and the leak is looked for, before you sign.

questions.q: First evening in the marina, your crew start cooking. The stove swings on its gimbals as soon as a pan goes on. What do you tell them?
options: Wedge the stove with a cloth; the lock is for the oven
Lock the gimbals at sea; free them in harbour
Free the gimbals at all times; that is what they are for
Lock the gimbals in harbour; free them only at sea so the pan stays level
questions.why: Gimbals keep the pan level when the boat heels; in a flat harbour the lock stops the stove tipping when someone leans on it.

questions.q: After a night of rain the cockpit looks like this. What do you ask for before you leave the base?

figure.title: Cockpit, Sunday 08:00
lines: Anchor locker: half full of water

options: The cockpit drains and the anchor-locker drain cleared and shown to run free
The anchor locker pumped out and the lid taped shut
The scuppers checked; cockpit water drains over the sole
A bucket; you will bail the cockpit after rain
questions.why: A cockpit that does not drain fills in a sea; a blocked anchor-locker drain puts the water in the forepeak. Both are cleared at the base.

questions.q: You take over the catamaran with this. How do you plan the week's water?
options: Fill once at the base; 600 l is plenty for 8 people for a week
Fill at every marina and make water only at sea, in clean water; 600 l will not last the week
Shower ashore only and never touch the watermaker all week
Rely on the watermaker; run it every morning while in the marina
questions.why: 600 l is under 11 l a day each for 8 people; a watermaker sucks oil and sewage in a harbour — it runs offshore in clean water.

questions.q: Your crew are filling tank 1 from the pontoon hose. You look over the side and see this. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Filling tank 1
lines: Hose in the deck filler, 6 min
Water spurting from a small hull fitting
Starboard side, below the side deck

options: Carry on — that is the bilge pump clearing hose water
Stop — a pipe has burst, call the technician
Stop — that is the tank vent, so the tank is full
Carry on — the tank spills there until the air is out
questions.why: The tank breathes through a vent in the hull; water out of the vent means the tank is full — close that filler and move to the next tank.

questions.q: Wednesday, 07:30. Your crew call you to the aft shower. You check the panel. What do you do?
options: Leave the pump on; it draws from tank 2 by itself when 1 is empty
Switch the pump off and wait an hour for the gauge to recover
Open every tap with the pump running to bleed the air out
Switch the pump off, turn the selector to tank 2, then switch it on again
questions.why: A pump running dry overheats and wears out; switch it off, change tanks, then let it prime with one tap open.

questions.q: After the engine test you lift the aft bunk with the technician and find this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Water heater, aft cabin
lines: Pool under the tank, draining to the bilge

options: The valve checked before you leave and the fault noted on the form
The valve's outlet plugged so the bilge stays dry
Nothing — a relief valve is meant to let water out
The water heater switched off and taped for the week
questions.why: A relief valve may drip as the water heats; a steady flow is a faulty valve or too much pressure — the base checks it, it is never plugged.

questions.q: Monday evening at anchor. The forward shower looks like this. What do you check first?

figure.title: Forward shower
lines: Tray full, water over the sill
Drain button pressed: no pump noise

options: The water-heater switch; the pump runs only with it on
The shower-pump breaker, then the hair filter on the sump
The tank selector; the shower drains back to the tank
The heads seacocks; the shower drains through the toilet
questions.why: A shower tray drains to a sump with its own pump, breaker and filter; hair clogs the filter and a tray left full floods the cabin sole.

questions.q: At check-in you pump the forward heads yourself. This is what you see. What do you do?

figure.title: Forward heads
lines: A minute later: half full again
Brown water, from the outlet side

options: Sign — set the lever to 'dry' after use and it stops
Sign; pump a few more strokes each time it is used
Ask for the joker valve to be changed and the heads tried again
Note it on the form and keep the inlet seacock closed
questions.why: Waste flowing back from the outlet is a worn joker valve, a cheap part the base changes in minutes — not a week of backflow.

questions.q: Wednesday in the Göcek bays, the holding tank is three-quarters full. You read the briefing notes again. What do you do?

figure.title: Briefing notes, Turkey
lines: Blue card: stamped at each pump-out
Pump-out boats and stations in the bays

options: Open the valve after dark, when the patrol boats have gone
Motor three miles out of the bay and open the valve there
Lock the heads and use the beach toilets until Friday
Pump out at a station or a pump-out boat and get the card stamped
questions.why: In Turkey the blue card records each pump-out; the tank is emptied at a station and the card shows it was, not over the side.

questions.q: Tuesday, 22:00. A crew member calls you to the aft heads. What do you do?

figure.title: Aft heads, electric
lines: Button pressed: motor hums, nothing moves

options: Stop pressing, switch its breaker off and use the other heads
Turn the Y-valve to overboard to take the load off
Keep pressing in short bursts until the blockage clears
Pour boiling water into the bowl and press again
questions.why: A humming macerator is jammed; pressed on, the motor burns out. Breaker off, then the jam is cleared — not more pressing.

questions.q: Going round the seacocks with the technician, you find this one. What do you do?

figure.title: Galley sink seacock
lines: Lever: will not move by hand

options: Lever it with the winch handle; a seacock has to turn
Leave it and ask the base to free or service it before you leave
Leave it open; it is only the sink and stays open anyway
Spray it with oil and try it again on Monday
questions.why: A seized seacock forced with a lever can snap off below the waterline; the base frees or services it before you sign for the boat.

questions.q: Monday at anchor there is water in the bilge again. You run this test. Where is it coming from?

figure.title: Bilge, Monday 08:00
lines: Pump off overnight: bilge stayed dry
Pump on: a trickle starts again

options: Rain through the deck fittings during the night
The stern gland, dripping since you motored in
A leak on the pressure side of the fresh-water system
The holding tank, spilling over through its vent
questions.why: Fresh water that comes only with the pump on is a pressurised pipe or joint; switch the pump off and trace the hoses from it.

questions.q: The technician says the gas 'has no leaks'. The regulator has a gauge. How do you check it yourself?

figure.title: Gas locker
lines: Bottle · regulator with a pressure gauge
Pipe to the galley: through a sealed gland

options: Light a burner and look for a steady blue flame
Open the bottle and check the gas alarm stays silent
Smell along the pipe from the locker to the stove
Open the bottle, close it again and watch the gauge hold for minutes
questions.why: With every burner off, a sound system holds its pressure; a falling gauge is a leak — then soapy water on the joints finds it.

questions.q: You find this in the gas locker. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Gas locker
lines: Rubber hose, regulator to the pipe

options: A new hose fitted before you leave
The cracks taped and noted on the form
A note on the form; you will check it daily
Nothing — the gas alarm will warn of a leak
questions.why: Gas hoses perish with age and sun and carry a printed date; a cracked one is changed at the base, not watched for a week.

questions.q: Monday, 12:30 in a bay. Your crew can't get the stove to light. You find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Galley, 12:30
lines: Burner: clicks, no gas, no smell

options: Call the base; the regulator has failed
Switch the red GAS switch on, then light the burner
Turn the burner knob harder to open the valve
Change to the spare bottle; this one has run out
questions.why: A solenoid valve at the locker opens only while its switch is on; it is the first thing to check when no gas reaches the stove.

questions.q: Tuesday afternoon, back from the beach, the fridge is warm. You find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Fridge
lines: Compressor running, hot to the touch
Seacocks: all closed when you went ashore

options: Turn the thermostat to maximum and keep the lid shut
Switch the fridge off for an hour to let it reset
Open the fridge cooling seacock and check its pump runs
Run the engine; the fridge is cooled by its water
questions.why: A water-cooled fridge needs its seacock open; when you close the seacocks to go ashore, reopening this one belongs in the routine.

questions.q: A 36 ft boat, six crew. After Sunday's swim the gauge already reads this. What rule do you set?

lines: One tank, 150 l, full on Saturday

options: Switch the pump off at night and carry on as usual
Carry on; half a tank lasts six people three days
Transom shower only, as long as each person likes
A short rinse after swims, wash up in seawater, drink bottled
questions.why: 75 l for six people for three days is about 4 l each a day, and the transom shower draws from the same tank at litres a minute.

questions.q: Sunday night in the town marina, your crew suggest this. What do you answer?

figure.title: The crew's plan
lines: Leave the marina hose in the filler

options: No — fill the tanks now, then take the hose out and close the filler
Yes, if the tap is only open a quarter turn
Yes — the tank vent spills anything extra over the side
Yes, if someone gets up at midnight to check the hose
questions.why: A hose left on keeps pushing water in; a split pipe or a stuck vent puts the town's supply into the bilge while you sleep.

questions.q: Tuesday at the town quay a neighbour points at your hull. You find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Starboard side, by the heads
lines: Heads used all day, valve to 'tank'

options: Open the holding tank's deck cap so the tank breathes
Stop using the heads: the tank is full; get it pumped out
Close the heads seacocks; one of them is leaking
Nothing — it is the shower sump pump clearing
questions.why: The holding tank vents through the hull; waste out of the vent means the tank is full — empty it before the heads are used again.

questions.q: Looking for the bucket in the cockpit, you find this. What do you ask the base?

figure.title: Port cockpit locker
lines: Spare gas bottle, full, on its side
Locker floor: open to the bilge
Gas locker: room for one bottle only

options: Nothing — it is full and its valve is shut tight
For it to be wedged upright in that locker
Where the spare goes, upright, in a locker that drains overboard
For it to be stowed below, out of the hot sun
questions.why: A bottle can leak at the valve; gas is heavier than air and runs into the bilge — spares stay upright in a locker that drains overboard.

questions.q: With a torch under the heads basin you find this. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Heads outlet seacock
lines: Hose on the tail: one clip
Clip: rusted through on one side

options: A note on the form; you will watch it all week
Tape round the clip to hold it until Friday
Nothing — you can close the seacock if it leaks
Two sound stainless clips on the hose before you leave
questions.why: A hose below the waterline is held by two good clips; a rusted one can let go at sea and flood the boat — a five-minute fix at the base.

questions.q: 42 ft catamaran. The technician lifts one floor panel and says 'bilges dry'. What do you ask?

figure.title: Catamaran bilges
lines: A bilge pump in each hull

options: To see every compartment of both hulls and each hull's pump run
For 'bilges dry' on the form, signed by him
Nothing — the two hulls share one bilge under the saloon
To see the starboard middle one; the ends stay dry
questions.why: Each hull is its own bilge, often in several compartments with their own pumps; one dry panel says nothing about the other five.

questions.q: Your crew have cooked their first supper aboard and ask how to turn the gas off. What do you show them?
options: Close the stove knob; the bottle valve is only for leaving
Close the valve at the bottle, let the flame die, then close the knob
Close the stove knob first, then the valve at the bottle
Close the stove knob; the bottle valve is closed in the morning
questions.why: Shutting the bottle first lets the flame burn the gas left in the pipe, so no gas sits in the line between meals.

questions.q: Your crew try the oven on Saturday evening. This is what happens. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Oven
lines: Knob pushed in and turned, lit
Flame dies as soon as the knob is let go

options: Keep relighting it; it stays lit once the oven is warm
Note it on the form: the oven's gas valve is faulty
Hold the knob in for 10–15 seconds after it lights, then let go
Wedge the knob in so the gas keeps flowing
questions.why: The flame-failure device shuts the gas until its sensor is hot; hold the knob in until it is, and never jam it in.

questions.q: Before going ashore you go to close these. Which position means closed?

figure.title: Heads seacocks, under the basin
lines: Inlet: lever in line with the hose
Outlet: lever in line with the hose

options: The lever in line with the pipe, as it is now
The lever pointing down, towards the hull
The lever turned round twice, clockwise
The lever across the pipe, a quarter turn
questions.why: A ball-valve seacock is open with the lever in line with the pipe and closed with it across — a quarter turn.

questions.q: Your crew ask whether they can drink the water from the galley tap. What do you tell them?
options: Drink bottled water; tank water is for washing and for boiling
Only from tank 1; tank 2 is for the showers
Yes — the base fills the tanks from the town supply
Yes, once it has run for a minute to clear the pipe
questions.why: Tanks and hoses are not kept to drinking standard and the source varies; boiled tank water is fine for cooking, bottled is for drinking.

questions.q: Your crew are washing up in a clear bay and ask whether the sink water goes to the holding tank. What do you answer?
options: Yes — so it does not matter how much soap they use
No — sink and shower water go over the side; use little soap
No — it drains to the bilge and the bilge pump clears it
Yes — everything that drains below goes to the holding tank
questions.why: On most charter boats only the toilets feed the holding tank; grey water drains straight into the bay you swim in.

questions.q: Tuesday, 18:00 at the town quay, the forward heads will not pump and you learn this. What do you do?

figure.title: Forward heads
lines: Handle: stiff, will not go down

options: Force the handle down hard to push the blockage through
Use it gently until Friday and tell the base at check-out
Stop pumping, close its seacocks, use the aft heads and call the base
Call the base and ask them to send someone at their cost
questions.why: Forcing a blocked pump breaks it; isolate it, call the base for where to get it cleared, and expect the charge — the blockage is the crew's.

questions.q: Thursday in a village harbour near Trogir: the gas runs out and there is no spare aboard. The shop has this. What do you do?

figure.title: Village shop
lines: Gas bottles: one brand, other valve
Your regulator: does not fit it
Shopkeeper: 'tape and a clip will do'

options: Buy it and fit your regulator with tape and a hose clip
Buy it and a camping stove to use on the saloon table
Buy it with the shop's own regulator and fit that one
Call the base for where your type is swapped; eat cold or ashore till then
questions.why: Bottle valves differ by brand and country; a gas fitting is never adapted. The base knows where its bottles are swapped.

questions.q: Thursday, 21:00 at anchor, wind forecast to rise in the night. You notice this. What do you do now?
options: Check each seacock, hose and the stern gland now, and call the base
Switch the bilge pump to manual to save the battery
Close every seacock, the engine's too, and wait for morning
Leave it; the pump keeps up, and you look at first light
questions.why: Salt water that keeps coming is a seacock, hose, gland or rudder seal; find it now, with light and the base on the phone, not at 02:00 in F6.

questions.q: Thursday, 07:00 in a bay. You will beat 15 miles back to the base in F5–6, heeled hard. You go below. What do you set?

figure.title: Below, 07:00
lines: Heads and galley sink: low when heeled
Gas valve at the bottle: open
Stove gimbals: locked since the marina

options: Heads and sink seacocks closed, gas on for tea, gimbals locked
Heads and sink seacocks closed, gas off at the bottle, gimbals free
Seacocks open to drain, gas off at the bottle, gimbals locked
Seacocks open, gas on at the bottle, gimbals free for the kettle
questions.why: Heeled, a sink or toilet below the waterline floods back through an open seacock; gas is off when nobody cooks, and the stove swings free.

questions.q: Croatia, 42 ft catamaran, eight crew. You plan two nights in a national-park bay. Reading this on Sunday, what do you plan?

figure.title: Holding tanks
lines: Base: 'full in about a day with eight'

options: Two nights; the tanks last two days if the crew are careful
Two nights; motor out on the second morning to empty them
One night in the park, then out past the limit to empty the tanks
Two nights in the park; empty the tanks at dawn when it is quiet
questions.why: Tanks that fill in a day are emptied daily; the park gets one night and the run past the limit comes before the tanks are full.

questions.q: Monday evening on the catamaran, eight crew. The water is going faster than you planned. You find this. What do you change?
options: Switch the pressure pump off between meals, nothing else
Leave the heads; no showers at all until the next marina
Set the heads to SEA flush; the showers do not matter
Set the heads to SEA flush and ask the crew for short showers
questions.why: Fresh-water flushing on four heads takes tens of litres a day; sea-water flushing and short showers make 400 l last to the marina.

questions.q: The technician switches on the chartplotter, waits for the fix, shows you this and turns to the VHF. What do you ask before he moves on?
options: Whether the card covers the whole cruising ground, and how old the chart is
Whether the plotter also drives the autopilot
Nothing — a plotter with a fix is a working plotter
Whether the screen can be dimmed for night passages
questions.why: Check the chart covers everywhere you will go and ask its edition: an old card misses new marinas, moles and shoals.

questions.q: At the berth the instruments show this, and the base's harbour plan gives 3.0 m here. What has happened?

lines: Harbour plan: 3.0 m at the berth

options: It shows the depth at the harbour mouth, not the berth
The sounder is set to feet — 9.8 ft is 3.0 m; switch the units to metres
The transducer is fouled — the reading is random
The offset is set below the keel — add the draught
questions.why: 9.8 ft = 3.0 m. Greek and Croatian charts are in metres: set depth to metres and distance to nautical miles before you sail.

questions.q: You check the sounder against the harbour plan at the berth. How much water is under the keel right now?

lines: Harbour plan: 3.5 m at the berth

options: 3.3 m — the reading is already the water below the keel
1.4 m — take the draught off the reading
About 1.6 m — the sounder reads from the transducer, not from the keel
3.5 m — the plan is right and the sounder is 0.2 m out
questions.why: No offset: the reading is depth below the transducer, 0.2 m under the surface here. Below the keel: 3.5 − 1.9 ≈ 1.6 m.

questions.q: Going through the plotter, the technician points at the MOB key and moves on. What do you do with it?
options: Press and hold it now to test the DSC distress alert
Note that it is the red button on the VHF handset
Leave it — a casualty is recovered by eye, not from a screen
Ask him to show how it marks and how it clears, then brief the crew on it
questions.why: MOB on the plotter drops a waypoint and shows bearing and distance back; the crew must know where it is before it is needed.

questions.q: On the test run outside the harbour the display shows this. What do you write on the check-in form?
options: Log reads zero — paddle wheel fouled; ask the base to clear it
Nothing — SOG from the plotter does for the week
GPS fault — SOG shows a speed with no log input
Plotter has lost its fix — reboot it at the berth
questions.why: A fouled paddle wheel reads 0; the base pulls and cleans it in the harbour. Note it: speed through the water feeds true wind and the log book.

questions.q: A steady breeze blows across the marina and the burgee flies at the masthead, yet the instruments show this. What do you do?
options: Go up in the bosun's chair and check the sensor yourself
Note it — masthead unit dead; ask the base to look at it before you leave
Tap the display — it needs some minutes to warm up
Accept it — the wind shows only once the boat is sailing
questions.why: The wind instrument should show direction and speed at the berth; a dead one is logged and fixed by the base, not by you aloft.

questions.q: This is the whole of the technician's autopilot briefing. What do you do?

figure.title: Autopilot
lines: Not tried on the test run

options: Accept it — AUTO is the only button you will need
Leave it switched off and hand-steer for the week
Ask to see Standby, a course change and the alarms, and try it on the test run
Read the manual the first time you need it at sea
questions.why: Know how to engage, disengage and what the alarm means before you rely on it — and never in harbours or close quarters.

questions.q: The technician finishes his radio check and leaves the set like this. What do you set before leaving the berth?
options: Channel 16 with squelch fully up to keep it quiet
Channel 16 alone — dual watch drains the battery
Leave 72 — the base calls you on it all week
Channel 16, dual watch on the base's working channel, squelch just above the hiss
questions.why: Under way you keep a watch on 16; dual watch adds the working channel. Squelch fully up mutes weak calls.

questions.q: The technician asks you to do the radio check yourself. How do you make the call?
options: Call the base on its working channel with the boat's name and ask for a readability report
Send a DSC test call to the base on channel 70
Call the base on channel 16 — a check must be heard by all
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for a check
questions.why: Radio checks go on a working channel, not on 16, which is kept for distress, safety and calling.

questions.q: You open the DSC page of the fixed VHF and look at the front of the set. What do you do?
options: Enter the MMSI printed on your own SRC certificate
Ask for the boat's MMSI to be programmed and the cover replaced before you sign
Ignore it — DSC is for ships, not charter yachts
Program the base's phone number in as the MMSI
questions.why: Without the ship's MMSI a DSC alert carries no identity; the cover prevents false alerts. Both are the base's job.

questions.q: The inventory lists a handheld VHF. This is what you find in the chart-table drawer. What do you do?
options: Leave it — the fixed set is the one that matters
Have it struck off the inventory to avoid a deposit claim
Ask for the charger and a full charge before you sign, and note it on the form
Take it as it is — one bar lasts a week on standby
questions.why: The handheld is the radio for the dinghy and the liferaft; flat and without a charger it is useless. Have it charged and listed.

questions.q: The plotter's AIS page shows the harbour traffic. What do you ask the technician?
options: Whether it shows yachts as well as ships
Whether the CPA alarm can be switched off at night
Whether the targets also appear on the VHF screen
Whether it is receive-only or a transponder — can the ferries see you?
questions.why: A receiver shows others to you; only a transponder shows you to them. Know which before you cross a ferry route at night.

questions.q: On the test run, in flat water with no current, you compare the steering compass with the plotter's course over the ground. What do you do?

figure.note: Plotter COG 098° T

options: Look for a phone or speaker by the binnacle, then note the deviation that remains
Set the plotter to magnetic north so that the two agree
Swing the compass yourself before leaving the harbour
Accept 8° — that is the variation in the Ionian
questions.why: Compass 090° + 3°E variation = 093° true; the other 5° is deviation — often a phone on the binnacle. Note it; the plotter steers by GPS.

questions.q: You tick the navigation kit off against the inventory. What do you ask the base for?
options: Nothing — the chartplotter replaces all of it
A pilot book of the area and a current chart, before you sign
A tide table and a set of tidal-stream atlases
A second pair of binoculars for the crew
questions.why: Paper chart and pilot book are the backup and the harbour detail the plotter lacks; an old chart misses new moles and depths.

questions.q: In the chart-table drawer you find this. The technician says nobody uses it any more. What do you do with it during the week?

figure.title: Log book
lines: Columns: time, position, course, log, wind, engine hours
Pencil on a string, half the pages left

options: Use it only if the port police ask to see a log
Fill it in on Friday evening from memory before the check-out
Keep it: each day's departure and arrival, positions and times, engine hours, weather, anything that broke
Leave it — the plotter's track is the boat's record
questions.why: The log is your record for the base, the insurer and the port police: when you were where, the engine hours, the damage you reported.

questions.q: Your mate, who has no radio certificate, asks whether she may use the VHF during the week. What do you tell her?
options: Yes, freely — the boat's ship licence covers the crew
Only the handheld, never the fixed DSC set
No — only the holder of the SRC may touch the set
Yes, under your supervision as the certificated operator — and anyone may call in distress
questions.why: The ship licence covers the set; an SRC holder is in charge of it and crew operate under supervision. Distress may be sent by anyone.
questions.ref: VHF licence — operator and ship station

questions.q: The base's briefing has a weather page. What do you take from it when you plan the week?
options: Sail early, reef before the afternoon, allow for the current in the channel
Ignore tide and current — there is none in the Med
Stay in the marina on every day the Meltemi blows
Plan the long legs for the afternoon, when the wind is up
questions.why: The Med has little tide, but wind-driven currents in channels are real; the Meltemi builds by afternoon, so passages go early.

questions.q: You switch the plotter on at the berth in the base and it shows this. What do you do?

figure.note: Plotter screen at the berth, Sat 17:00

options: Enter a position correction so the boat sits on the berth
Treat it as a stale fix — wait for a lock, then check the position against the berth
Accept it — plotters are good to about half a mile
Assume the base moved the boat overnight
questions.why: Until it has satellites the plotter shows the last stored position. Check the fix time and that the boat sits on its berth before trusting it.
questions.ref: Check-in: GPS fix at the berth

questions.q: You set up the sounder's shallow-water alarm from these figures. What do you set it to?
options: 5 m — anything closer is a nuisance in Greek bays
2.1 m — the draught, exactly
About 3 m — the keel touches at 1.7 m on this sounder, plus a margin
1.0 m as found — the alarm is about the hull, not the keel
questions.why: The keel touches when the sounder reads 2.1 − 0.4 = 1.7 m; add a metre or so of margin. Set it, and tell the crew what the alarm means.

questions.q: The depth sounder is blank and the base answers as shown. What do you do?
options: Sail anyway — the Ionian is deep and you know the bays
Sign now and raise it by phone with the base on Monday
Refuse the boat and demand the deposit back
Have it written on the form as unserviceable and ask for a fix or a lead line before you sail
questions.why: A dead instrument is noted at hand-over so it is not charged to you, and a boat without depth is not fit to anchor: push for a fix.

questions.q: The plotter's display menu looks like this, and Tuesday's plan is to leave Kos at 03:00 for Astypalaia. What do you set up now, at the berth?
options: Find the night palette and the dimmer and try them, so that you can set them in the dark
Switch the plotter off at night and steer by the compass alone
Leave it at 100 % — the brighter the screen, the safer the night
Set AUTO and forget it — the plotter knows when it gets dark
questions.why: At 100 % the screen kills your night vision; the night colours and the dimmer are found in daylight, not fumbled for at 03:00.

questions.q: Reading the plotter again on Sunday morning, before the lines come off, you find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Plotter — routes
lines: XTE alarm: on · arrival alarm: 0.1 M

options: Keep it and mute the two alarms for the week
Clear the active route and the old waypoints, then build your own from the chart
Follow it — the previous crew clearly knew the area
Delete everything, including the base's own harbour marks
questions.why: A stranger's route steers you to their anchorages with their alarms; a plotter left clean shows only what you put in it.

questions.q: The contract allows the Turkish coast from Bodrum to Datça, and the plotter shows this. What do you do before you sign?

figure.title: Plotter — cartography
lines: Turkey coast: base map only, no depths

options: Cross anyway — the AIS and the depth sounder will show the shoals
Rely on the phone app — it streams the Turkish coast when you need it
Ask the base for a card that covers Turkey, or paper charts of that coast — before you sign
Sail by the base map — the harbours over there are easy
questions.why: A base map has no depths or hazards; for every mile the contract lets you sail you need a chart, electronic or paper.
questions.ref: Check-in: chart coverage vs cruising area

questions.q: The technician calls the tablet in the chart table 'the backup plotter'. What do you check before it earns that name?

figure.title: Tablet
lines: Charger: USB lead, no 12 V plug

options: That it has a SIM card — the charts stream from the internet
That it shows AIS targets like the fixed plotter does
Nothing — a backup is only looked at when the plotter dies
That the charts are downloaded for offline use and that it charges from the boat's 12 V
questions.why: A backup that needs a phone signal and a wall socket is no backup: offline charts of the whole area and a 12 V lead, checked now.

questions.q: Your crew's navigator says she will do the week on her phone app and the paper chart is 'for the port police'. What do you tell her?

figure.title: Phone chart app
lines: Battery: 40 % · in the sun at the helm

options: Fine as a third source — the plotter is the primary and the paper chart the backup
Fine, as long as she keeps it in a waterproof case at the helm
Fine — a modern app is more up to date than any plotter card
No — phones are banned from navigation on a charter boat
questions.why: A phone overheats, goes flat and dies with the signal; its crowd-sourced depths are not surveyed. Use it, but not alone.

questions.q: Monday, 11:00, motoring north in the Kos–Kalymnos channel at cruising revs, the displays show this. What is happening?

lines: Cruising revs, flat water, no wind

options: The log is over-reading — the paddle wheel needs calibrating
Nearly 2 kn of current against you — the log is through the water, SOG over the ground
The GPS has a stale fix — SOG lags behind the real speed
The engine is losing power — check the fuel filter
questions.why: STW is what the paddle wheel sees; SOG is what the ground sees. The difference is the current — the briefing warned of 2 kn here.
questions.ref: SOG vs speed through the water

questions.q: Sunday, at anchor in a bay you came into in daylight, your crew ask what the thin line behind the boat on the plotter is. What do you tell them?
options: The route — where the plotter wants to take you next
The anchor circle — the plotter's drag alarm
The track — where the boat has been; it is your way back out in the dark
The chart's depth contour — the boat sits on the 5 m line
questions.why: The track records your positions; following it back out is the safest line in a bay you have already crossed.

questions.q: Thursday's plan is a night passage across the Piraeus ferry route. You set the plotter up on Wednesday evening. What do you set?
options: Alarms off — they wake the off-watch for every fishing boat
CPA 0.1 M, so that only a real collision course sounds
Nothing — with a transponder the ferries will avoid you
A CPA alarm on AIS targets at a range that leaves time to act, and test that it sounds
questions.why: A guard zone or CPA alarm is your second lookout at night; set it wide enough to act on and check that you can hear it from the helm.
questions.ref: AIS — CPA alarm and guard zone

questions.q: Monday, 09:30, weighing anchor in a crowded bay. The crew member at the wheel presses AUTO so that he can go forward and help. What do you do?
options: Take him off it and keep a hand on the wheel — nobody leaves the helm in a crowded anchorage
Have him use wind mode instead — it reacts faster to gusts
Let him — AUTO holds a heading better than a hand does
Let him, but set the heading at the gap between the boats
questions.why: The autopilot steers a heading, not round boats and chains; in harbours and anchorages a person steers and the pilot stays on Standby.

questions.q: Running home under main and genoa with a preventer rigged, the pilot is in wind mode. What happens when the wind veers 20° — and what do you do?
options: The pilot gybes the boat — switch to compass mode at once
The pilot follows the wind 20° to starboard; check the new heading on the chart, then alter or change mode
The pilot alarms and drops to Standby — hand-steer until it settles
Nothing changes — wind mode holds the course over the ground
questions.why: Wind mode keeps the apparent wind angle, so it will not gybe you — but it steers where the wind goes; someone must watch the course.

questions.q: On the test run the autopilot's heading agrees with neither the steering compass nor the plotter. The technician's answer is shown. What do you do?

figure.title: Test run, headings
lines: Technician: “do a couple of circles, it learns”

options: Do the circles yourself after leaving the harbour on Sunday
Set the plotter's heading source to the pilot so that they agree
Ask the base to do the calibration and the heading alignment now, in calm water, and check again
Ignore it — the pilot holds a course even if its number is wrong
questions.why: A pilot with an uncalibrated fluxgate steers badly, especially on turns; calibration is the base's job, done before the boat is signed for.

questions.q: The technician leaves the VHF on low power 'because the base is close'. Thursday you will be 20 miles offshore. What do you do with the setting?

figure.title: Fixed VHF
lines: Base: “leave it, we are 200 m away”

options: Set 25 W now for everything — more power is always better
Leave 1 W all week — 25 W drains the batteries
25 W only on channel 16; the working channels stay on 1 W
1 W in harbour for the base, 25 W for calling at sea — and a distress call always on 25 W
questions.why: Low power keeps a harbour chat local; at sea and in distress you want the full 25 W. Know which key switches it before you need it.

questions.q: Sunday evening, stern-to in Fiskardo, the VHF chatters on 16 all evening and your crew want it off. What do you tell them?
options: In harbour it may go off or down; the watch on 16 is for when you are under way
Switch it to the base's channel — they may call you
It stays on 16 at full volume all week — that is the law
Leave it on 16 at the lowest volume so that nobody hears it
questions.why: A listening watch on 16 is kept under way; alongside at night the set may be off or turned down — the harbour office has its own channel.

questions.q: Tuesday, 15:00, at anchor off Vathi. You come below to the alarm and this screen; your seven-year-old is at the chart table. What do you do, in order?
options: Call the base on the working channel and ask them to cancel it
Cancel on the set, then call the coastguard on 16: boat's name, MMSI, position, 'false alert, cancel'
Nothing — it was undesignated, so nobody will respond to it
Switch the set off — the alert stops when the power goes
questions.why: A DSC distress alert is live until cancelled by voice on 16; the coastguard needs your name, MMSI and position to stand down.
questions.ref: DSC — cancelling a false distress alert

questions.q: The technician does the radio check from the office 50 m away and gets 'loud and clear'. What does that tell you about the masthead antenna?

figure.title: Radio check
lines: Antenna: masthead; deck plug taped up

options: That the antenna is at the masthead, so the range is 25 miles
That the set is on 25 W — on 1 W the office would not hear it
Little — at 50 m a broken antenna cable still gets through; ask for a check from a station miles away
Everything — if it reaches the office, it reaches the coastguard
questions.why: Range comes from the antenna and its cable; a check across the pontoon proves only that the set transmits. Call a station on the horizon.

questions.q: At the helm the depth display is blank, while the one at the chart table shows the depth. What do you tell the base?

figure.title: Instruments
lines: Chart table: depth 3.4 m, wind 8 kn

options: Switch everything off and on again; it will come back by itself
The transducer is dead — a diver must look at the hull before you sail
Nothing — the chart-table display is enough for the week
The helm display or its network plug has failed — the sounder is fine; fix it or note it on the form
questions.why: One instrument reading at one display and not at another is the network, not the sensor: the connector at the helm is the usual culprit.

questions.q: Wednesday morning after a rolly night at anchor, the spare halyard has been slapping the mast and the wind display shows this in a flat calm. What do you do?
options: Look up — the halyard has likely fouled the masthead unit; free it from the deck, tell the base, sail by eye
Reef now and keep it in — the instrument knows better than your eye
Switch the instrument off — a reading like this means the electronics are failing
Stay put and call the base for a replacement unit before you move
questions.why: A halyard wrapped on the masthead unit jams the cups or bends the vane; free it, tell the base, and sail without the number until it is fixed.

questions.q: Sunday evening you motor-sail into the dusk with the main up and the engine on. Which switches go on?
options: TRICOLOUR and STEAMING — the two brightest, at the top
NAV and STEAMING — sidelights, sternlight and the masthead steaming light
NAV alone — the engine is only helping the sail
TRICOLOUR alone — the sail is up, so you are a sailing vessel
questions.why: Engine on means power-driven: sidelights, sternlight and the steaming light (Rule 23). The tricolour is for sail alone.

questions.q: Monday, 22:00, under sail alone, your crew set the panel like this 'to be seen'. What do you change?
options: Add ANCHOR too, so that the ferries see a white light
Leave it — an extra light never hurt anyone at night
Tricolour alone, or NAV alone — never both — and the deck light off; it blinds the helm
Add STEAMING as well — the more light, the better you are seen
questions.why: Rule 25: a sailing vessel shows either the deck-level set or the tricolour, not both; a deck light hides your lights and your night vision.

questions.q: Tuesday, 23:00, anchored in a bay with dinghies crossing to the taverna. The panel is set like this. What do you change?
options: Add STEAMING — a second white at the top is seen further
Swap ANCHOR for TRICOLOUR — it is higher and brighter
Leave it — in a busy bay more lights are safer
NAV off — at anchor you show only the all-round white; sidelights say you are under way
questions.why: Rule 30: an anchored vessel shows an all-round white; sidelights and sternlight are for a vessel under way and confuse a dinghy at night.

questions.q: Ticking off the inventory, your crew ask why the panel has a HORN button when there is an aerosol foghorn in the locker. What do you tell them?
options: The electric horn is the boat's whistle for manoeuvring and fog signals; the aerosol is the backup — test both
The aerosol is for fog only; the button is for calling the marina
The button is for the anchor-drag alarm — the aerosol is the horn
Either will do — a sailing yacht is not required to carry a whistle
questions.why: A vessel over 12 m carries a whistle (Rule 33); the electric horn is it, and a can that sounds without power is the sensible spare.

questions.q: The radar display says this and the contract forbids night sailing. The base cannot fix it this week. Do you accept the boat?
options: Yes, but only after they fit a working scanner, whatever it takes
Yes — written on the form as unserviceable so it is not charged to you; your plan needs no radar
Yes, and say nothing — an unused radar is not your problem
No — refuse the boat, a radar on the list must work
questions.why: Weigh a dead item against your plan: no night or fog passages, so radar is not needed — but it goes on the form, or the check-out charges it to you.
questions.ref: Check-in: radar and defects on the form

questions.q: Your crew plot the plotter's position on the paper chart and it lands 100 m inland. Reading the chart's title block you find this. What is going on?
options: The chart is old and the coast has been built out since
The GPS is 100 m out — normal for a charter plotter
The chart is on another datum — apply the printed shift to GPS positions, or set the plotter to the chart's datum
The plotter's position offset is wrong — reset it to zero
questions.why: GPS positions are WGS84; an older chart on ED50 needs the shift printed in its title block before a GPS position goes on it.

questions.q: Thursday, 07:00, anchored in a bay with no phone signal and a hard sky to the north. How do you get a forecast before deciding to move?

figure.title: Briefing — forecast sources
lines: Coastguard weather: announced on 16, read on a working channel
No phone signal in the northern bays

options: Go by the barometer — a Med summer has no fronts to speak of
Call the coastguard on 16 and ask them to read you the forecast
Motor towards the base until the phone finds a signal, then open the app
Keep 16 on for the coastguard's announcement, listen on the channel the briefing gave, and ask the base on 72
questions.why: Coast stations announce their weather broadcasts on 16 and read them on a working channel; the base knows the local pattern. Both are on the VHF.

questions.q: You take the hand-bearing compass from the drawer and try it on the way out of the harbour, as shown. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Hand-bearing compass — harbour mole
lines: Steering compass, bow on the mole: 093°

options: Use it well away from the binnacle and the winches — at the bow it agrees with the steering compass
Take bearings from the plotter's cursor from now on
The steering compass is 11° out — ask for it to be swung
Average the two readings and use 098° for the week
questions.why: A hand-bearing compass has no deviation card: it is read where there is no iron or magnet — the bow, the pushpit — never beside the wheel.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician briefs the instruments at the starboard helm and heads for the galley. What do you ask?

figure.title: 42 ft catamaran — helms
lines: Starboard: plotter, pilot, depth, both tachos

options: Whether the two helms can run the plotter at the same time
Which readouts repeat at the port helm — you will steer from there when the quay is to port
Whether the port wheel can be locked for the week
Nothing — a catamaran is steered the same from either side
questions.why: On a cat you moor from the helm nearest the quay; if depth, engine revs and the pilot's Standby are only to starboard, you need to know it now.

questions.q: Reading the plotter's set-up page on Sunday morning you find this, left by the last crew. What do you change?
options: Position to decimal degrees, to match the phone app
Depth to feet, to match the depth sounder's display
Distance to nautical miles and speed to knots — the chart, the log and the forecast all use them
Nothing — kilometres are more precise than miles
questions.why: One mile is one minute of latitude on the chart; km on the plotter and miles on the chart is how distances get doubled or halved.

questions.q: Tuesday, in a bay, your crew mark 'the good spot for tomorrow' by pressing the plotter's MOB key. What do you do?
options: Leave it — a waypoint is a waypoint, whatever key put it there
Press MOB again — the second press turns it into a waypoint
Rename it to “anchor spot” in the waypoint list and keep it
Clear it and explain: MOB starts a man-overboard display, on some sets an alert; a spot is a normal waypoint
questions.why: The MOB key is for one thing; a plotter left in MOB mode steers back to a false casualty and, with DSC linked, can send an alert.

questions.q: Tuesday afternoon, under way, the VHF shrieks and shows this. What do you do?
options: Silence it, listen on 16 and note the position; call the coastguard if nobody answers and you can help
Send your own distress relay at once on DSC
Switch the set off — the alarm resets itself on power-up
Press Acknowledge — it stops the alert for everybody at once
questions.why: A received alert is answered by the coast station; a yacht listens on 16, logs the position and acts only if nobody else does.

questions.q: Thursday, 11:00, 24 miles from the base, the displays show this and the base closes at 18:00. When do you arrive, and what do you do?
options: About 13:00 — allow for the current easing as you go
About 17:00 — plan by SOG, six hours at 4 kn; call the base now and say so
No way to tell — the current changes every hour
About 15:00 — the log gives the speed, four hours at 6 kn
questions.why: Time to go is distance over speed over the ground: 24 M / 4 kn = 6 h. Tell the base early — a late boat is a late check-out.

questions.q: The technician counts the lifejackets with you: eight for eight people. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Lifejackets, cockpit locker
lines: Crew list: 6 adults, 2 children (24 kg, 31 kg)

options: Two more adult jackets, straps pulled tight for the children
Nothing — eight jackets for eight people is the rule
Two child lifejackets sized by weight, plus a spare adult one
A note on the form that the children stay in the cockpit
questions.why: One lifejacket per person of the right size, plus spares; an adult jacket slides straight off a child.

questions.q: You open the cover of one inflatable lifejacket and find this. What do you do?
options: Pull the toggle to prove it inflates, then sign the form
Accept them — a jacket is only serviced after it has been used
Screw the cylinder home by hand and sign — the rest is cosmetic
Ask the base to service or replace the jackets before you leave
questions.why: Loose cylinder, red indicator, overdue service: the jacket may not inflate. The base replaces it, you note it.

questions.q: You plan an overnight passage to Kos. What do you do about this before you sign?

figure.title: Harnesses and jackstays
lines: Stowed in the locker, not rigged

options: Ask for new webbing and a tether, rig the jackstays and test each clip
Leave them in the locker — the Dodecanese is coastal sailing
Run a mooring line along the deck instead and sign for them
Rig them as they are; the webbing is only used in daylight
questions.why: You clip on at night and in a sea; faded webbing and a bent hook will not hold a fall.

questions.q: The technician says the liferaft 'is fine, nobody has ever opened it'. What do you do?
options: Take it, but note the date on the form in case
Refuse to sail until an in-date raft is aboard
Accept it — a raft is only serviced after inflation
Ask for a second raft to make up for the old one
questions.why: A raft past its service date may not inflate; an expired raft means you do not leave the pontoon.

questions.q: The raft is in date. You look at the cradle on the coachroof. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Liferaft in its cradle
lines: Painter: coiled in the cradle, not tied

options: Nothing — six is enough: the dinghy takes the other two
A second 6-person raft, with its painter tied to the first
An 8-person raft, painter made fast, padlock swapped for a quick-release
The padlock key kept at the chart table, noted on the form
questions.why: Raft capacity covers everyone aboard; the painter is tied on, and the lashings open by hand or hydrostatic release.

questions.q: You check the flares in the container against the base's list. What goes on the form?
options: 6 flares as counted — the dates are the base's responsibility
2 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — the list is for bigger yachts
4 in date — expired flares still fire, only less reliably
In date: 0 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — base to make up the list
questions.why: Only in-date flares count; write the real count on the form and the base makes up the shortfall before departure.

questions.q: You walk the boat with the base's list of fire gear. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Fire gear, base's list: 3 extinguishers
lines: Aft cabin: 1 kg powder, gauge red, 2022
Engine bay: fire port, no extinguisher beside it

options: Aft cabin extinguisher replaced, one at the engine port, a fire blanket
The aft cabin one shaken hard — settled powder lifts the gauge
Nothing — the galley extinguisher covers a 45 ft monohull
A bucket on a lanyard by the galley instead of a blanket
questions.why: Count, type, gauge in the green and service date per extinguisher; the engine port needs its own, the galley its blanket.

questions.q: The technician hands you a new fire blanket and asks where you want it. Where does it go?
options: In the engine bay, next to the extinguisher port
By the galley, reachable without leaning over the stove
In the cockpit locker, together with the flares
In the forepeak, with the spare sails and the tools
questions.why: A blanket is for a pan or stove fire: mounted beside the galley, on the side away from the flames.

questions.q: You press the EPIRB's test button and read the label. What do you do?

figure.title: EPIRB, bracket by the companionway
lines: Registered: this yacht, MMSI on the label

options: Pull the sea switch to prove it transmits, then sign
Take it — in an emergency you would use the VHF first
Ask for a replacement — battery expired, self-test fails
Write 'EPIRB tested' on the form — the light is just weak
questions.why: Registration, battery date and a passed self-test are the three checks; a dead EPIRB is replaced, never 'tested live'.

questions.q: You open the first-aid kit against the inventory list. What do you do?
options: Sign — a first-aid kit is a courtesy, not an inventory item
Take the whole kit ashore and bring your own instead
Sign — you will buy what you need at the pharmacy in town
List the missing and expired items on the form; the base restocks it
questions.why: The kit is inventory: contents and dates are checked, shortfalls are written down and made up by the base.

questions.q: At the pushpit the technician shows you the horseshoe. You picture this moment on Monday. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Horseshoe lashed on with a knot · no light · no danbuoy

options: The horseshoe on a quick-release clip, with a light and a danbuoy
Nothing — the fenders float and are quicker to throw
The horseshoe lashed tighter so a sea cannot take it
A second horseshoe at the bow for a bow-first pick-up
questions.why: MOB gear goes in seconds: horseshoe and danbuoy on a quick release, a light for the night, a throwing line within reach.

questions.q: The technician points at the emergency tiller under the bunk and moves on. What do you do?

figure.title: Emergency tiller
lines: Found: under the aft cabin bunk
Rudder-stock plate: cockpit sole, aft of the wheel

options: Ask the technician to confirm it fits, and sign
Open the deck plate and fit it on the rudder stock yourself, now
Lash it in the cockpit so it is ready when needed
Note where it is kept — fitting it is for an emergency
questions.why: Find it and try it: a tiller that does not fit, or a plate that will not open, is found at the base, not in a gale.

questions.q: You lift the floorboards with the technician and find this. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Below the floorboards
lines: Bag of softwood bungs: chart table
Electric bilge pump: runs on test

options: Nothing — the electric pump works and the bungs are aboard
The bungs hammered into the seacocks now, to be ready
A bung tied to each seacock and the manual pump handle
A spare electric pump in place of the manual one
questions.why: A bung lives tied to its seacock; the manual pump needs its handle in place — power is the first thing to go.

questions.q: This is what the safety locker holds against the base's list. What goes on the form?
options: The bolt cutters only — the rest you can buy in town
Nothing — a knife, a phone light and AIS cover all of these
The foghorn only — the rest is for offshore boats
Bolt cutters, a full foghorn and spare batteries — base to supply
questions.why: Cutters or a rigging knife for a lost mast, a working horn, a torch with spares; the grab bag you pack yourself.

questions.q: Two of your crew are weak swimmers. Before you leave you ask the technician how a person in the water gets back aboard. What answer do you want?

figure.title: Getting back aboard
lines: Bathing ladder: folds down from the platform
Spare halyard: topping lift to a cockpit winch

options: The bathing ladder drops from the water and a spare halyard reaches a cockpit winch to hoist someone up
The dinghy is launched and the casualty climbs into it
The liferaft is thrown to the casualty as a float
The crew pull the casualty in over the guardrail together
questions.why: Recovery is planned at the base: a ladder that opens from the water and a halyard to a winch for someone who cannot climb; try both.

questions.q: The base manager reads out the emergency numbers at the briefing. Where do they go?

figure.title: Base briefing — numbers
lines: Base office: phone on the key fob

options: In your head — three numbers are easy to remember
On a card by the VHF and in your phone, before you leave
In the base's folder — it stays aboard anyway
In the ship's log, to look up when they are needed
questions.why: Channel 16, the base's phone and the local emergency number: written where any crew member can find them.

questions.q: The technician shrugs: 'the lifebuoy light is extra, nobody checks it'. What do you do?
options: Take his word for it — the base knows the local rules
Buy a light in town and claim it back from the deposit
Ask for the light — the base's list is the law's minimum for the boat
Cross the light off the list before you sign the form
questions.why: The base's list is the national equipment regulation for the flag; every item on it is aboard before you sign.

questions.q: The raft cannot be swapped before Monday. What do you do?
options: Sail with the dinghy inflated on deck in place of the raft
Sign for the boat and ask for a discount instead of a raft
Sail Sunday inside the Ionian and come back Monday for the raft
Stay at the base until a serviced raft is aboard; note it on the form
questions.why: Out-of-date safety gear is replaced before you leave; the base's problem does not become your crew's risk.

questions.q: The boat is signed for and the crew are aboard. What do you do before supper?
options: Walk them through lifejackets, MOB, gas, heads and who does what
Brief the two who have sailed; they pass it on to the rest
Show them the lifejackets; the rest is covered on the first sail
Let them settle in — the briefing is better once under way
questions.why: Your own safety briefing before leaving: jackets and where they are, MOB, gas and heads, swim rules, jobs.

questions.q: The technician shows you the swim ladder. What rule do you set for your crew before anyone swims?
options: Engine in neutral, ticking over to charge the batteries
Engine off and key out, ladder down, then into the water
Engine off, ladder up so nobody climbs near the propeller
Lifejackets on for everyone who goes in the water
questions.why: A turning propeller kills; a ladder down means a tired swimmer can get back aboard.

questions.q: You read the lifejacket labels while the crew are still at the airport. What do you ask the base for?

figure.title: Lifejackets, 6 of 6
lines: Crew: two non-swimmers, one child of 9

options: One auto jacket for the helm; the rest stay in the cabin
Manual jackets for everyone, with a demonstration of the toggle
Auto-inflating jackets with spray hoods for the non-swimmers and the child
Nothing — a manual toggle is easier for a child to find
questions.why: A stunned or weak swimmer cannot pull a toggle; auto inflation and a spray hood keep the airway clear in a sea.

questions.q: Reading the form again on Sunday morning you write your lifejacket rule for the week. Which one?
options: Only when the base's wind limit is reached, as the contract says
Children only; adults decide for themselves when to wear one
Everyone until the first swim stop, then as each one likes
Children always on deck; everyone at night, when reefed, and in the dinghy
questions.why: The skipper sets the rule before leaving: children whenever out of the cabin, all hands at night, in a reef and in the dinghy.

questions.q: The technician walks the side deck with you. With two small children coming aboard, what do you ask for?
options: Netting on the guardrails and two child harnesses, gates clipped shut
Nothing — the children stay below while the boat is moving
Adult harnesses on the shortest setting and the gates tied open
A second guardrail wire run at knee height instead of netting
questions.why: A child slides under a guardrail wire: netting, a harness that fits and closed gates are the base's job before you leave.

questions.q: Tuesday, 23:00, at anchor off Fiskardo. Two crew want to take the dinghy ashore for a drink. What do you insist on?
options: Oars only — the outboard is too loud for the anchorage at night
Lifejackets on, a torch, kill cord on the wrist and a time to be back
Nothing — 300 m is a short run and the outboard is reliable
A lifejacket for the one who drives; the passenger holds the torch
questions.why: A dinghy at night is where charter crews drown: jackets worn, a light to be seen, the kill cord on, and the skipper knows when they are due.

questions.q: Your crew ask how the liferaft is actually launched. What do you tell them?
options: Open the canister on deck, inflate the raft and lower it over the side
Throw the canister to windward so the raft drifts back to the boat
Check the painter is tied on, throw the canister to leeward, pull the painter until it fires, board dry
Throw the canister, swim to it and pull the painter from the water
questions.why: Painter made fast to the yacht, canister over the lee side, a sharp pull on the painter inflates it; step in dry, cut the painter last.

questions.q: Monday, motoring out of Alimos, smoke comes from the engine box under the companionway steps. What is the drill you set on Saturday?

figure.title: Engine fire drill
lines: Fire port: on the step panel, cap on
Gas valve: at the bottle, cockpit locker
Fuel shut-off: by the engine panel

options: Open the engine box, find the flame and aim the extinguisher at it
Pour sea water down the step while someone calls the base
Keep the engine running to reach the quay, then fight the fire
Stop the engine, fuel and gas off, extinguisher through the port, bay kept shut
questions.why: Opening the bay feeds the fire with air; through the port the powder fills the space while fuel and gas are cut and the crew get ready to call.

questions.q: The 36 ft boat has no fire port. The technician says the engine is 'right under the steps anyway'. What do you ask for and plan?

figure.title: Engine access, 36 ft
lines: Engine box: lifts with the companionway steps

options: A second extinguisher by the companionway; lift the step a crack and aim through the gap
Nothing — on a small boat one extinguisher in the forecabin is enough
A port drilled in the step by the base before you leave on Sunday
The forecabin extinguisher moved to the engine box, inside the lid
questions.why: Without a port you open the box the least you can and discharge through the crack; the extinguisher lives where the fire is fought, not in the bow.

questions.q: You find this in the cockpit locker. The technician says 'they are all together, easier to count'. What do you ask?
options: Two in the locker and one by the wheel, where the skipper sits
Each one mounted in its bracket — galley, companionway, aft cabin — before you sign
All three by the engine, where a boat fire usually starts
Nothing — three in date, counted and photographed, is the check
questions.why: A fire below is fought from where you are, with the extinguisher at hand: one by each escape route and the galley, not in a locker on deck.

questions.q: The EPIRB passes its self-test. You read the label against the boat's papers. What do you do?

figure.title: EPIRB label
lines: MMSI: not the one on the radio licence

options: Stick the boat's name over the label and note it on the form
Nothing — the beacon transmits a position whatever name it carries
Ask the base to swap it for this yacht's own EPIRB, or re-register it, before you leave
Take it — the base's phone number is what the rescue centre uses
questions.why: A beacon alerts under its registration: rescuers look for the wrong yacht, crew and base contact. The base fixes the registration, not you.

questions.q: Friday evening at anchor, last night of the week. Your crew find the expired flares the base left aboard and want a show. What do you say?

figure.title: Flares aboard
lines: 3 expired — in a bag, 'for the base'

options: Yes, one handheld well away from the other boats, as practice
Yes, if you call the coastguard first so they do not come out
Yes, the smoke only — orange is not a distress colour at night
No — a red flare is a distress signal; the expired ones go back to the base for disposal
questions.why: Any red flare means distress and launches a rescue; expired pyrotechnics are returned to the base, never fired for fun or practice.

questions.q: Saturday evening, the crew unpack. One of them hands you this list. What do you do with it?
options: Write it on your crew sheet, stow each medicine where you both know, tell the co-skipper
File it with the base's papers so the office has it
Keep it to yourself — medical details are private aboard
Ask them to manage it themselves; your job is the boat
questions.why: The skipper knows who takes what and where it is, and a second person knows too, so a collapse at sea is not a mystery.

questions.q: Sunday, 08:00, departure at nine. A crew member who has never sailed asks when to take the seasickness tablet. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Sunday morning
lines: Forecast: F4–5 on the nose, short sea
Tablets: in the first-aid kit, in date

options: Not at all — tablets make him drowsy and useless on the winch
Now, with breakfast — an hour before leaving, then stay on deck and take the helm
After an hour at sea, once he knows whether he needs it
When he first feels queasy — before that it is wasted
questions.why: Tablets work only if taken before the motion starts; food, fresh air, the horizon and a job at the wheel do the rest.

questions.q: Monday, the genoa sheet runs through a crew member's palm during a tack. The first-aid kit is as restocked on Saturday. What do you do?

figure.title: Rope burn, right palm
lines: Skin red and raw across the palm
Kit: burn dressings, sterile water, bandages

options: Ice from the fridge straight on the skin until it goes numb
Cover it in antiseptic cream and tape it tight so he can winch
Cool it under fresh water for 15–20 minutes, then a burn dressing, loosely bandaged
Rinse it in sea water and let the sun dry it out
questions.why: A rope burn is a burn: cool with fresh water, cover with a clean non-stick dressing; no cream, no ice, no sea water in an open wound.

questions.q: Your crew gather for the safety briefing. One of them says he has sailed for twenty years and goes below. What do you do?

figure.title: Saturday 19:30, briefing
lines: His boat: a tiller 30-footer, no gas, no raft
This boat: 45 ft, gas, raft on the coachroof
Jackets: a type he has not used

options: Skip the briefing — with an old hand aboard you have backup
Make him give the briefing instead, since he knows the drills
Let him go — an experienced hand will find things when needed
Call him back — the gear and its places are this boat's, and he may be the one who needs them
questions.why: The briefing is about this boat: where the gas valve, the raft and the jackets are and who does what. Experience elsewhere does not cover it.

questions.q: Going through the companionway with the technician you check what closes the boat in a sea. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Companionway and hatches
lines: Washboards: one of two, no lanyard
Companionway hatch: slides, no lock from inside

options: The second washboard with a lanyard, the hatch dog fixed and the seal replaced
A sheet of plywood cut to size, kept in the lazarette for storms
The forehatch taped shut for the week; the rest is fine
Nothing — in the Med you sail with the companionway open anyway
questions.why: Washboards and hatches are what keep a knockdown or a boarding sea out of the boat: both boards, tied on, and dogs that close.

questions.q: The base's grab bag turns out to be an empty dry bag. Sunday morning you fill it yourself. What goes in?

figure.title: Grab bag — your list
lines: Boat: handheld VHF, EPIRB on its bracket
Papers: passports, boat papers in the chart table

options: The passports only — everything else is replaced by the base
Handheld VHF, flares, torch, water, the papers, the medicines, phone in a dry pouch
The liferaft's own pack is enough; the bag is for valuables
Food for a week, the chart folio and the ship's log
questions.why: The bag goes into the raft with you: a way to call and be seen, water, documents, the crew's medicines, a phone; packed before leaving.

questions.q: The technician hands you the throwing line in its bag. Your crew ask how it is used. What do you show them?

figure.title: Throwing line
lines: Floating line, 20 m, in a bag
Bag end: loop for the hand

options: Tie the bag to the horseshoe and throw both at the person
Throw the bag straight at the person so it lands in their hands
Keep hold of the loop, throw the bag past and upwind of the person, let them grab the line, pull in
Take the line out of the bag, coil it, and throw the coil
questions.why: Hand loop held, bag thrown beyond the casualty so the line falls across them; it lives in the cockpit, not under the fenders.

questions.q: A crew member shows you his own personal locator beacon. What do you tell him?
options: Hand it to you; the skipper holds all the beacons
Leave it in the bag — the yacht's EPIRB covers everyone aboard
Register it to the yacht at the base office before you sail
Clip it to his lifejacket and tell his contact which yacht and where he is this week
questions.why: A PLB is personal: worn on the jacket, and the registered contact knows the trip so the rescue centre has the right picture.

questions.q: Your crew ask what to do if the frying pan catches fire. What do you tell them?
options: Gas off at the stove, fire blanket over the pan from the side, leave it covered
A pan of water over it, quickly, before it spreads to the curtains
The powder extinguisher straight into the pan from above
Carry the pan up to the cockpit and throw it over the side
questions.why: Water on burning oil explodes into flame; the blanket smothers it, the gas is shut, the pan stays where it is until cold.

questions.q: Your crew ask why the base's equipment list is different from the one they know from home. Whose rules apply to this boat?
options: The skipper's licence country — German rules follow the skipper
The flag of the boat — the Croatian regulation on the base's list
Whichever is the strictest of the countries represented
The country of the majority of the crew aboard
questions.why: Safety equipment is required by the flag state of the vessel; the base's list is that regulation for this boat.

questions.q: You find this in the locker. The technician says 'hang it up if it gets foggy'. What do you do?

figure.title: Cockpit locker
lines: Radar reflector: folding octahedral, in its bag

options: Lash it to the pushpit where it is quick to reach
Leave it in the bag — fog is rare in the Ionian in summer
Hoist it under the spreader now and leave it up all week
Hoist it only at night, and take it down for sailing by day
questions.why: A GRP hull barely shows on a ferry's radar: the reflector goes up high at the base and stays there, day and night.
