questions.q: The technician shows you where the lifejackets live. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Lifejackets found
lines: Forepeak, under the spare genoa and the fenders

options: One in the cockpit for the helm; the rest stay in the bow
Put on now and worn until the crew are used to them
Left where they are — the forepeak is dry and they stay clean
Moved to the cockpit locker or by the companionway, one per person, reachable in seconds
questions.why: Jackets are reached in seconds from the cockpit when it goes wrong, not dug out from under a sail in the bow.

questions.q: Your crew ask what the little light and the whistle on the lifejacket are for. What do you tell them?
options: To be found at night — the light is seen, the whistle is heard over the engine
To attract the next ferry so it alters course
To mark the jacket as serviced — the base checks both
To be used at the swim stop when the ladder is up
questions.why: A head in the water is invisible at night: the light and the whistle are how the boat finds you; show the crew where they are.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician shows you the liferaft. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Liferaft, catamaran
lines: Stowed: cockpit locker under the table
On top: 6 fenders, the passerelle, the hose
Painter: tied to a ring in the locker

options: Nothing — a locker keeps the raft dry and out of the sun
The locker cleared so the raft comes out in seconds, nothing stowed on top
The fenders left on top — they float and are useful too
The raft moved to the trampoline, lashed to the crossbeam
questions.why: A raft under the fenders and the passerelle is not launched in a hurry; its locker holds the raft and nothing else.

questions.q: Thursday, 02:00, on passage to Rhodes. The lazyjack has parted and the crew on watch wants to go forward to clear it. What do you insist on?

figure.title: Night watch, 02:00
lines: He has a tether, clipped nowhere
You are asleep; one other crew below

options: Wait till daylight — nobody goes forward at night, whatever breaks
Go without the tether — it snags on the lazyjacks at the mast
Clip on before leaving the cockpit, on the high side, and wake you first
Clip on at the mast once he gets there, so the tether does not drag
questions.why: Nobody leaves the cockpit at night unclipped or unseen; the jackstays you rigged at the base are for exactly this moment.

questions.q: Thursday, 05:30. You have decided to leave this bay now, ahead of Friday's gale; the passage home is forecast as shown. What do you do before the anchor comes up?

figure.title: Thursday 05:30, at anchor
lines: Crew: 6, two never sailed in a blow

options: Shake out the reefs and set full sail to make the most of the morning breeze
Leave the reefing and harnesses until the wind reaches F6 on the way
Keep the washboards out and the forehatch open for air until the sea builds
Reef at anchor, jackstays rigged, everyone in jackets and harnesses, washboards in, hatches dogged, loose gear stowed
questions.why: Everything is done in the calm of the bay: a reef, harnesses or a forehatch are hard and dangerous to sort out once the wind arrives.

questions.q: Wednesday, motoring on the 42 ft catamaran, a crew member falls off the transom steps. You come back to him. What do you do before anyone reaches down?

figure.note: Both engines ahead · recovery at the stern steps

options: Both engines off and the keys out, then bring him to the steps
Keep steerage on both and let him swim to the steps
Port engine off — the steps are on the port hull
Both in neutral, ticking over, so you can hold position
questions.why: Two propellers either side of the steps: a catamaran recovers at the transom only with both engines stopped, as in your swim rule.

questions.q: Thursday, entering a bay in Croatia, the wheel suddenly turns freely. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday, 16:00
lines: Under full main and genoa, F4
Emergency tiller: tried at check-in, aft cabin

options: Steer with the sails to the harbour 3 miles on and berth under sail
Sails down, engine idle, fit the emergency tiller you tried on Saturday, anchor in the bay and call the base
Drop the anchor where you are and wait for the base to send a tow
Send someone to find the tiller while you hold course on the engine
questions.why: What you tried at the base works now: way off, tiller on the stock, somewhere safe to anchor, then the base; the harbour can wait.

questions.q: Thursday, 22:00: engine dead, drifting onto a lee shore, MAYDAY sent. A ferry's lights appear 2 miles off. Which flare, and how?
options: The orange smoke first — it lasts longest and is seen furthest
A handheld aimed at the ferry's bridge so the officer sees it
A parachute first, downwind, then a handheld over the lee side as the ferry closes
Both parachutes at once, straight up, then the smoke
questions.why: Parachute to be seen far off, handheld to be pinpointed; fired downwind over the lee side, never at a vessel, and night is no time for smoke.

questions.q: Tuesday, 14:00, motoring in no wind at 36 °C. Your crew report this about the one who was on the foredeck all morning. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday, 14:00
lines: Drank one small bottle since breakfast

options: A swim stop — the sea cools him faster than anything
A cold beer and a salt tablet, then back on deck in a hat
Send him to his bunk to sleep it off till the harbour
Into the shade now, cool him with wet cloths and fanning, sips of water, and call for medical advice
questions.why: Hot dry skin and confusion is heatstroke, not tiredness: cool him fast, fluids if he can swallow, and get advice — it kills.

questions.q: The technician reads you the ground-tackle line of the inventory in the office and offers you the pen. What do you do?
options: Go to the bow first and see the anchor and the chain yourself
Sign, and check the anchor on the first evening at anchor
Ask for a heavier anchor; 25 kg is too light for 45 ft
Sign — the inventory is the base's own record of the boat
questions.why: You sign for what you have seen: anchor type and size on the roller, chain in the locker.

questions.q: You ask about the chain marks. 'Every ten metres, you will see them,' says the technician. What do you do?

figure.title: Anchor chain
lines: Colour code: not on the form

options: Count the marks yourself the first time you anchor
Ask for the colour code and write it on the check-in form
Take his word — paint marks are the same across the fleet
Ask for the chain to be re-marked before departure
questions.why: Scope is laid by the marks; without the code you do not know how much chain is out.

questions.q: You lift the locker lid and trace the chain to its end. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Anchor locker
lines: Bitter end: shackled hard to the eye bolt

options: Ten metres of rope spliced on to make the chain longer
Nothing — a shackled end can never be lost overboard
A rope lashing at the bitter end that you can cut in an emergency
A bigger shackle — the last link takes the whole load
questions.why: The bitter end is tied with rope so the whole rode can be cut away if you must leave the anchor fast.

questions.q: On the foredeck the technician points at the two foot switches and hands you the windlass remote. What do you do before you leave the bow?
options: Note 'windlass OK' — he has just shown you the controls
Try the remote only — the foot switches are a backup
Try it on the first anchorage, with a real load on the chain
Run the chain out and in from both switches and from the remote
questions.why: Test every control both ways at the pontoon; a dead 'up' switch is found at the base, not in a bay.

questions.q: During the test the windlass motor hums and runs, but the gypsy does not turn and the chain stays where it is. What do you do?
options: Tighten the clutch with the windlass handle and try again
Reset the breaker at the panel and try again
Note the windlass as faulty and plan to anchor by hand
Ask for the windlass motor replaced before departure
questions.why: A slipping clutch: the gypsy is not locked to the shaft. The handle tightens it — and frees it to lower by hand.

questions.q: You press the foot switch and nothing happens. You go below and find the panel like this. What do you do?
options: Write 'windlass dead' on the check-in form and ask for an electrician
Switch the windlass breaker on, start the engine and try again
Ask the base to charge the batteries overnight before you test it
Lower the anchor on the clutch to test the chain run instead
questions.why: The windlass has its own breaker and is used with the engine running — its current would flatten the house bank.

questions.q: The technician showed you the snubber at check-in. On your first night you are anchored as drawn and the wind is building. What do you do with the chain?
options: Set the chain stopper and keep the snubber for a real gale
Leave the chain on the gypsy — the windlass brake is made for it
Hook the snubber on, take the load to a cleat and slacken the chain on the gypsy
Lead the chain round the mast foot and make it fast there
questions.why: The windlass is not a mooring point: the snubber takes the snatch loads, the chain stopper backs it up.

questions.q: At the bow the technician opens the locker and you see this. He says the shower hose does the chain. What do you do?
options: Ask for a bucket and bail the locker out once a day
Accept it — the locker empties itself once you are sailing
Accept the shower hose — it rinses the chain just as well
Ask for the drain cleared and the washdown shown working, and note both
questions.why: Standing water and mud in the locker rot the chain and the boat; the washdown is listed, so it must work.

questions.q: You find the bow roller like this. 'It has been that way all season,' says the technician. What do you do?
options: Photograph it, write it on the check-in form and ask for a pin before you leave
Refuse the boat until the roller is replaced with a new one
Say nothing now and call it pre-existing damage at check-out
Take his word — a season of use shows that it holds
questions.why: Damage not on the form is yours at check-out; the pin keeps the anchor from jumping the roller at sea.

questions.q: The technician ticks the second anchor without going aft: 'It is in the lazarette.' What do you do?
options: Check the warp length only; the anchor is a standard item
Ask him to dig it out and show you the anchor, the warp and the shackle together
Ask for a second all-chain rode in place of the rope warp
Tick it — a kedge is hardly ever used on a week's charter
questions.why: A kedge without its warp or shackle is no anchor; see the whole kit and where it lives.

questions.q: You anchor for lunch where the figure shows, the way the briefing described. How much chain do you lay, counting the marks?
options: Two marks, 20 m: three times the charted depth
Seven marks, 70 m: all of it, nothing held back
Three marks, 30 m: 4–5 × the 7 m from roller to seabed
One mark, 10 m: the chain's own weight holds in F3
questions.why: Med scope with all chain is 4–5 × the depth measured from the bow roller, not the waterline.

questions.q: You read the mooring kit against your week. What do you ask the base for before you sign?
options: Nothing — the lazy lines take the load, and 10 m reaches any quay
A second pair of springs; stern-to is held by the anchor chain
Only the long line — 10 m stern lines are the standard kit
Stern lines of at least a boat length, and a long line for taking lines ashore
questions.why: A stern line goes to the quay and back; in a bay or at a quay without lazy lines you need a long line ashore.

questions.q: The technician makes a stern line up on the midships cleat to show you the cleat hitch. The line looks like this. What do you do?

figure.note: Hard, kinked; cover worn through in one place

options: Ask for it replaced before departure and note the swap on the form
Accept it and turn it end for end so the chafe sits inboard
Tape over the worn part and keep that line as a spring only
Accept it — a stiff line is a strong line, it has not stretched
questions.why: A chafed, hardened line parts in the first Meltemi night; mooring lines are the base's to replace, not yours.

questions.q: The technician counts the fenders out on the pontoon. What do you do?
options: Ask for all the fenders replaced with new ones for a 45 ft boat
Ask for the flat one pumped or swapped, and note the torn cover on the form
Accept them all — fenders are consumables and the deposit covers them
Say nothing — a half-flat fender still works against a quay
questions.why: Count, size and condition go on the form; a flat fender is a scraped hull you will pay for.

questions.q: The passerelle is lying on the coachroof, untied. The technician says you will rig it at the first quay. What do you do?
options: Tie it to the guardrail with its own bungee for the passage
Leave it — a passerelle does not move on a coachroof
Have him show you the fitting and the lashing, and lash it down before you leave
Ask for it stowed in the base until you need it at a quay
questions.why: A loose plank goes overboard on the first heel; see how it fits and how it is lashed for a passage.

questions.q: At the quay demonstration the technician hauls the lazy line up bare-handed. You will also pick up buoys in the bays. What do you check is aboard before you sign?

figure.note: Slime line hauled up by hand

options: A second boat hook and a bucket for the mud off the line
Spare lazy lines of your own for quays that have none
A long lanyard so the lazy line can be tied to the pulpit
Gloves for the slime line and a boat hook that locks when extended
questions.why: Lazy lines are slimy and cut hands; the boat hook that does the buoys and lines must lock, not telescope back.

questions.q: The dinghy is in the water at the pontoon. The technician goes through it with you and you note this. What do you do?

figure.title: Dinghy on the inventory
lines: Boat name: not on the tubes

options: Ask for a plug and the boat's name on the tubes before you sign for it
Sign and buy a plug and a marker pen in town
Sign — a missing plug only matters when you tow it
Refuse the dinghy and ask for the deposit reduced
questions.why: No plug means a swamped dinghy; without the boat's name a stolen or drifted tender cannot be returned.

questions.q: First evening, stern-to on the Lefkas town quay on your 42 ft catamaran. You read this clause again. What do you do with the dinghy?

figure.title: Contract — dinghy & outboard
lines: Not covered by the damage waiver
Lifted at night; not towed at sea

options: Leave it afloat on its painter — the quay is lit and busy all night
Dinghy up on the davits, lifting lines cleated, cable and padlock on
Tow it tomorrow and padlock it only in the empty bays
Tie it alongside, outboard on, with the kill cord in your pocket
questions.why: The dinghy is the first thing stolen and the one thing the deposit does not cover; lift it and lock it every night.

questions.q: The technician lifts the outboard onto the dinghy and says it 'runs fine'. What do you do?
options: Check the fuel level only — the engine was serviced over the winter
Ask him to start it and watch from the pontoon
Start it at the pontoon yourself, in neutral, and pull the kill cord to see it stop
Take his word and start it the first time you need to go ashore
questions.why: An outboard is tested where help is: it starts, it stops on the cord, and you have seen fuel in the tank.

questions.q: The base manager shows you the plan for Friday. Where and how do you bring the boat back?

figure.note: Briefing: back by 17:00 on Friday

options: Stern-to at C on your own anchor, as at a town quay
Alongside at A for fuel, and leave the boat there
On a buoy at D and wait for the base to call you in
Stern-to at B on the lazy line, by 17:00 on Friday
questions.why: The base takes the boat back where and how the briefing says: its own berth, the lazy line, no anchor, on time.

questions.q: You find this in the cockpit locker during the inventory count. When does it go up during your week?
options: Hoisted forward whenever you lie at anchor by day
Hoisted at night with the anchor light, as a pair
Hoisted at the masthead when you motor-sail by day
Only in a channel, where ships must see you anchored
questions.why: COLREGs Rule 30: a vessel at anchor shows one ball forward by day and the all-round white light at night.

questions.q: Sunday, 09:00, you are leaving the base for a 20-mile passage. What do you do at the bow before you go?
options: Switch the breaker off and leave the chain on the gypsy
Close the stopper, fit the pin and switch the windlass breaker off
Leave all three as they are — you may need the anchor in a hurry
Tie the anchor to the pulpit and leave the breaker on
questions.why: At sea the chain sits on the stopper and the pin, not the gypsy; a live breaker lets a kicked foot switch drop the anchor.

questions.q: Your crew ask how to tie the fenders on before the first quay. What do you show them?

figure.note: Height set for the quay, then made fast

options: A bowline round the guardrail, so the fender can never slip down
A reef knot round the stanchion, pulled tight
A clove hitch with a slipped half hitch, so the height changes fast
Two half hitches on the top wire, pulled hard by hand
questions.why: A clove hitch is re-set in seconds for a quay or a pontoon; the slipped half hitch stops it shaking loose.

questions.q: The technician hands you the boat's keyring. On the dinghy's transom you find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Outboard on the dinghy
lines: Lock key: on the boat's keyring

options: Keep the key in the dinghy so any of the crew can unlock it
Take the lock bar off — it gets in the way of lifting the outboard
Lock it only at night, when the dinghy is up on the davits
Try the key in the lock now, and lock it whenever the dinghy is left
questions.why: An outboard on open clamp screws is lifted off in a minute; a key that will not turn is found at the pontoon, not ashore.

questions.q: The catamaran's dinghy hangs on the davits at the base, and rain is forecast tonight. What do you do with the drain plug?

figure.title: Davits, at the base
lines: Bow and stern lifting lines: cleated

options: Pull it out so the rain drains, and fit it again before launching
Lower the dinghy into the water for the night instead
Leave it in and bail the dinghy out in the morning
Leave it in — the water steadies the dinghy on the davits
questions.why: Rain in a hanging dinghy weighs hundreds of kilos on the davits; the plug goes back in before it touches the water.

questions.q: Monday afternoon the crew take the dinghy to a shingle beach. The one at the tiller asks you how to land. What do you tell him?
options: Come in fast so the dinghy slides up the beach clear of the waves
Stop the outboard and tilt it up before the shallows, then row or wade in
Keep it running in gear until the bow touches the shingle
Tilt it halfway and leave it idling so you can back off later
questions.why: A propeller in shingle loses its blades and its shear pin; the motor is stopped and lifted, the dinghy walked in.

questions.q: Your first anchoring on the 42 ft catamaran: the chain is out and the boat is lying back. What do you do with this from the locker?

figure.title: Anchor locker, catamaran
lines: Bridle: two legs, one to each bow

options: Hook it on, then winch the chain tight so the bridle stays slack
Keep it for a gale — in a settled bay the chain alone is enough
Hook it on and ease chain until both legs take the load, chain slack behind
Make one leg fast on the windlass side and leave the other loose
questions.why: The bridle spreads the load to both bows and stops the cat sheering about; the chain behind it carries nothing.

questions.q: Tuesday, 18:00, a paid buoy field in a Croatian bay. Your crew member at the bow has the buoy's ring on the boat hook. What does he do next?

figure.title: Buoy field, Croatia
lines: Buoy with a ring on top

options: Hold the ring while you motor gently to keep the boat on it
Lead the buoy's pick-up line onto the gypsy and take it in
Hook the boat hook on and tie its handle to the pulpit
Pass a line through the ring and back to the same cleat, then a second one
questions.why: A line doubled through the ring is let go from aboard; two lines share the gusts, and none goes on the windlass or the hook.

questions.q: This week's boat is a 36 ft monohull with a mixed rode. You look at the bow fitting and the locker. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: 36 ft — ground tackle
lines: Chain: 25 m, then 40 m of rope
Bow roller: sharp edge on the cheek

options: The sharp cheek smoothed, and a chafe sleeve where the rope meets the roller
Nothing — rope stretches and takes the snatch better than chain
Twenty more metres of chain, so the rope never leaves the boat
A second rope rode, in case the first one parts
questions.why: A rope rode on a sharp roller chafes through in one windy night; the edge and the sleeve are sorted before you sign.

questions.q: Thursday night, stern-to at a town quay with a swell running in. The stern lines are creaking and you see this. What do you do?

figure.note: Line sawing on the fairlead and the quay edge

options: Swap it for a spring line until the swell dies down
Fit chafe guards at the fairlead and the quay edge, and ease the line a little
Take the line in hard so it stops working on the fairlead
Leave it — the base replaces worn lines at check-out
questions.why: Chafe, not strain, parts mooring lines; a sleeve or a length of hose where the line moves keeps it whole till morning.

questions.q: Monday, 17:00, your crew have hung the fenders as they were on the base pontoon. You are coming alongside this quay for fuel. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Fuel quay, Lefkas
lines: Stone quay: top 1.2 m above water
Fenders: hung low, as at the pontoon

options: Lay them on deck and hold one by hand at the bow
Leave them low — the boat touches a quay at the waterline
Raise the fenders to where the topsides will touch the quay face
Take them in — the tyres on the quay do the fenders' job
questions.why: Fenders go where hull and quay meet; at a high quay that is up the topsides, and tyres leave black marks you pay for.

questions.q: Wednesday evening, stern-to at a quay. You plan to leave at 06:00, when nobody will be ashore. How do you get the stern lines back aboard?

figure.note: Leaving at 06:00, nobody on the quay

options: Leave them on the rings and ask the base to collect them later
A crew member casts off and jumps aboard as the boat moves away
Untie them tonight and lie on the anchor alone till morning
Just before leaving, double each one back through its ring and slip it from aboard
questions.why: A line doubled through the ring is let go from the boat: nobody jumps a widening gap, and nothing is left on the quay.

questions.q: Monday, 18:00, a Croatian marina with lazy lines. Your crew member lifts the lazy line off the quay and walks it forward while you hold the boat in reverse. What do you tell him first?

figure.title: Lazy line, marina
lines: Line from the quay to a block on the seabed
Stern 2 m off, engine in reverse
Crew walking it forward, slack in the water

options: Keep the slack out of the water and away from the stern — it fouls the propeller
Make it fast on the stern cleat first and walk it forward later
Let it sink as he walks, so it does not catch on the keel
Take it to the windlass and haul the bow down onto it
questions.why: A slack lazy line under a boat in reverse wraps the propeller; keep it taut and high until it is on the bow cleat.

questions.q: Monday, 17:00, a town quay with no lazy lines; you will go in stern-to between two boats. Where do you drop the anchor?

labels: town quay · gap between two boats
figure.note: Boat 14 m · depth 5 m · chain 70 m

options: At A, and pay out more chain once the stern lines are on
At B: about four boat lengths out, square to the gap, then reverse in
At C: far out, so you have all the scope there is
At A: close in, so your chain stays clear of the others' anchors
questions.why: Four boat lengths in 5 m gives real scope and still reaches the quay with chain to spare; too close and it never bites.
questions.ref: Base briefing: stern-to with the anchor

questions.q: Monday, 13:00, your first anchoring of the week: the chain is out and the boat is lying back. How do you know the anchor holds before the crew swim?
options: Read the depth twice; if it has not changed, it holds
Wait ten minutes; if the boat has not moved, it is set
Reverse slowly, then to about 1,500 rpm, and watch a transit on the shore
Look at the chain: tight and straight down means it holds
questions.why: An anchor is set by backing down on it under power; a transit or the plotter shows a drag before the crew are in the water.

questions.q: Tuesday, 09:00, leaving a bay in F4. Your crew member on the remote starts the windlass with the chain bar-tight and the boat lying well back. What do you do?
options: Let him carry on — the windlass is rated to pull the boat
Give more revs astern to break the anchor out first
Have him lift in short bursts so the motor can cool between them
Motor slowly up towards the chain so the windlass only lifts the slack
questions.why: The windlass lifts chain, it does not haul the boat; motor up gently while the bow shows the helm where the chain leads.

questions.q: Your crew member at the bow guides the chain onto the gypsy with his hand while you press the remote. What do you tell him?
options: Hands clear: stop the windlass, clear the chain with it off, then carry on
Fine at slow speed — the motor stops itself if it jams
Gloves on, and then it is safe to guide the chain by hand
Fine, as long as your thumb stays near the up button
questions.why: A gypsy takes a finger off with one link; chain is cleared with the windlass stopped, never by hand while it runs.

questions.q: In the windlass test the anchor comes up the wrong way round and jams in the roller; the last metres of chain are twisted. What do you ask the base for?
options: The chain turned end for end in the locker
A swivel at the anchor, its pin moused, before you leave
Nothing — you will turn the anchor by hand at the bow each time
A heavier anchor, which settles the right way up
questions.why: A swivel lets the anchor turn as it comes home; a twisted chain jams the roller and the gypsy just when you need them.

questions.q: Tuesday, 22:00, anchored for the night. You set the plotter's anchor alarm. What radius do you give it?

figure.title: Night anchorage, F4
lines: Boat 14 m, GPS at the stern
Alarm centred on the drop point

options: 200 m: wide, so the swinging at night does not wake you
15 m: tight, so it warns you as soon as the boat moves
About 55 m: the chain out plus a boat length, with a little margin
35 m: the chain out, nothing added for the boat
questions.why: The GPS swings on the chain plus the boat's length; tighter wakes you all night, wider tells you too late.

questions.q: The dinghy is on the pontoon, soft. The technician hands you the foot pump and goes off to another boat. What do you check as you pump it up?

figure.title: Dinghy, soft on the pontoon
lines: Valve stems: some up, some down

options: Pump one chamber hard — the others share the same air
Pump until just soft to the touch — the sun will do the rest
Leave the valves as they are and pump until the pump goes stiff
Each valve in the inflate position, every chamber hard, then listen for a leak
questions.why: A valve left open empties as fast as you pump; each chamber is filled on its own and checked for a slow leak before you sign.

questions.q: Monday, 12:30, you come into a clear-water bay for lunch. Where do you drop the anchor?

figure.note: Depth 6–8 m across the bay

options: B: on the pale sand, where the anchor digs in and you can see it
C: close under the rocks, sheltered from the wind
Anywhere — in 6–8 m all chain holds on any bottom
A: in the dark weed, which holds the anchor like a net
questions.why: An anchor skids over thick weed and jams in rock; in clear water the pale sand is the holding ground.

questions.q: Wednesday, a 4-mile hop in a calm on your 36 ft monohull, which has no davits. Your crew want to tow the dinghy as it is, outboard on. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — dinghy
lines: Outboard: on the pushpit when towing

options: Tilt the outboard up and leave it on the dinghy's transom
Outboard onto the pushpit bracket, then tow on a painter clear of the propeller
Tow it as it is — 4 miles in a calm is too short to matter
Tow it on a 1 m painter, tight to the stern, outboard on
questions.why: A towed dinghy can flip and drown its outboard, which the deposit does not cover; the motor rides on the pushpit.

questions.q: Monday, at anchor, you move the outboard from the pushpit bracket onto the dinghy for the first time. How do you do it?
options: Pass it down by hand, then climb in and fit it on the transom
Lower it on its own fuel line and do the clamps up once afloat
On a lanyard, one person in the dinghy, clamps tight before letting go
Carry it down the swim ladder and step into the dinghy holding it
questions.why: Outboards are dropped between boat and dinghy; a lanyard, and the clamps tight before anyone lets go, keep it out of the sea.

questions.q: Monday, 10:00, at anchor. The outboard ran at the base; now it coughs and dies after a few seconds every time. You find this. What do you do?
options: Call the base for a mechanic before you pull it again
Take the plug out, dry it and try again on full choke
Pull the cord until it catches — it runs once it is warm
Open the vent on the tank cap, squeeze the bulb firm, then start it again
questions.why: A closed vent starves the motor of fuel within seconds; open it and prime the bulb until it is firm.

questions.q: Thursday, 16:00, a northerly F5–6 is forecast overnight and you have 70 m of chain. Which bay do you choose for the night?

figure.title: Bays within reach
lines: A: 18 m, sand, open to the S
B: 7 m, sand, open to the S
C: 7 m, weed, open to the N

options: B: 7 m of sand, sheltered, with chain for five times the depth and more
A: the deep water gives the boat room to swing in the gusts
A: 70 m of chain is enough for any depth in these bays
C: the same depth as B, and the weed holds well
questions.why: 70 m in 18 m is under 4:1 in a blow; shelter, sand and a depth where the chain gives 5:1 or more win.

questions.q: Friday, 08:00, leaving a town quay. As your anchor comes up, the neighbour's chain comes up with it, lying across the shank. What do you do?
options: Lower both back down and wait for the neighbour to leave first
Pass a line under their chain, lower your anchor clear, then let the line go
Unshackle your anchor, leave it, and call the base about it
Motor ahead hard so your anchor drags their chain off
questions.why: Take their chain's weight on a line of your own, drop your anchor clear, then slip the line — their anchor never moves.

questions.q: Monday, 18:00, the briefing's notes on tonight's bay are in front of you. How do you anchor?
options: In the SW half; if it fouls, power it out with the windlass
In the NE half, with all 70 m out so the anchor lies flat
In the SW half, with a buoyed trip line on the anchor's crown
In the NE half — old chains hold an anchor like a hook
questions.why: Keep clear of known chains; a trip line pulls a fouled anchor out backwards without a diver or a cut chain.

questions.q: Wednesday, 17:00, near Göcek. The bay is filling up and the boats along the shore lie on anchors with lines ashore. Where do you go?

figure.note: Long line: 50 m, on board

options: B: anchor in the gap and swing free, with no line ashore
A: swing free among them — they hold still, so there is room
C: in the entrance, 30 m deep, where nobody else is
B: drop well out and back in, with a long line to the shore like the others
questions.why: Boats on lines ashore do not swing; a free-swinging boat among them hits one at the first wind shift — do as they do.

questions.q: Thursday, 07:00, on the catamaran: 25 miles back to the base with F6 and a short sea forecast. The dinghy is on the davits as it has hung all week. What do you do before you leave?

figure.title: Dinghy on the davits
lines: Hung on its two lifting lines only
Plug in, 20 l of rainwater inside

options: Outboard to the pushpit, dinghy drained, hauled up tight and strapped to the davit bar
Leave it as it is — the davits are built to carry it at sea
Lower it and tow it on a long painter for the passage
Lash the outboard tighter and leave the water in as ballast
questions.why: In a seaway a hanging dinghy swings and fills; weight off, water out, and strapped so it cannot work the davits loose.

questions.q: Thursday, 21:00, stern-to on a town quay. The wind has turned onshore and is building, and the stern is surging towards the stones. What do you do?
options: Leave it as it is and put every fender on the transom
Passerelle up, chain in to pull the stern off, stern lines eased to match
Tighten the stern lines to hold the boat hard on the fenders
Pay out more chain so the boat rides softer on its lines
questions.why: In an onshore wind the anchor keeps you off the stones: chain in, stern lines eased, the gangway up before it is crushed.
questions.ref: Mooring: stern-to in an onshore wind

questions.q: The technician hands you the inventory list and you count the galley gear together. What do you do before you sign?

figure.title: Inventory list — galley
lines: You count: forks 6, pans 2, the rest OK

options: Sign it and count again properly on the first evening
Sign it — two forks and a pan are not worth the time
Have him write 'forks 6, pans 2' on the list and sign that
Sign it and buy the missing ones in town for the base
questions.why: What is written as missing at check-in cannot be charged as lost at check-out.

questions.q: Three items on the deck inventory are not aboard. The technician says they are in the store and will be brought before you leave. What do you do?

figure.title: Deck inventory
lines: Technician: 'in the store, I'll bring them'

options: Sign the list and remind him again on Monday by phone from the first bay
Refuse to take the boat until the store has delivered all three
Sign the list as it is — he said he will bring them before you leave
Note all three as missing on the list now; strike them out when they arrive
questions.why: The list you sign is the check-out baseline; a promised item that never comes is charged at list price.

questions.q: You look into the cabins while the technician is on deck. What do you do?

figure.title: Cabins
lines: Stbd aft: door latch broken, door swings

options: Ask for the mattress dried or changed and the latch fixed, and note both on the form
Note the latch only — a damp mattress is normal on a boat
Air the mattress at sea and tape the door; neither is deposit material
Say nothing now and raise both at check-out so they are not charged
questions.why: Faults you accept silently become yours at check-out; the base can still fix them on Saturday.

questions.q: The technician points at the galley and says everything in it works. What do you do?
options: Test it all on the first evening and call the base if anything fails
Switch the fridge on, light every burner and the oven, boil the kettle before he leaves
Take his word for it — galley gear is not part of the deposit anyway
Light one burner; the fridge needs hours to get cold anyway
questions.why: Test what you are told works while the technician is aboard; a failure at sea is yours to live with.

questions.q: On Wednesday you touch the quay at Fiskardo and chip the gelcoat at the bow. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday, Fiskardo quay
lines: Gelcoat chip at the bow, 3 cm
Contract: any damage reported at once

options: Say nothing — a chip that size is either found at check-out or it is not
Wait and point it out yourself at the check-out, which is honest enough
Photograph it and phone the base the same day; the repair comes off the deposit at check-out
Touch it up with a repair kit from the chandler so that it is not found
questions.why: Reporting at once keeps the insurance and the waiver valid; hidden or late damage can cost the whole deposit.

questions.q: Thursday evening you are in an anchorage 30 miles from the base and see this forecast. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday 18:00
lines: Forecast Fri: NW 7, gusts 8, easing Sat noon
Contract: back at base Fri by 18:00
Late return: €500 a day + next crew's costs

options: Stay put and call the base on Saturday morning once it has eased
Leave Friday morning regardless — the penalty is worse than a rough passage
Slip at 04:00 without telling anyone and hope to beat the wind
Call the base now, say where you are, and decide with their advice: move tonight or sit it out
questions.why: The decision is the skipper's, but a base warned the day before can plan; a penalty is never a reason to sail into a gale.

questions.q: Friday afternoon you are approaching the base. The briefing said return berths are assigned on arrival. What do you do?

figure.note: Friday 16:30 · contract: alongside at the base by 18:00

options: Call the base on the VHF or phone before entering and take the berth they give you
Go alongside the fuel dock at A and wait there for a marinero
Anchor off at C tonight and come in at 08:00 for the check-out
Take the first empty berth on the base pontoon — their boats all come back tonight
questions.why: The return berth, the time and the mooring are the base's; 'back at the base' means alongside, before the deadline.

questions.q: Friday 15:30, the fuel gauge shows half. The base has given you berth B for the night. Where do you go first?

figure.note: Contract: full tank, or pump price + €50 service

options: Berth B — half a tank is enough for the base's next crew
Fuel dock A: fill the tank and keep the receipt, then berth B
Berth B now, fuel dock A at 08:00 before the technician comes
Berth B — the base refuels every boat and takes it from the deposit
questions.why: 'Returned full' is in the contract; the base's own refuelling adds a service charge, and the receipt is your proof.

questions.q: You are three miles from the base on Friday afternoon with these tanks. What do you do before the check-out?

figure.title: Check-out form — tanks
lines: Contract: water full, holding tank empty
Your water: ¼ · holding tank: ½
Gas: in use ⅓, spare full — write it down

options: Pump the holding tank out in the base marina after dark, when nobody is watching
Fill the water from jerry cans and leave the holding tank for the next crew to empty
Pump the holding tank out where allowed offshore or at the base, and fill the water at the berth
Leave both as they are — filling water and pumping out are part of the final cleaning
questions.why: Water full and holding tank empty are check-out items; discharge only offshore where the local rules allow, or at a pump-out.

questions.q: It is Friday evening at the base and the crew asks how much cleaning the boat needs. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Contract — cleaning
lines: Final cleaning: included in the price
Galley, fridge and heads left clean

options: Leave it all — the final cleaning is paid for in the price
Scrub the whole boat inside and out — cleaning is the charterer's job
Pay the €80 — it is cheaper than the crew's last evening
Clean the galley, fridge and heads and take the rubbish ashore; the base does the rest
questions.why: Read the clause: the included cleaning covers the boat, not your rubbish or a dirty fridge and heads.

questions.q: You are back at the base on Friday with the dinghy still in the water and the outboard on it. What do you do before the check-out?
options: Rinse both with fresh water and lift them back to where they were at check-in
Tie them off astern and tell the technician at check-out where they are
Leave both in the water at the berth — the base lifts them with the crane
Deflate the dinghy and stow it with the outboard in the aft locker
questions.why: The dinghy and outboard go back washed, lifted and stowed as at check-in; they are inventory, checked like the rest.

questions.q: Saturday 07:30, the technician is due at eight. The crew is still in their bunks and the saloon is full of bags. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — handover
lines: Boat back at base: Friday by 18:00

options: Pack after the inspection — the boat is yours until the next crew boards
Get the crew up, bags into the cockpit, cabins stripped and clear by eight
Ask the technician to come back at eleven when the boat is empty
Let them sleep — the check-out is the skipper's business
questions.why: The inspection needs empty cabins and lockers; the base turns the boat round the same day.

questions.q: At the check-out the technician fills in the engine hours on the form. What do you do?
options: Write 1 371 plus the hours you logged each day instead of the meter
Let it go — nine hours matter only to the base's service schedule
Read the meter with him and have the form corrected to 1 412 before you sign
Sign it — the figure is the base's, not yours, and the fuel is full
questions.why: Both readings are compared on the form you sign; a wrong figure is argued later only with your photo.

questions.q: The technician's walk-round finds nothing new. Then the diver comes up. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-out inspection
lines: Diver: scratch on the keel, 20 cm, 'fresh'

options: Accept the €350 — at every base the diver's word on the hull is final
Sign now and dispute the €350 by e-mail with the base once you are home
Refuse outright — the check-in form already says the keel has scratches
Ask for the diver's photo and compare it with your check-in photos of the keel before agreeing
questions.why: New damage is settled against the check-in form and photos; 'old scratches' on the form only covers what the photos show.

questions.q: At the check-out the technician marks a scratch on the starboard quarter as new. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-out — hull
lines: Your photo, Sat 15:42: the same scratch

options: Show the dated check-in photo and ask for the charge to be withdrawn and the form amended now
Offer to split it — the form is against you but the photo is for you
Pay now and claim it back from your deposit insurance when you are home
Pay the €200 — you signed 'hull OK' and the form you signed is the contract
questions.why: A dated check-in photo is the evidence the base itself asked you to take; a charge is disputed at the base, before signing.

questions.q: The cockpit table came off its hinge on Thursday. At the check-out the base wants a new table. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-out — cockpit table
lines: Base: new table €420 from the deposit
You reported it on Thursday by phone

options: Pay half — the hinge was old but the break happened to you
Point to the check-in note: a fault recorded as old is wear, not new damage, and not yours
Pay — it broke on your watch and the deposit covers wear and tear
Refuse to sign anything and leave the base with the deposit still held
questions.why: The check-in form is the baseline: what was noted as old or defective at check-in cannot be charged as new damage.

questions.q: A winch handle and a fender went overboard during the week. What do you expect at the check-out?
options: A claim on the deposit insurance, which pays for losses too
No deduction — the deposit covers damage, not lost gear
A €150 deduction at the base's list prices, shown on the settlement
A deduction at the chandler's retail price plus the base's time
questions.why: Lost inventory is charged from the deposit at the base's list price; deposit insurance normally excludes it.

questions.q: The technician shows you this settlement and asks you to sign. What do you ask for first?

figure.title: Deposit settlement
lines: Release of the rest: 'in a few days'

options: The €2,590 in cash — a hold on the card can take weeks to come back
Only the keel estimate — the fender is a fixed price from the list
Nothing more — the settlement is written out and signed by the base
An itemised receipt with the repair estimate, and the date the card hold is released
questions.why: Every deduction comes with a receipt and the repair cost; the pre-authorisation is released by the base, not by your bank on its own.

questions.q: During the week you noted the autopilot dropping out above 20 knots, a stiff heads pump and a flickering port light. Nobody is charging you for any of it. What do you do at the check-out?
options: Give the technician a short written list for the base's job sheet
Mention the port light only — the rest is normal charter wear
Post it in an online review so the next crew is warned
Keep it to yourself — anything you report may end as a deduction
questions.why: A fault list costs you nothing, gets fixed before the next crew and shows the base you sailed with care.

questions.q: Saturday morning you lock the boat. A crew mate says to switch everything off, as on his own boat. What do you do?

figure.title: Base note — leaving the boat
lines: Battery switches: house ON, engine OFF
Hatches and ports closed, bimini folded
Keys: to the office, not left aboard

options: Switch everything off and leave the key in the ignition for the technician
Follow the base's note: shore power on, house on, engine off, hatches shut, keys to the office
Switch everything off and unplug the shore cable, as on his boat
Leave everything on, instruments too, so the base sees they work
questions.why: The base's note is what the next check-in depends on: the charger keeps the batteries up and the fridge cold.

questions.q: On a 42 ft catamaran the inventory says only 'cockpit and flybridge cushions 10'. You count ten. What do you do before you sign?
options: Turn the torn cushions over so the seams don't open further
Tell the technician and leave the list as it is
Write the torn seams and the broken zip on the list, with photos
Sign it — ten out of ten is all the list asks for
questions.why: A count proves the item is there, not its state; a tear not written down is charged as new at check-out.

questions.q: Saturday 18:00, the technician says the inventory is always complete and he has no time to wait while you count. What do you do?

figure.title: Inventory list — 4 pages
lines: Deck: winch handles, boat hook, cushions

options: Count the galley only — the deck gear is seen on the walk-round
Sign it, and count on Monday so you know what you have
Sign page 4 — the base would not hand over an incomplete boat
Count it with the crew this evening and hand the list in, with what is short, before you sail
questions.why: What you sign uncounted is what you owe at check-out; the count can wait for the evening, the signature waits for the count.

questions.q: The check-in form of your catamaran has one line for engine hours. You look at the two engine panels. What do you do?

lines: No line for the starboard engine

options: Have both meters written on the form and photograph each panel
Write the starboard figure in your own log and say nothing
Leave it — the base only tracks the port engine's hours
Add the two together and have the total written on the form
questions.why: Each engine is read against the form at check-out; a meter that is not on it is your word against the base's.

questions.q: Thursday at Sivota, a crew member drops the key ring into the harbour. What do you do?
options: Wait for the check-out and see whether the technician asks for them
Phone the base now so they can arrange spares, and expect the €80 at check-out
Say nothing — a set of keys is not worth a call mid-week
Cut the dinghy padlock with the bolt cutters and buy a new one
questions.why: Report a loss when it happens: the base can get spares to you, and the list price is all you pay.

questions.q: Tuesday the gas runs out in Vathi and you swap the bottle at a shop. At the check-out the technician sees a different bottle in the locker. What do you show him?

figure.title: Gas — the week
lines: Tue: bottle swapped at a shop, €32
Contract: gas used is the charterer's
Locker now: the shop's bottle, full

options: Your card statement — the €32 comes back to you from the deposit
The log entry for Tuesday — gas needs no receipt
The shop's receipt, so the swap and the bottle deposit are on record
Nothing — the bottle in the locker is full, which is all he needs
questions.why: A swapped bottle is accounted for by its receipt; without one the base may charge its own bottle as lost.

questions.q: Wednesday night in Kioni the outboard is stolen from the dinghy, tied astern with its cable locked. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — theft
lines: Outboard theft: insured if locked on
Cut cable: keep it for the base

options: Buy a second-hand outboard ashore so the inventory is complete
Tell the base at the check-out, with the cut cable as proof
Call the base only — they deal with the police and the insurer
Report it to the port police that morning, take their report, and call the base
questions.why: The insurer pays only for a locked motor and a timely police report; without them its full value comes off your deposit.

questions.q: Friday, a crew member admits he cracked the forward hatch lens with a winch handle on Tuesday and asks you to keep it quiet. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Contract — damage
lines: Damage reported to the base at once
Check-out: every hatch, from below too

options: That you will report it now: reported it costs €180, hidden it voids the waiver
Fine — tape over it and the technician won't see it from the deck
Fine — if it is found you will say it happened on Friday
Fine, as long as he pays the €180 himself if it is found
questions.why: The crack will be found at check-out anyway; reported, it is a list-price repair, hidden, it breaks the reporting clause.

questions.q: With a gale due on Friday you are back at the base on Thursday afternoon. Your crew want to fly home on Friday morning. What do you arrange with the base?

figure.title: Contract — early return
lines: Boat stays on the base's berth
Disembark by Saturday 09:00 at the latest

options: Nothing — leave the keys at the office and let them inspect on Saturday
An early check-out with the technician before you leave on Friday
Nothing — the boat must be sailed until Friday 18:00, gale or not
A refund of Friday's charter, since the boat is back a day early
questions.why: The boat is yours until it is inspected; leave before the check-out and you have no say in what is found.

questions.q: Friday 13:00, the breeze is dying and your crew want to drift home under sail. What do you do?

figure.title: Friday 13:00
lines: Contract: alongside at the base by 18:00

options: Sail until 16:00 and motor the rest if you are still out
Sail on — the base cannot charge you for a calm
Motor now, to be at the fuel dock and alongside well before 18:00
Sail on and call the base at 18:00 to say you are late
questions.why: At 2–3 kn the 22 M run past 18:00; a calm is not weather that excuses a late return, and fuelling takes time too.

questions.q: Friday you fill up at Nidri and motor two hours to the base. The technician reads the gauge and wants to top up at the base's price. What do you show him?

lines: Contract: full, or a receipt within 20 M

options: Your log — it shows you left Nidri straight after fuelling
Nothing — pay the top-up; the gauge reading is what counts
The engine hours — two hours of motoring is not an eighth
The Nidri receipt — the contract takes it as full from within 20 miles
questions.why: Read the fuel clause: a receipt from close by counts as full, and most fuel gauges are too coarse to argue over.

questions.q: Friday 17:30, berthing stern-to at the base in a crosswind, your quarter touches the next charter yacht. Nobody is aboard her. What do you do?

figure.title: Friday 17:30, base pontoon
lines: Your stbd quarter touched her topsides
Her: another company's boat, nobody aboard

options: Photograph both boats and tell the base office now, before the check-out
Mention it at tomorrow's check-out if the technician asks
Leave a note with your phone number on her wheel and go
Rub the scuff off and say nothing — it may be an old mark
questions.why: Damage to another boat is a third-party claim: your base reports it to the insurer and needs to hear it from you first.

questions.q: Friday 20:00 at the base, a marina attendant comes along the pontoon asking for tonight's berthing fee. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Charter price
lines: Included: base marina, first and last night
Showers: marina block, code at the office
Not included: other harbours and marinas

options: Pay him, and ask the base to refund it at the check-out
That the night is included for base boats, to be settled with the base office
Nothing — move out and anchor off for the night instead
Nothing — pay him; the base marina is a harbour like any other
questions.why: The last night in the base marina is in the charter price; a fee asked for it is for the base to settle with the marina.

questions.q: Friday 18:30, you are alongside at the base and the crew want to go straight to dinner. What do you do first?

figure.title: Friday 18:30 at the base
lines: Inventory list: in the chart table
Not seen today: a bucket, the boat hook

options: Buy a bucket and a boat hook in town in the morning before eight
Go to dinner — the technician counts it all in the morning anyway
Count the inventory against the list with the crew and hunt for what is missing
Count it at 07:30 tomorrow while the crew are packing
questions.why: Your own count the evening before finds the boat hook under a berth, not on the settlement; by morning there is no time.

questions.q: Friday night a glass of red wine goes over the saloon cushion. What do you do?

figure.title: Saloon cushion, 23:00
lines: Cream cover, red wine across it
Fresh water and a sponge aboard

options: Leave it till the morning and ask the technician what to use
Turn the cushion over and leave it for the base's cleaners
Scrub it with the galley bleach until the stain is gone
Blot and rinse it with cold fresh water now, and show the technician in the morning
questions.why: Treated at once a stain is often a cleaning; left to set or bleached it is a new cover — and it is shown either way.

questions.q: Friday evening, the fridge and lockers still hold food and drink. Your crew suggest leaving it all for the next crew. What do you do?

figure.title: Base note — food aboard
lines: Fridge emptied, cleaned, door left open
Food left aboard is thrown away
Unopened food: the box at the office

options: Empty the fridge and lockers: unopened food to the office box, the rest ashore
Leave it in the fridge — the next crew will be glad of it
Leave the unopened food in the lockers and bin the fridge's
Wipe the fridge out and leave the drinks for the technician
questions.why: The fridge goes back empty and clean; food left aboard becomes the base's rubbish and your cleaning charge.

questions.q: Saturday 07:00, your last morning aboard. This note is taped inside the companionway. What do you do with the beds?

figure.title: Base note — departure
lines: Beds stripped, sheets and pillowcases bagged
Towels in the same bag, one bag per cabin
Duvets and pillows left on the berths

options: Strip everything, duvets and pillows too, and pile it on deck
Strip them, bag sheets and towels by cabin, and leave duvets and pillows on the berths
Leave them as slept in — the cleaners strip them anyway
Make them up again neatly so the next crew finds them ready
questions.why: The base's note says how bedding goes back; following it avoids a cleaning charge and a sheet counted as missing.

questions.q: Saturday 08:45, no technician yet; the office says the base is short-staffed and he will be 'an hour or two'. What do you do?

figure.title: Saturday at the base
lines: Boat: clean, full, on berth B12

options: Miss the flight and wait — leaving before the check-out admits the damage
Leave the keys on the chart table and go — the base is late, not you
Photograph the boat, and have the office sign 'returned 08:45, not yet inspected'
Leave a crew member behind to do the check-out and sign for you
questions.why: A timed note signed by the office and your photos record the boat as you left it; a late inspection is then the base's to justify.

questions.q: Saturday 08:00, the technician starts the check-out walk-round. A crew mate says you can wait in the café: 'they'll message if anything's wrong'. What do you do?

figure.title: Check-out, Saturday 08:00
lines: Your check-in photos: on your phone

options: Send the crew mate to watch and meet them both at the office
Leave your number and the photos with him and go to breakfast
Wait in the café — the inspection is the base's job, not yours
Go round with him, phone in hand, and see each point as he finds it
questions.why: A point you see found you can answer on the spot with a check-in photo; one reported to you later is harder to dispute.

questions.q: At the check-out the technician finds the genoa's UV strip coming away along the leech and wants €250 from the deposit. What do you say?

figure.title: Check-out — genoa
lines: UV strip: stitching rotten, 2 m loose
Contract: fair wear and tear not charged

options: That rotten stitching is wear, not damage, and the contract does not charge it
Agree, and offer to have it restitched by a sailmaker at home
Nothing — pay; 'sails OK' on the form means the strip was sound
Offer half — you did not photograph the strip at check-in
questions.why: Rotten thread is sun and age, not misuse; the wear-and-tear clause covers it even without a check-in photo.

questions.q: At the check-out the technician offers to settle the broken saloon locker hinge 'off the books'. What do you do?
options: Pay the €50 — cheaper, and the hinge gets fixed either way
Take it through the settlement at €90, with a receipt
Pay the €50 and have him strike the line from the form
Pay nothing — a reported hinge is the base's to repair
questions.why: Cash with no paper leaves the damage open on the base's books; a receipted line on the settlement closes it.

questions.q: The settlement charges both of the week's incidents. You bought the waiver. What should come off the deposit?

figure.title: Settlement — damage
lines: Mon: gelcoat chip at the bow — €350
Thu: pulpit bent on a quay — €900

options: €500 — one excess covers the whole charter
€1,000 — the full excess for each incident
€850 — the chip in full, the pulpit up to the excess
€1,250 — the waiver covers the first incident only
questions.why: Per incident, each repair is charged up to the excess: the €350 chip in full, the €900 pulpit capped at €500.

questions.q: On Wednesday a motorboat hit your bow; you took her details and reported it. At the check-out the base takes the pulpit repair from your deposit. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Check-out — pulpit
lines: Wed: hit by a motorboat, reported at once
You have: her name, insurer, photos
Base: claim against her insurer opened

options: Nothing — the deposit settles it, whoever was at fault
That the base drops it now and chases the motorboat itself
Nothing yet — you will claim from her insurer once you are home
A written note on the settlement that it is refunded when her insurer pays
questions.why: Damage caused by a third party is held, not lost: put the refund on recovery in writing before you sign.

questions.q: At the settlement the base charges a late-return fee. You came in on Saturday morning after the base told you to stay in harbour. What do you do?

figure.title: Settlement — late return
lines: Your log: left Vathi Sat 06:00, NW 4

options: Show the base's messages and ask for the fee to be struck before you sign
Pay it — the deadline was Friday 18:00, whatever the reason
Sign, then dispute it by e-mail with the messages from home
Offer half — the weather was neither your fault nor the base's
questions.why: You were late on the base's own instruction; its messages settle that, at the desk and before you sign.

questions.q: Saturday 08:30, the office is busy and the manager hands you a check-out form with nothing filled in: 'sign here, the technician will do it after you've gone'. What do you do?
options: Sign it, and photograph the boat before you leave just in case
Sign only after the inspection, on the completed form, and keep a copy
Leave it unsigned and go — no signature means no charge
Sign it — the check-in form protects you from anything unfair
questions.why: A blank signed form lets anything be written in later; you sign what was found, with you there.

questions.q: The technician has signed the check-out form 'no damage, nothing missing'. What do you photograph before you leave the boat?

figure.title: Check-out — signed
lines: Boat on berth B12, keys at the office

options: Nothing more — the signed form is all the proof you need
Only the form — the hull photos were taken at check-in
The signed form, the hull from the pontoon, the fuel gauge and the hour meter
The cabins and the galley, to show they were left clean
questions.why: Your copy and photos of the boat as handed back answer any later claim of damage 'found after you left'.

questions.q: Saturday, the check-out is signed and the document folder is still at the chart table. What do you do with it?

figure.title: Document folder
lines: Transit log, stamped at the base
Contract: folder to the office at check-out

options: Keep the transit log and crew list as your record of the week
Hand it to the next crew's skipper when they board tonight
Leave it at the chart table — it lives with the boat
Check it is complete and hand it in at the office with the keys
questions.why: The papers are the base's and go back with the keys, as the contract says; one that goes missing is your problem.

questions.q: You left the deposit in cash at check-in, and the check-out is clean and signed. What do you get back at the office?

figure.title: Deposit — cash
lines: Check-out form: no damage, nothing missing

options: The €2,500 in cash, against the receipt you were given at check-in
Nothing yet — the base waits a week in case the diver finds more
A bank transfer in 30 days — cash is never paid back in cash
The €2,500 less a fee for keeping the cash for a week
questions.why: A cash deposit with a clean signed check-out comes back in full against its receipt; the signed form closes the inspection.

questions.q: Three weeks after a clean check-out your card still shows the deposit blocked. What do you do?

figure.title: Your card, three weeks on
lines: Card issuer: holds lapse within 30 days

options: Phone the technician who signed the form and ask him to release it
Write to the base with the signed form and ask them to cancel the hold
Wait — a hold always clears by itself, however long it takes
Dispute the €3,000 with your bank as a fraudulent charge
questions.why: Only the base can cancel its hold early; the signed clean form is your proof that it owes you that.

questions.q: Ten days after a clean check-out, the base e-mails a €400 charge for a keel scratch 'found when the boat was lifted'. What do you reply?

figure.title: E-mail from the base
lines: Keel scratch found at haul-out, Tuesday
Two crews have sailed her since

options: Nothing — they cannot charge a card once the hold is released
Accept — a lift shows what the diver could not see
That the signed clean check-out closed your charter, and you refuse the charge in writing
Offer half, since the keel was under water at check-out
questions.why: The signed check-out ends your liability; damage found after later charters is not yours, and you say so in writing.

questions.q: Back home, you write an online review of the base. What goes in it?
options: A star rating only — written details can be used against you
The technician's name and your dispute, to make the base pay
Only the problems — the good parts are what you paid for
Facts: the boat's state, the check-in, the help mid-week, the deposit's return
questions.why: A factual review helps the next crew and the base; a dispute goes to the base in writing, not into a review.
